1	# Track L — Lean MVP loop: method
2	
3	Status: approved as a track on 2026-09-14 (`PLAN.md` Track L, `README.md` decisions table). Round 1's cut is decided (`Q-MVP-01`: every major feature at its most minimal; `Q-MVP-02`: auto-resolved mission card while the tactical slice is unbuilt). The Round 2 and 3 cuts and the thresholds are proposals for Westley to review. The backlog's Round column is the next follow-up. Open questions for this track are `Q-MVP-##` rows in `../ambiguity_register.md`.
4	
5	## Why this track exists
6	
7	The stage pipeline builds the game epic by epic and has no way to learn from a player until the game is done. That is the waterfall failure in agile clothing: every story could be Ready, Tested, and Built and still be something nobody wants to play. Track L puts a player in the loop as early as the C/Agora path allows, in rounds, and uses what they say and do to decide what gets built next. Its two questions are: which of the bible's ideas are actually good, and what does player satisfaction mean for this specific game, as opposed to what the bible assumes it means.
8	
9	## Lean vocabulary, mapped to this project
10	
11	| Lean term | Here |
12	|---|---|
13	| Hypothesis | A bible claim about what players value, rewritten as a falsifiable statement with a metric and a threshold. Listed in `experiments.md`. |
14	| Experiment | A round: a cut shipped to a defined tester group with defined instruments. |
15	| Build | The cut: a subset of stories, chosen by omission, plus marked stand-ins for epics the round needs but does not build. `feature_mvps.md`. |
16	| Measure | Telemetry file, structured feedback form, scripted interview, and (Round 3) Steam's own numbers. |
17	| Learn | The gap review: assumed value versus observed, one row per hypothesis. |
18	| Pivot or persevere | A change-protocol PR, a new `Q-` flag, a kill, or a keep. Never a silent edit. |
19	
20	## Rounds
21	
22	| Round | Testers | Delivery | Instruments | Gate to open the round |
23	|---|---|---|---|---|
24	| 0 | none | none | Hypotheses written, metrics defined, feedback instruments drafted, and a two-week Agora velocity baseline recorded in `../proving_ground/BUILD_LEDGER.md`. | This track merged. |
25	| 1 | 10 to 20 friends over the round, at most 4 active at once, Windows assumed, in a small Discord server | ZIP posted to Discord; `README.txt` with hotkeys and where logs go; structured feedback form; bug-report capture hotkey; a bug channel. | Scripted 30-minute interview per tester; feedback form; local session telemetry file with opt-in upload. | Every Round 1 story Built; probes H and I passed; one cold-machine smoke test by a friend with no dev tools. |
26	| 2 | 10 to 30 people, the Round 1 Discord widened | ZIP posted to Discord; bug channel; a pinned survey. | Same as Round 1 plus aggregated telemetry and a weekly digest written offline from the files. | Round 1 gap review done and its actions landed; every Round 2 story Built. |
27	| 3 | Steam Playtest | Steam build: store page, export presets, store copy worded in Round 2 testers' own words (`Q-MVP-06`). | Steam retention and wishlist numbers, in-game survey, Discord. | Round 2 gap review done; the layer-system option chosen in its design phase; onboarding passes the 30-minute personality-load check (below). |
28	
29	Rounds open on evidence. No round has a date, because Agora's throughput on this project is unmeasured: at the time of writing it has completed zero cards for Ouroboros. `build_path.md` defines the velocity measurement that must exist before any forecast is shown to Westley.
30	
31	## What player satisfaction means here
32	
33	Each metric ties to a hypothesis in `distinctiveness.md`. Everything below is measurable without a model API, in keeping with the no-runtime-API rule.
34	
35	**Engagement**
36	- Chapters completed per session, sessions per tester, and return within seven days. The research band for the tribe's paid titles (D7 of 40 to 75 percent) is a comparison point, not a target for a friends build.
37	- Time from first screen to first order; whether the first mission was abandoned; whether the tutorial was skipped. These are the UI-bounce signals the research names as the tribe's number one complaint.
38	
39	**The world moves without me** (H1)
40	- Free answer after the first time jump: "What changed in the galaxy while you were away?" Scored yes/no on whether the tester names a change they did not cause, and whether they call it interesting or random.
41	
42	**Carry-forward** (H2)
43	- Free answer after chapter three: "Name something that happened because of a mission you played earlier." Scored yes/no.
44	
45	**Chronicle** (H3, H8)
46	- Telemetry: read time per jump, expand-clicks per jump.
47	- Interview: one entry recalled unprompted; one line quoted.
48	- Any tester describing the text as filler or placeholder is a fail on its own.
49	
50	**Tragedy of understanding** (H4)
51	- After a loss: "Why did you lose?" Scored on whether the answer names a positional or force cause, versus "the game cheated" or "no idea."
52	
53	**Commander, not king** (H5)
54	- Interview count of testers who ask for base building or economy, and whether "freeing" or "missing" wins when they describe the absence.
55	
56	**Intent to continue**
57	- Would you play another chapter? Would you pay $12 for this? Both yes/no, asked last.
58	
59	The thresholds attached to these in `distinctiveness.md` are live kill criteria from Round 1 for every hypothesis, prototypes included (`Q-MVP-04`, answered 2026-09-14). A threshold miss on a prototype surface is still a finding; the gap review decides whether the idea or the stand-in failed.
60	
61	## Feedback instruments
62	
63	- **Feedback form.** A rewrite of the existing `build/feedback.txt` template so that every question maps to one metric above. Free text where the metric is a scored free answer; yes/no where it is a count. Delivered inside the ZIP as a text file for Round 1, as a pinned form for Round 2, in-game for Round 3.
64	- **Interview script.** Ten questions in fixed order, thirty minutes, after the tester's second session. Recorded with consent. The scored questions are asked verbatim so answers are comparable across testers.
65	- **Telemetry file.** Local, plain JSON, written by the client: session start and end, chapter index, mission outcome band, orders issued per mission, chronicle read time and expand-clicks, screens visited, first-order latency. Stored locally; the tester may send it back with the form or opt in, from the first-launch notice, to an upload to the project's R2 bucket (`Q-MVP-03`, answered 2026-09-14). Consent follows the pattern the legacy client's privacy modal used; nothing uploads without the opt-in.
66	- **Bug capture.** A hotkey that zips logs, the telemetry file, and a screenshot, and copies the path to the clipboard. The legacy client's F12 flow is the reference for behavior, not for code.
67	- **Discord (from Round 1).** Opens with the friends round and widens for Round 2 (`Q-MVP-05`, answered 2026-09-14). One bug channel, one feedback channel, one pinned survey, a weekly digest written by Claude from the files. The research names this "support-shaped" Discord as the norm for small strategy teams.
68	
69	All of the above are stories in the proposed epic E-22 (`feature_mvps.md`), built by Agora like anything else.
70	
71	## Gap review
72	
73	Run after every round, before any Round N+1 story enters Stage 3. One table, one row per hypothesis:
74	
75	| Hypothesis | Bible source | Assumed value | Observed | Gap | Action | Owner |
76	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
77	
78	Action is exactly one of: **change protocol** (story and rules rewritten, tests revised, card respec'd, one PR); **flag** (a new `Q-` row when the result raises a question only Westley can answer); **kill** (story status Killed, recorded in `experiments.md` under "Killed by evidence"); **keep** (recorded under "Confirmed by evidence" with the number that confirmed it). A gap with no action is not allowed; "watch it next round" is a keep with a note.
79	
80	The review also produces the next round's cut: the ranking in `distinctiveness.md` is re-scored with the new evidence, and `feature_mvps.md` is rewritten (not annotated) to match.
81	
82	## What Track L may not do
83	
84	- Weaken a rule or test to fit a round. Cuts are by story omission only.
85	- Loosen a scale gate or a speed budget.
86	- Build on the legacy Python slice, or use it for a playtest.
87	- Call a model at runtime, including for feedback digests inside the game.
88	- Put a human in the build loop. Client and packaging cards wait for probes H and I like any other capability.
89	- Claim Ready for a story outside a round's scope because its epic's e2e file exists. A round-scoped e2e file lists the stories it does not cover.
90	
91	## Relationship to the stages
92	
93	Stages 3, 4, and 5 are unchanged in content. Track L decides their order: the next epic into Stage 3 is the one whose Round N stories are not yet Ready, in dependency order within the round. Stage 4's backlog gains a Round column (`build_path.md`). Stage 5 writes tests only for stories in the current or next round. The proving ground gains probes H and I. The layer-system design phase (README decision of 2026-09-13) is unchanged and sits between Round 2 and Round 3.

The review also produces the next round's cut: the ranking in `distinctiveness.md` is re-scored with the new evidence, and `feature_mvps.md` is rewritten (not annotated) to match.

## What Track L may not do

- Weaken a rule or test to fit a round. Cuts are by story omission only.
- Loosen a scale gate or a speed budget.
- Build on the legacy Python slice, or use it for a playtest.
- Call a model at runtime, including for feedback digests inside the game.
- Put a human in the build loop. Client and packaging cards wait for probes H and I like any other capability.
- Claim Ready for a story outside a round's scope because its epic's e2e file exists. A round-scoped e2e file lists the stories it does not cover.

## Relationship to the stages

Stages 3, 4, and 5 are unchanged in content. Track L decides their order: the next epic into Stage 3 is the one whose Round N stories are not yet Ready, in dependency order within the round. Stage 4's backlog gains a Round column (`build_path.md`). Stage 5 writes tests only for stories in the current or next round. The proving ground gains probes H and I. The layer-system design phase (README decision of 2026-09-13) is unchanged and sits between Round 2 and Round 3.

# C4 model — MVP version

## Purpose

This is the first C4 model of Ouroboros Manifold, required by `CLAUDE.md`'s "C4 model per version"
rule: drawn before the MVP becomes the full game, kept beside the bible, read before designing a
manager-mode cascade or authoring Agora tests. It is **descriptive, not aspirational**: every
element and relationship here is traceable to a file on `origin/main`, or is explicitly marked
`planned` (bible/doc only, no code) or `unverified` (claimed by a doc but no call site found).
It documents the system as of:

```
commit 47bfaeed63a17d6cbde4d138700c66ba9ccfc9fd
origin/main, read 2026-09-28
```

This is not a redesign and does not resolve any open design question. Where the model surfaces a
question the code cannot answer (an ambiguous boundary, a duplicated responsibility, a doc that no
longer matches the code), it goes in `gaps.md`, not into an invented answer.

## How to read this model

- `1-context.md` — Level 1 (System Context): the player, Westley, Agora's QA loop, the offline
  library builder, and any external services (storefront, CDN) the code actually references.
- `2-containers.md` — Level 2 (Containers): the Godot client, the C sim library, the pipe
  transport process, save files, the generated content library, the legacy Python reference sim,
  the test harness, and Agora, with the protocol and entry point for each relationship.
- `3-components-sim.md` — Level 3 for the C simulation library: one component per `csrc/<module>.c`
  file, grouped by owning epic, with the real tick-order call trace.
- `3-components-client.md` — Level 3 for the Godot client: autoloads, scene groups, how scenes
  reach the sim, and the QA daemon.
- `4-flows.md` — three runtime sequence flows (new game → galaxy; briefing → deploy → tactical →
  debrief; time jump → chronicle), each step naming the pipe command and the handler function.
- `gaps.md` — every place the model and the running code disagree, a boundary is unclear, a
  bible-named container does not exist yet, or a responsibility is duplicated. Cited to file:line.

Every diagram is Mermaid (`C4Context`/`C4Container`/`C4Component`, or `flowchart` where the C4
syntax cannot express something — GitHub and most Markdown viewers render Mermaid inline). Every
diagram is followed by a table repeating each element with its source file, so the model is
checkable without a renderer.

## Status legend

Used throughout this model to classify every component, entry point, and container:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **built** | Code exists on `origin/main` and is reached by the running game (the live scene-router flow, the pipe's command dispatch, or the strategic/tactical tick) — not merely present in a source file. |
| **wired-untested** | Code exists and something in the running game calls it, but no test exercises that call path directly (rare in this codebase; most wired code has a fenced test — flag explicitly where this applies). |
| **tested-unwired** | Code exists and is covered by tests (`tests/csim/*.py`, `tests/*.gd`), but nothing in the running game (tick, pipe dispatch, scene graph) ever calls it. A real function, provably unreached. |
| **planned** | Named in the bible or `docs/northstar/` but no corresponding code exists in this checkout. |

A component can be `built` for some entry points and `tested-unwired` for others in the same file
(e.g. `csrc/tactical_mapgen.c`: `om_map_add_cover`/`om_map_add_obstacle` are built; most
`om_map_get_*` accessors are `/* STUB */`). Where that split matters, the component tables call it
out per entry point rather than giving the whole module one status.

## Sources read

`CLAUDE.md`, `docs/bible/game_bible.md`, `docs/architecture.md`, `docs/northstar/PLAN.md` ("The
Factory"), `docs/northstar/plans/push/pieces.toml`, `docs/northstar/spec_factory/symbol_modules.toml`,
`csrc/*.c`, `csrc/ouroboros_sim.h`, `csrc/om_internal.h`, `csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c`, `Makefile`,

`scripts/qa_harness.sh`, `autoload/qa_daemon.gd`, `simulation/` (read for what still calls it),
and `~/Projects/agora/projects/ouroboros/qa.toml` plus `~/Projects/agora/scripts/qa_explore.py`
(read-only, outside this repo).

This is not a redesign and does not resolve any open design question. Where the model surfaces a
question the code cannot answer (an ambiguous boundary, a duplicated responsibility, a doc that no
longer matches the code), it goes in `gaps.md`, not into an invented answer.

## How to read this model

- `1-context.md` — Level 1 (System Context): the player, Westley, Agora's QA loop, the offline
  library builder, and any external services (storefront, CDN) the code actually references.
- `2-containers.md` — Level 2 (Containers): the Godot client, the C sim library, the pipe
  transport process, save files, the generated content library, the legacy Python reference sim,
  the test harness, and Agora, with the protocol and entry point for each relationship.
- `3-components-sim.md` — Level 3 for the C simulation library: one component per `csrc/<module>.c`
  file, grouped by owning epic, with the real tick-order call trace.
- `3-components-client.md` — Level 3 for the Godot client: autoloads, scene groups, how scenes
  reach the sim, and the QA daemon.
- `4-flows.md` — three runtime sequence flows (new game → galaxy; briefing → deploy → tactical →
  debrief; time jump → chronicle), each step naming the pipe command and the handler function.
- `gaps.md` — every place the model and the running code disagree, a boundary is unclear, a
  bible-named container does not exist yet, or a responsibility is duplicated. Cited to file:line.

Every diagram is Mermaid (`C4Context`/`C4Container`/`C4Component`, or `flowchart` where the C4
syntax cannot express something — GitHub and most Markdown viewers render Mermaid inline). Every
diagram is followed by a table repeating each element with its source file, so the model is
checkable without a renderer.

## Status legend

Used throughout this model to classify every component, entry point, and container:

| Status | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **built** | Code exists on `origin/main` and is reached by the running game (the live scene-router flow, the pipe's command dispatch, or the strategic/tactical tick) — not merely present in a source file. |
| **wired-untested** | Code exists and something in the running game calls it, but no test exercises that call path directly (rare in this codebase; most wired code has a fenced test — flag explicitly where this applies). |
| **tested-unwired** | Code exists and is covered by tests (`tests/csim/*.py`, `tests/*.gd`), but nothing in the running game (tick, pipe dispatch, scene graph) ever calls it. A real function, provably unreached. |
| **planned** | Named in the bible or `docs/northstar/` but no corresponding code exists in this checkout. |

A component can be `built` for some entry points and `tested-unwired` for others in the same file
(e.g. `csrc/tactical_mapgen.c`: `om_map_add_cover`/`om_map_add_obstacle` are built; most
`om_map_get_*` accessors are `/* STUB */`). Where that split matters, the component tables call it
out per entry point rather than giving the whole module one status.

1	# Gaps — where the model and the running code disagree, or a boundary is unclear
2	
3	Every item cites file:line. Nothing here is a design decision; where a real choice is needed, it
4	is phrased as a question for Westley, not answered.
5	
6	## 1. `docs/architecture.md` documents a fog function that is never called
7	
8	`docs/architecture.md:288` states the tactical frame's `visible[faction]` field is
9	`"om_visibility_compute's set for that faction"`. The actual code building that field,
10	`csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c:1094-1129`, calls `om_player_can_see_unit` (`csrc/fog.c:470`) per unit
11	instead. `om_visibility_compute` (`csrc/fog.c:615`) has no caller anywhere in `csrc/` except its
12	own definition (`grep -rn "om_visibility_compute" csrc/` returns exactly one line). Both
13	functions do real fog work (`om_player_can_see_unit` calls `om_fog_faction_sees`,
14	`csrc/fog.c:474`), so this is not a stub standing in for the documented function — it is a second,
15	working implementation that the doc doesn't mention, while the one the doc names sits unused.
16	**Question for Westley**: should `docs/architecture.md` be corrected to name
17	`om_player_can_see_unit`, or should the pipe be rewired to call `om_visibility_compute` (unclear
18	which is the intended long-term API)?
19	
20	## 2. `csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c`'s own file-header comment is stale against its body
21	
22	The comment block at `csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c:1-65` (dated to the "T1-2" wiring pass, 2026-09-24)
23	states flatly: `"map.nodes" reflects the stub (always empty), "map.cover" and "map.obstacles" are
24	always empty, and "units"/"visible" are always empty"` (`:50-52`) because "there is also no
25	enumerator for live tactical unit ids at all" (`:47-48`). Checked against the current body, all
26	three parts of this claim are now stale, not just the units/visible part:
27	
28	- **units/visible**: `csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c:1043-1048` enumerates real unit ids via
29	  `om_unit_count`/`om_unit_id_at` and builds populated `units[]` and `visible{}` entries, using
30	  `om_unit_get_faction`/`om_player_can_see_unit` (`csrc/fog.c:470`). `om_unit_count`/`om_unit_id_at`
31	  are real, non-stub E-11 accessors (piece B10, attached per `pieces.toml:196-210`).
32	- **map.nodes**: `om_map_get_node_count`/`om_map_get_node_pos`/`om_map_get_node_type`
33	  (`csrc/tactical_mapgen.c:454-476`) are real, non-stub accessors reading a live `om_mapgen_state`
34	  struct, not hardcoded returns. Every mission populates three real nodes: `om_mission_setup`
35	  (`csrc/mission.c:2054-2065`) calls `om_mission_instantiate_map`, which calls
36	  `om_map_add_spine_node` and `om_map_add_spawn_point` twice (`mission.c:2046,2048-2049`), both
37	  real functions (`tactical_mapgen.c:288-295`, backed by the same `om_mgs_add_node` helper `cover`
38	  uses). `"map.nodes"` is not always empty; it is always (at least) 3 after `mission_start`.
39	- **map.cover**: also real and populated — `om_map_add_cover` (`mission.c:2047`) places the
40	  objective's cover circle, read back by `om_map_cover_count`/`om_map_cover_at`
41	  (`csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c:1012-1015`), both real (see gap 7's correction).
42	- **map.obstacles**: this part of the original claim is still accurate.
43	  `om_map_add_obstacle` (`tactical_mapgen.c:306`) is real and not a stub, but no production code
44	  was found to call it (`grep -rn "om_map_add_obstacle(" csrc/*.c` outside `tactical_mapgen.c`
45	  itself returns nothing), and separately `csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c:1033-1036` has its own comment
46	  confirming no accessor enumerates obstacles at all, so the field is hardcoded `[]` regardless.
47	
48	A comment that is right about one field, wrong about two, and half-right about the reason (a real
49	unit enumerator now exists) is worse than a comment that is simply outdated; it should be re-split
50	or re-dated at the next touch of this file.
51	
52	## 3. Two live simulation transports, both spawned by the running client
53	
54	`autoload/sim_bridge.gd:58-61` (`SimBridge._ready()`) unconditionally spawns
55	`simulation/pipe_transport.py` (the legacy Python sim) on every boot, because `USE_LIVE_SIM`
56	(`sim_bridge.gd:29`) is a hardcoded `true` with no code path that sets it `false` in this
57	checkout. Independently, `autoload/sim_session.gd`'s `SimSession.bridge()` lazily spawns
58	`pipe/ouroboros_pipe` (the C sim) the first time any live-flow scene calls it
59	(`scenes/galaxy/galaxy_view.gd:97`, etc.). Both subprocesses can be running at once during
60	ordinary play, one of them (the Python one) doing real, non-trivial work
61	(`autoload/tactical_bridge.gd`, `autoload/ui_data_bus.gd` via `autoload/sim_bridge_data_source.gd`)
62	that has nothing to do with the scenes the player actually sees in the live flow, except for
63	save-slot listing, era library, and settings, which genuinely do read from it. See `gap 4` for the
64	concrete visible consequence.
65	
66	## 4. `scenes/load_game/load_game.gd` renders two independent save-slot lists in one screen
67	
68	`load_game.gd:74` calls `_refresh_slots()` (`:101-109`), which reads `UIDataBus.get_save_slots()`
69	(the legacy `SimBridge`-backed source) and builds `tm_card` UI rows. Separately, `_render_bridge_rows()`
70	(`:272-297`, called after a `list_saves` round-trip through the C-bridge) builds a second set of
71	plain `HBoxContainer` rows from `_bridge.load(slot_id)` (the new C-transport save format). Both
72	write into the same `_slot_list` container. Only the C-bridge rows' Load button actually navigates
73	to `"galaxy"` (`load_game.gd:294`, inside `_render_bridge_rows`); the legacy cards' click handler
74	was not traced as reaching the live galaxy scene. **Question for Westley**: is the legacy
75	`UIDataBus` save-slot card meant to be removed now that the C-bridge path (piece `T2g`, attached)
76	covers real loading, or is it still load-bearing for something the C-bridge path doesn't yet do
77	(e.g. showing era/name/playtime metadata `UIDataBus`'s mock schema carries and the sidecar JSON
78	does not)?
79	
80	## 5. `new_game` / `onboarding` / `time_jump_sequencer` are a three-scene chain, all orphaned from the live boot path
81	
82	`scenes/main_menu/main_menu.gd:71` binds the `"NEW GAME"` label directly to `action: "galaxy"`, and
83	`_on_menu_action`'s `"galaxy"` arm (`main_menu.gd:314-320`) calls `SceneRouter.go_to("galaxy")` with
84	no intermediate scene. A repo-wide search finds **no** `go_to("new_game"` call site anywhere in
85	`scenes/`, so `scenes/new_game/new_game.tscn` is unreachable from the confirmed live flow, even
86	though it is registered in `SceneRouter.SCENES` (`scene_router.gd:7`) and is a complete, working
87	scene (creates a save slot via `UIDataBus.create_save_slot`, `new_game.gd:205`, then calls
88	`go_to("onboarding", ...)`, `new_game.gd:206`). Since that caller never fires,
89	`scenes/onboarding/onboarding.tscn` is unreachable too, and since `onboarding.gd:386` is the only
90	caller of `go_to("time_jump", ...)`, `scenes/world/time_jump_sequencer.tscn` — the scene driven by
91	`SimBridge`'s `time_jump_started`/`time_jump_keyframe`/`chronicle_entry`/`time_jump_ended` signals,
92	relayed through `UIDataBus` (`autoload/ui_data_bus.gd:5-8`), i.e. the **legacy Python transport** —

is phrased as a question for Westley, not answered.

## 1. `docs/architecture.md` documents a fog function that is never called

`docs/architecture.md:288` states the tactical frame's `visible[faction]` field is
`"om_visibility_compute's set for that faction"`. The actual code building that field,
`csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c:1094-1129`, calls `om_player_can_see_unit` (`csrc/fog.c:470`) per unit
instead. `om_visibility_compute` (`csrc/fog.c:615`) has no caller anywhere in `csrc/` except its
own definition (`grep -rn "om_visibility_compute" csrc/` returns exactly one line). Both
functions do real fog work (`om_player_can_see_unit` calls `om_fog_faction_sees`,
`csrc/fog.c:474`), so this is not a stub standing in for the documented function — it is a second,
working implementation that the doc doesn't mention, while the one the doc names sits unused.
**Question for Westley**: should `docs/architecture.md` be corrected to name
`om_player_can_see_unit`, or should the pipe be rewired to call `om_visibility_compute` (unclear
which is the intended long-term API)?

## 2. `csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c`'s own file-header comment is stale against its body

The comment block at `csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c:1-65` (dated to the "T1-2" wiring pass, 2026-09-24)
states flatly: `"map.nodes" reflects the stub (always empty), "map.cover" and "map.obstacles" are
always empty, and "units"/"visible" are always empty"` (`:50-52`) because "there is also no
enumerator for live tactical unit ids at all" (`:47-48`). Checked against the current body, all
three parts of this claim are now stale, not just the units/visible part:

- **units/visible**: `csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c:1043-1048` enumerates real unit ids via
  `om_unit_count`/`om_unit_id_at` and builds populated `units[]` and `visible{}` entries, using
  `om_unit_get_faction`/`om_player_can_see_unit` (`csrc/fog.c:470`). `om_unit_count`/`om_unit_id_at`
  are real, non-stub E-11 accessors (piece B10, attached per `pieces.toml:196-210`).
- **map.nodes**: `om_map_get_node_count`/`om_map_get_node_pos`/`om_map_get_node_type`
  (`csrc/tactical_mapgen.c:454-476`) are real, non-stub accessors reading a live `om_mapgen_state`
  struct, not hardcoded returns. Every mission populates three real nodes: `om_mission_setup`
  (`csrc/mission.c:2054-2065`) calls `om_mission_instantiate_map`, which calls
  `om_map_add_spine_node` and `om_map_add_spawn_point` twice (`mission.c:2046,2048-2049`), both
  real functions (`tactical_mapgen.c:288-295`, backed by the same `om_mgs_add_node` helper `cover`
  uses). `"map.nodes"` is not always empty; it is always (at least) 3 after `mission_start`.

  itself returns nothing), and separately `csrc/pipe/om_pipe.c:1033-1036` has its own comment
  confirming no accessor enumerates obstacles at all, so the field is hardcoded `[]` regardless.

A comment that is right about one field, wrong about two, and half-right about the reason (a real
unit enumerator now exists) is worse than a comment that is simply outdated; it should be re-split
or re-dated at the next touch of this file.

## 3. Two live simulation transports, both spawned by the running client

`autoload/sim_bridge.gd:58-61` (`SimBridge._ready()`) unconditionally spawns
`simulation/pipe_transport.py` (the legacy Python sim) on every boot, because `USE_LIVE_SIM`

checkout. Independently, `autoload/sim_session.gd`'s `SimSession.bridge()` lazily spawns

concrete visible consequence.

Independent of gap 1's doc mismatch: `om_visibility_compute` itself is a real, non-trivial function
covered by `tests/csim/test_E12_S089_i_see_what_my_units_see.py` through
`test_E12_S094_how_fog_looks.py` (six files), reached only via ctypes in tests, never from the
tick or the pipe. This is a clean instance of the model's **tested-unwired** status: a piece of the
sim that is provably correct in isolation but provably never runs during play.

## 9. Legacy `scenes/tactical/` is a full, built, unreached scene stack

`scenes/tactical/` contains a complete tactical presentation
(`tactical.gd` 13.1K, `hud.gd` 26.4K, `terrain_renderer.gd` 12.3K, `unit_renderer.gd` 16.7K,
`input_router.gd` 11.2K, plus `visuals/*`), wired to `SimBridge`/`TacticalBridge`/the client-side
`Visibility` autoload (`scripts/tactical/visibility.gd`). It is registered in
`autoload/scene_router.gd`'s `SCENES` dict as `"tactical"` (`scene_router.gd:13`) but no
`go_to("tactical")` call site exists anywhere under `scenes/` — the live flow always uses
`"tactical_c"` instead (`scenes/mission_briefing/mission_briefing.gd:668`). It is exercised by
`tests/test_b3_tutorial_integration.gd` and `tests/test_qa_state_scenes.gd`. This is the client-side
equivalent of a tested-unwired component: real, tested, unreachable from the player's actual path
through the game. Given `scenes/tactical_c/` is comparatively minimal (11.8K, one file), the two
stacks are not equivalent in feature completeness — `scenes/tactical/`'s HUD, terrain renderer, and
visual-effects managers (`combat_heatmap.gd`, `ability_overlay_manager.gd`,
`destruction_manager.gd`, `attack_visual_manager.gd`, `ambient_density_manager.gd`, all under
`scenes/tactical/visuals/`) have no equivalent under `scenes/tactical_c/` yet. Agora's QA profile's
**QA-001** ("tactical view renders completely blank (flat grey) after Deploy... The frame IS loaded
(daemon state tick > 0) but nothing renders on screen",
`~/Projects/agora/projects/ouroboros/qa.toml`) is filed against `tactical_c`, the thinner of the
two stacks — consistent with, but not proven caused by, its comparative thinness.

## 10. Client-side fog-of-war logic exists in two more places than `csrc/fog.c`

`scripts/tactical/visibility.gd` (the `Visibility` autoload) is described as "single source of
truth for fog of war" (`visibility.gd:1`) for `scenes/tactical/`'s renderer, HUD, and input router
— a client-side predicate, independent of `csrc/fog.c`'s server-side computation, and applying only
to the unreached legacy tactical scene (gap 9). `scenes/tactical_c/` reads visibility from the
pipe's `visible{}` map instead (gap 1/2). No shared fog implementation exists between the two
tactical stacks.

## 11. The bible's E-19 multiplayer epic has no corresponding container

`docs/bible/epics/E-19-multiplayer.md` exists and describes lockstep two-client play (rung P9 in
`docs/northstar/PLAN.md:174`, "Two clients, lockstep... Checksums agree per tick; desync detector
silent; two-window QA session"). No networking code, no second-client launch path, and no lockstep
message format exist anywhere in this checkout. Every container and flow in this model assumes
exactly one player, one client process, one pipe process, one world. The single-player assumptions
most likely to need revisiting for multiplayer: `autoload/c_bridge.gd`'s one shared
`SimSession.bridge()` singleton per process (`sim_session.gd:14`, "the one pipe session of the
run"); the pipe's `player_faction` being a single scalar on the `hello`/`snapshot` frames
(`docs/architecture.md:238,244`) rather than per-client; and `QADaemon`'s single-port,
single-connection `TCPServer` (`autoload/qa_daemon.gd:33-34,87-94`), which has no notion of a
second player's session at all. **Planned, not built** — status per this model's legend.

## 12. The documented offline library builder does not match the one that exists

`CLAUDE.md:9` names `claude-sonnet-4-20250514` as the offline content-generation model (library
builder). The only concrete builder script in this checkout,
`scripts/library/emit_chronicle_fragments.py`, makes no model API call at all — it regex-parses
hardcoded C string literals out of `csrc/chronicle.c`'s `CHRON_FRAGMENTS[]` array
(`emit_chronicle_fragments.py:1-13,25-38`) and writes them to
`library/chronicle/fragments.json`. This is consistent with (does not violate) the "No runtime API
calls during play" rule, since it makes no call at all, runtime or otherwise, but it means the
actual chronicle prose in the running game today is hand-written placeholder text embedded in C
source, not model-generated content. If real content generation is expected before ship, no code
path for it exists yet in this checkout.

## 13. `csrc/om_internal.h`'s hook hint says B4's freeze dependency

`csrc/worldgen.c` (piece `B4`) is marked `depends_on = ["freeze"]` in `pieces.toml:74` with the
size-estimate note "needs F2's weak `om_world_generate` attribute" — the weak/strong override
pattern (`csrc/region.c:321`'s `__attribute__((weak))` `om_world_step`, similarly `region.c:217`'s
weak `om_world_generate`) is a real, load-bearing mechanism for how these pieces attach
independently without editing a shared dispatch table. It is unverified whether this pattern is
documented anywhere outside the C source comments themselves (`worldgen.c:4-8`) — a reader of
`docs/architecture.md` alone would not learn that world generation is wired this way. Noted here
as a documentation gap, not a code defect.

## 14. Cloudflare R2 and the GDExtension path are named only in `CLAUDE.md`/research notes

Both are stated intentions with zero corresponding code: R2 (`CLAUDE.md:9`, no other reference
anywhere in the checkout) and GDExtension (`CLAUDE.md:9`; `docs/northstar/research/c_rewrite.md:9`,
"Phase 2 adds a thin GDExtension binding and deletes the pipe"). Neither is a defect — both are
explicitly forward-looking — but both are listed here so a reader of this model does not mistake
"named in the tech stack" for "exists."

## 15. The Factory's documented QA verb vocabulary does not match the shipped daemon

`docs/northstar/PLAN.md:143` ("QA architecture") lists an intended actor vocabulary including
`goto`. The shipped `autoload/qa_daemon.gd:183-212` (`_dispatch`) has no `goto`/`nav` case at all,
and the project's own QA profile documents this explicitly and prominently:
`~/Projects/agora/projects/ouroboros/qa.toml` ("IMPORTANT navigation rule: there is NO 'goto' or
'nav' verb in this game. This is not a web browser."). This is the one place in the model where
the general Factory design doc (which is intentionally project-agnostic, `PLAN.md:98`: "it must
serve a second project... not a fork") and this specific project's implementation are already known
and documented (by the project's own profile) to diverge — included here for completeness, not as
a new finding.

## Proposed epic E-22 Playtest delivery and telemetry

Not in the bible yet. Proposed here; the epic file and catalog rows are a follow-up PR through the normal Stage 2 gate. Story list in the commander's words:

- "I download one file, unzip it, double-click it, and I am at the main menu with nothing else installed." (Round 1; export preset and ZIP card; probe I is its proving-ground twin.)
- "The first screen tells me what is recorded on my machine and asks before recording anything." (Round 1; consent per `Q-MVP-03`.)
- "A session file on my machine records what I did, in plain text I can read, and never leaves my machine unless I send it." (Round 1.)
- "One key captures a bug report with logs and a screenshot and tells me where it went." (Round 1.)
- "A feedback form in the download asks me questions I can answer in ten minutes." (Round 1; the form is the metric list in `README.md`.)
- "A build I get from Discord tells me its version and which round it is." (Round 2.)
- "A weekly digest of what testers reported is written from the files, with no model reading my session." (Round 2; offline script.)
- "The Steam Playtest build asks the same questions in-game." (Round 3.)

Every one of these is an Agora card, gated on probes H and I.

## Stories cut from every round on purpose

S-040, S-041 (E-05 flags); S-054 (deferred); S-151 (deferred); S-157 (deferred); all of E-19; S-146, S-147, S-148, S-150 (E-20 pack mechanics). They stay Spec'd or Deferred in the catalog. A gap review may pull any of them forward; nothing here kills a story.

Every status below comes from reading the docs and the C4 model (dated 2026-09-28) and the `pieces.toml` piece statuses on `main`. I did not run the game or the test suites.

## 1. The 21 epics

Counts come from `stories.md` and the register: 161 stories, 57 open flags out of 214 rows.

| Group | Epic | Covers | Stories |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sim core | E-02 | Region fields and drift | S-012 to S-020, S-160 |
| | E-03 | World generation | S-021 to S-025 |
| | E-04 | Events and chains | S-026 to S-031 |
| | E-05 | Faction agents and conflict | S-032 to S-041 |
| | E-06 | Diplomacy and technology | S-042 to S-048 |
| | E-07 | Civilizational lifecycle | S-049 to S-054 |
| | E-08 | Generational structure | S-055 to S-064 |
| | E-09 | Chronicle | S-065 to S-071 |
| | E-10 | Missions | S-072 to S-080 |
| Tactical | E-01 | Layer system | S-001 to S-011 |
| | E-11 | Units and combat | S-081 to S-088 |
| | E-12 | Fog and sensors | S-089 to S-094 |
| | E-13 | Movement and command | S-095 to S-102 |
| | E-14 | Enemy macro behavior | S-120 to S-125 |
| | E-15 | Reinforcement, supply, hazards | S-126 to S-131 |
| | E-17 | Map generation | S-112 to S-119 |
| Client and cross-cutting | E-16 | Camera, HUD, world view, screens | S-103 to S-111, S-161 |
| | E-18 | Visual style and combat visuals | S-132 to S-138 |
| | E-19 | Multiplayer (plus the deferred economy story S-159) | S-139 to S-144, S-159 |
| | E-20 | Multi-era and monetization | S-145 to S-151 |
| | E-21 | Offline AI pipeline | S-152 to S-158 |

**Gate status.**
- Only E-02 to E-05 have passed their gate, and only those four have e2e files.
- E-04 and E-05 are the only epics whose stories are marked Tested. E-02 and E-03 are Ready.
- The epic files' "not passed" verdict lines look stale. For example, E-06 says it is blocked on 5 flags, but most of its flags are closed in the register.

## 2. Epics compared with the built MVP

The MVP plan (Track L, `docs/northstar/mvp/`) cuts every epic except E-19 to its thinnest form for Round 1. It proposes a new epic, E-22, and five prototype stories. `build_path.md` is dated 2026-09-14 and says "functionally zero built". That is stale.

The C sim now has about 21k lines of C. The live C tick covers events, agents, collisions, friction, admin revolts, diplomacy, technology, lifecycle and drift.

# Options pass: design options for TBD features

Opened 2026-09-22. Eleven features have a high-level idea in the bible but no defined player-facing behavior. This folder holds, per feature, a perception brief (what the docs say, what Westley said, what is fixed, what is contradictory) and, once Westley confirms the brief, a set of 2 to 4 design options with a diagram each. Options describe the "what" from the player's chair. No implementation, no recommendation. Westley picks; a pick becomes a flag answer and a rule rewrite through the Design Lane.

Precedent for this shape: `../landscape_design/README.md`, the P2 design phase. Nothing here is bible text. `docs/bible/**` and `docs/northstar/ambiguity_register.md` do not change in this pass.

## Method

1. Perception brief per feature (this chat): documented goal, Westley's verbatim words, fixed constraints, prior art, contradictions as questions.
2. Westley confirms or corrects each brief in three chat batches; his answers land verbatim in the brief's "Westley confirms" block.
3. One sub-agent per feature writes `options.md` and one SVG per option against the confirmed brief. Sub-agents research and enumerate; they never decide, recommend, or rank.
4. Review against the checklist below, then one HTML atlas for side-by-side reading.
5. Optional Blue Ocean fusion pass on features Westley names (ERRC grid, strategy canvas, fused options).

## Folder shape

```
<slug>/brief.md                 perception brief, Westley's confirmation, sub-agent brief
<slug>/options.md               2 to 4 options, A to D
<slug>/diagrams/<option>.svg    one diagram per option
```

`.gdignore` keeps Godot from generating `.import` files for the SVGs.

## Atlas

All eleven option sets, side by side with their diagrams, on one page: https://claude.ai/artifact/6571aySFhmoQ1i4XswDhNm (private to Westley). Rebuilt from the files here whenever an options.md changes.

## Decisions (2026-09-23)

Westley read the atlas and answered per feature; his words are verbatim in each brief's section 10, and every pick is folded into the bible with its flag id.

| Feature | Outcome | Decision |
|---|---|---|
| camera | picked | Angle Rack and Layer Peel both, Layer Peel as a player option, plus a 180-degree flip key; control specifics later (Q-103-03, Q-103-04). |
| map-view | prototype | Sand Table is the candidate, prototype before commitment (block-resolution table with a grain-size dial, plus a 45° view with layers separated); more layer-mark ideas beyond pins wanted (Q-103-05, Q-103-06; E-16 S-161). |
| control-groups | picked | Recall and Narrow as the default for groups and multi-layer movement, the Comb for moving individual layers within a group (Q-105-02). |
| layer-system | picked | Terrace Reading combined with Floor Spindle, both subdued; an occlusion indicator for hidden units is open (Q-E01-08 closed, Q-009-02). |
| era-transitions | picked | The Long Horizon (Q-148-01 closed; the reach measure is Q-148-05). |
| era-feel | picked | The Climate of War (Q-151-01). The Long Look is not an era-feel strategy; its idea became a decision that loading screens carry interesting information (E-16 R-110-04, Q-110-03). |
| paired-economy | second pass | None yet. The Works is good but not unique; the Two Clocks needs concrete player actions; the Commons is too broad and not about emotions. Second pass: building and designing efficient pathways and systems as the economy player's task. |
| city-spectacle | second pass | None. New direction: static architecture expands outward on its own as the city grows; small settlements crop up at production facilities and resource objectives and can grow into cities around a critical resource; trade moves visibly between cities; the home base has a resource reason to exist but is not the only source; people go where money and resources are. Second pass with a couple of ideas on this. |
| unit-traits | picked | Unlockable trait cards (Dead by Daylight, Age of Empires 3 register) under a core rule: cards and abilities never outrank positioning, layer damage weighs more, cross-layer-vision cards minimized. Decided, no second pass (Q-083-02, Q-083-03). |
| complications | picked | Crossed Signals (Q-080-02). |
| difficulty-knobs | picked | Neither. Difficulty scales the enemy's economic prosperity and its multi-layer intelligence; a costly seer unit is a desired piece of the layer system (Q-125-02, Q-125-03, Q-E12-01). |

Cross-cutting from the same answers: cross-layer damage and vision are the game's most important undefined mechanic and get a research program with prototypes and humans in the loop (register Q-008-02, research queue Q76); a costly seer unit is a desired piece of the layer system (Q-E12-01); loading screens carry chronicle-register information (E-16 R-110-04); and before the MVP becomes the full game a C4 model of the system is drawn and kept beside the bible (CLAUDE.md).

Second pass owed: paired economy (building and efficient pathways as the task, concrete actions) and self-running city (settlements at resource sites, trade between cities, the home base as one source among many).

One agent per feature, launched only when Westley says so. The agent reads, in order: `docs/bible/game_bible.md`, the feature's epic file, its `brief.md` (sections 4 and 8 are the constraints; section 8 wins), and the prior research the brief names. Then it writes `options.md` and one SVG per option in `diagrams/`.

- Role: research and enumerate. Never decide, recommend, or rank. Player perspective only: what the player sees, does, feels, and learns. No implementation, no engine or data language, no file paths, no code.
- Options: the count and wild count in the brief's section 9, labeled A to D. A wild option is a shape no shipped game has and may have no precedent.
- Per option: a name; one paragraph on how it works from the player's chair; a 30 to 60 second play vignette in second person; the brief constraints it honors and the ones it strains, named; prior art with a confidence tag (VERIFIED, REPORTED, ESTIMATED, AMBIGUOUS) or "none"; player-side tradeoffs as consequences; one SVG diagram. Camera and control groups also carry a control table per option.
- Diagram: hand-authored SVG, 960 wide, either a screen wireframe (what the player sees at one moment, labeled regions) or a flow (states the player passes through). Real labels, no lorem, no external images, plain SVG 1.1 with no scripts and no foreignObject, so GitHub renders it.
- Research: WebSearch and WebFetch allowed; cite every prior-art claim; `docs/research/games/*.md` may be read.
- Write access: only `docs/northstar/research/options/<slug>/`. Never `docs/bible/**`, `docs/northstar/ambiguity_register.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, tests, code.
- Prose: normal prose in `options.md`; caveman only in the report back to the main agent.
- Length: 600 to 1,500 words plus tables unless the brief says otherwise; the required elements per option set the floor. Longer means the option is drifting into "how".

## Review checklist for an options.md

- Option count matches the brief; the required wild options are present.
- Each option has: a name, one paragraph from the player's chair, a 30 to 60 second second-person vignette, the brief constraints it honors and the ones it strains, prior art with a confidence tag or "none", player-side tradeoffs, one SVG.
- No implementation language. No recommendation or ranking language.

1	# Layer system look and feel: perception brief
2	
3	## 1. Feature and status
4	
5	E-01 "Layer system", the game's defining mechanic (`docs/bible/epics/E-01-layer-system.md`). The mechanics are largely decided (Q-E01-01 to Q-E01-07, Q-001 to Q-009 closed). What is open is how it reads on screen: Q-E01-08 (references missing, `docs/northstar/ambiguity_register.md:32`) and A-299 (the layer-preference indicator visual, deferred to research, `docs/northstar/stage1_audit.md:471`). `docs/bible/references/E-01/notes.md` records the plan: "Westley does not yet know exactly what it should look like; he will decide by interacting with real options." A two-layer P6 mockup exists (`docs/northstar/plans/briefs/2026-09-22-p6-layers-mockup.md`). This brief covers the look and feel: how the stack, a height change, the ring and strip, the pulse, and the preference indicator read to the player. It does not reopen closed mechanics unless Westley says so in section 8.
6	
7	## 2. Player-facing goal as documented
8	
9	"The layer system is the game's strategic defining characteristic. The battlefield is not a flat plane. It is a stack of three to five vertical layers, and a unit is always on exactly one of them. Terrain blocks layers at specific places, so a force can go over an obstacle on a high layer or around it on a low one. Vision across layers is worse than vision on your own layer, so a force on a layer you cannot see is a threat you do not know about. Changing layers costs time and leaves the unit briefly vulnerable." (`E-01:18`)
10	
11	"As a commander, I want to see at a glance which layer each unit is on and which layer I am focused on, so that I never have to guess who can see whom." (S-009, `E-01:148`) "As a commander, I want a unit on a higher layer to sit visibly higher than one on a lower layer, so that the layer stack reads as a stack and not as a color code." (S-010, `E-01:161`)
12	
13	## 3. Westley's own words
14	
15	Vision v2 Q6, 2026-09-10 (`docs/northstar/vision_v2.md:65`): "A player with an inferior force but understanding of positional tactics (surround, high ground, game theory positioning) can overcome the opposition, the goal is to construct a situation with enough variables that creates a really high skill ceiling, and significantly favors players with an understanding of the layer system, specific units, and such. (we're really heavily basing based off of Starcraft 2 here, surrounds and high ground were really important in that game, we're trying to turn it up to 11 in our game)."
16	
17	Q-E01-01, 2026-09-12 (`ambiguity_register.md:9`): "There should always be 5 layers, regardless of era. Only 3 may have been an idea from when we were just implementing a toy version, but we're not doing that anymore, so every era should be a 5 layer system."
18	
19	A-299, Stage 1 (`stage1_audit.md:471`): "Westley's initial (non-final) idea: a mostly translucent grid around the unit, fading with distance, brightest on the unit's current layer and faded on adjacent layers, so layer membership reads visually at a glance." Same row: "good visualization tools exist for this kind of 3D-layer cueing and deserve a look."
20	
21	Q-001-02 (`:20`): "The bottom layer is layer 1 (lowest in terms of height)." Q-001-03 (`:21`): "Units shoudl route around obstacles, just like classic starcraft 2 RTS." Q-002-01 (`:22`): "it should be 'reasonable' how quickly a unit traverses from one layer to another, between 1 and 2 seconds is a good starting point, to be tuned if needed." Q-004-02 (`:26`): "It should still be attackable by those units until the transition is halfway completed. New layer can attack it after it's halfway completed." Q-006-01 (`:28`): "Give the interceptor the pulse, mark it as a 'for now' ability, we'll modify units a lot when we have playtesters." Q-009-01, 2026-09-16 (`:31`): "(a), purely visual presentation (non-focused layers dim slightly; commands and box-select still function normally across all layers)." Q-008-01 (`:30`): "(a), prototype attacks are same-layer only. Cross-layer strikes deferred to dedicated layer tuning research."
22	
23	E-17 references, 2026-09-13 (`docs/bible/references/E-17/notes.md:42`): "Dramatic elevation differences. Real earth-era height changes; the player should physically feel the height and get a real sense of scale. This ties to the E-01 layer system — vertical space must read."
24	
25	Mockup review 2, 2026-09-21 (`docs/northstar/research/landscape_design/README.md:63`): "Though Halo Wars had small changes, I want this game to have big changes for vastly different heights."
26	
27	## 4. Fixed constraints any option must honor
28	
29	- Always 5 layers, layer 1 at the bottom; the generator never varies the count (Q-E01-01, Q-001-01, Q-001-02).
30	- A ring under every unit, one color per layer, changing on the tick the layer changes (R-009-01, `E-01:151`). A second, smaller preference indicator, distinct from the ring; exact visual open (R-009-02, `:152`).
31	- A layer strip on the HUD; click or Tab changes focus and the strip highlights (R-009-03, `:153`); vertical five-slot strip on the right edge (`docs/bible_history/bible_2_00_combat.md:199`); focus is purely visual, non-focused layers dim (Q-009-01).
32	- Height reads: a unit's drawn height is the layer's elevation; a transition tweens, never snaps; one layer step moves the unit by more than 5 percent of viewport height at a fixed camera (R-010-01 to 03, `E-01:164-166`).
33	- Transition: one tween of 1 to 2 seconds regardless of distance, per-type durations (Raider 1.0 s to Bastion 5.0 s); the old layer can hit until halfway, the new layer from halfway (Q-002-01, Q-004-01, Q-004-02, A-354).
34	- No automatic layer change ever; the player owns the layer (Q-001-03).
35	- Cross-layer vision: adjacent layer at half range, two away at a fifth, three or more none (Q-E01-03); the pulse is the Interceptor's ability, reveals all layers briefly, leaves a ghost marker for 10 s (Q-006-01, Q-006-02).
36	- Fog is binary hidden or revealed; no special silhouette for another layer (Q-E01-06).
37	- Combat is same-layer only for the prototype; layers change pathing and vision, not damage (Q-008-01, Q-E01-04).
38	- Alt plus 1 to 5 sets preference, Alt plus 0 clears (Q-003-01).
39	- Visually quiet: "the world, not the interface, stays the thing the player is actually looking at" (A-313, `stage1_audit.md:492`).
40	- Era-agnostic: the engine says which layers are blocked; the pack says whether that is an asteroid, a mountain, or a reef (`E-01:22`).
41	- The camera is never bound to a layer (E-16 R-103-04).
42	
43	## 5. Prior art already named
44	
45	By design, none external for the look: "Not external screenshots — a design phase." (`references/E-01/notes.md:3`). Mechanic bar: StarCraft 2 high ground and surrounds (vision Q6). Terrain scale: the Roblox biome and island generators (`references/E-17/notes.md:28-36`). Camera height floor: Halo Wars. HUD register for the strip's host bar: Immortal: Gates of Pyre. Readable-toy register: Age of Empires Online, Art of Rally.
46	
47	## 6. Contradictions, as questions for Westley
48	
49	1. Vertical scale. Q-E01-01 records three elevation bands (0 to 30, 30 to 100, 100 to 300 wu) for five layers; R-010-01 calls that a defect; the P6 mockup uses 600 wu between layers; pass 3 terrain peaks are 3,000 to 5,000 wu. Should the five layers be tied to terrain height (a layer is a terrace of the mountain) or float above it (a layer is an altitude band the terrain pokes through)? What should one layer step look like next to a cliff?
50	2. Cross-layer combat. `references/E-01/notes.md:15` records it as "an intended strategic tuning lever (range/damage vary by layer offset), still under research"; Q-008-01 closes the prototype as same-layer only. May the options explore how cross-layer strikes would read, or must they assume same-layer only?
51	3. "Non-focused layers dim slightly" versus the spec's 60 percent dim (`docs/stage_specs/stage_11c_layer_visuals_and_fog_spec.md:59`). How much should the other four layers fall back when one has focus?
52	4. A-299's translucent grid around each unit versus the P6 mockup's translucent plane for a whole layer. One idea or two? Is a whole-layer plane wanted at all?
53	5. The E-01 purpose still says "three to five" layers. Confirm the options assume exactly five everywhere.
54	
55	## 7. Proposed option width
56	
57	Four options, two wild. Each option describes, from the player's chair: the stack at normal camera distance, a unit changing height, the per-unit ring and the preference indicator, the HUD strip and what focus does to the picture, and the pulse reveal and fade.
58	
59	## 8. Westley confirms
60	
61	Batch 1, 2026-09-22, verbatim: "no specific scale numbers, that's for the agents to decide based on their specific option, layer differences will also change per-era: in space layer differences can be quite large, but on land layer differences are a lot smaller in small-scale combat (pre-high altitude planes or deep sea submarines). For the dimming, layer it's on should be around 50%, adjacent layers 10-20%, layers 2 away are 5%. The idea behind it is visible but not in the way. - When the player toggles to a different layer we should show them a little icon or something to indicate which layer the unit would be moving too, like a waypoint or something. Grid around each unit, not whole layer, players need to be able to see the battlefield and the background and things behind the grid view (think Autocad, Unreal engine, tools that visualize 3D objects well and clear to the user and user friendly). Exactly 5 for each, for eras that don't have units that can literal "fly" (roman/greek), the escelation will still be land, it'll just be mountains or something reasonable to get that high/low."
62	
63	Folded into the brief:
64	
65	- Vertical scale (question 1): no numbers from Westley; each option sets its own scale and says why. The spacing is a per-era value: large in a space era, small in a land era before high-altitude flight or deep submarines. Exactly five layers in every era; in a land era without flying units the upper layers are still land (mountains or something reasonable).
66	- Dimming (question 3): confirmed 2026-09-22, verbatim "Layer dimming: grid visibility per layer". The per-unit grid shows at about 50 percent on the unit's own layer, 10 to 20 percent on adjacent layers, 5 percent two layers away: "visible but not in the way". How far non-focused layers fall back under strip focus stays "slightly" (Q-009-01) and is each option's call.
67	- Cross-layer combat (question 2): not answered in batch 1. Options assume same-layer combat (Q-008-01) and may note where a cross-layer variant would change the picture.
68	- Layer-change indicator: when the player toggles a unit toward another layer, a small icon shows which layer it is moving to, like a waypoint. This is the R-009-02 preference indicator, now given a direction.
69	- Grid (question 4): a grid around each unit, never a whole-layer plane. The battlefield, the background, and anything behind the grid must stay visible. Reference register: AutoCAD, Unreal Engine, and other 3D visualization tools that read clearly.
70	- Five layers (question 5): confirmed.
71	
72	## 9. Sub-agent brief
73	
74	Follow the common template in `../README.md` ("Sub-agent template"). Sections 4 and 8 of this file are the constraints; where they disagree, section 8 wins.
75	
76	- Options: 4, of which 2 wild.
77	- A grid around each unit, never a whole-layer plane; the battlefield and everything behind the grid stays visible. Register: AutoCAD, Unreal Engine, and other 3D visualization tools that read clearly.
78	- A waypoint-like icon that shows which layer a unit is moving to when the player toggles it.
79	- The per-unit grid's visibility is about 50 percent on the unit's own layer, 10 to 20 percent on adjacent layers, 5 percent two away. Strip focus dims non-focused layers "slightly"; each option shows how much.
80	- No fixed spacing: each option sets its own vertical scale and says why; spacing is per era (large in space, small on land). Five layers in every era, including land eras without flying units.
81	- Assume same-layer combat; note where a cross-layer variant would change the picture.
82	
83	## 10. Decision (2026-09-23)
84	
85	Westley, verbatim: "For layer system I'd like to combine Terrace Reading with Floor Spindle and have both display, but the neither should be visually loud, just a subdued indicator (not blocking the view). We'll need to come up with a method to indicate to the player that there are units blocked by their current perspective, like a little exlamation point on the blocking units, this is to be determined and open, but I think it'd be good game design for us to indiciate to the user that they're not seeing the whole picture in some fashion."
86	
87	Recorded as: Terrace Reading combined with Floor Spindle, both subdued; an occlusion indicator for hidden units is open (Q-E01-08 closed, Q-009-02).

- Dimming (question 3): confirmed 2026-09-22, verbatim "Layer dimming: grid visibility per layer". The per-unit grid shows at about 50 percent on the unit's own layer, 10 to 20 percent on adjacent layers, 5 percent two layers away: "visible but not in the way". How far non-focused layers fall back under strip focus stays "slightly" (Q-009-01) and is each option's call.
- Cross-layer combat (question 2): not answered in batch 1. Options assume same-layer combat (Q-008-01) and may note where a cross-layer variant would change the picture.
- Layer-change indicator: when the player toggles a unit toward another layer, a small icon shows which layer it is moving to, like a waypoint. This is the R-009-02 preference indicator, now given a direction.
- Grid (question 4): a grid around each unit, never a whole-layer plane. The battlefield, the background, and anything behind the grid must stay visible. Reference register: AutoCAD, Unreal Engine, and other 3D visualization tools that read clearly.
- Five layers (question 5): confirmed.

## 9. Sub-agent brief

Follow the common template in `../README.md` ("Sub-agent template"). Sections 4 and 8 of this file are the constraints; where they disagree, section 8 wins.

- Options: 4, of which 2 wild.
- A grid around each unit, never a whole-layer plane; the battlefield and everything behind the grid stays visible. Register: AutoCAD, Unreal Engine, and other 3D visualization tools that read clearly.
- A waypoint-like icon that shows which layer a unit is moving to when the player toggles it.
- The per-unit grid's visibility is about 50 percent on the unit's own layer, 10 to 20 percent on adjacent layers, 5 percent two away. Strip focus dims non-focused layers "slightly"; each option shows how much.
- No fixed spacing: each option sets its own vertical scale and says why; spacing is per era (large in space, small on land). Five layers in every era, including land eras without flying units.
- Assume same-layer combat; note where a cross-layer variant would change the picture.

## 10. Decision (2026-09-23)

Westley, verbatim: "For layer system I'd like to combine Terrace Reading with Floor Spindle and have both display, but the neither should be visually loud, just a subdued indicator (not blocking the view). We'll need to come up with a method to indicate to the player that there are units blocked by their current perspective, like a little exlamation point on the blocking units, this is to be determined and open, but I think it'd be good game design for us to indiciate to the user that they're not seeing the whole picture in some fashion."

Recorded as: Terrace Reading combined with Floor Spindle, both subdued; an occlusion indicator for hidden units is open (Q-E01-08 closed, Q-009-02).

1	# Layer system look and feel: options
2	
3	These four options show how the five-layer stack, a unit's own layer marker, the HUD strip, and the sensor pulse could read on a commander's screen, at a vertical scale each option sets for its own stated reason. None ranks or recommends.
4	
5	## Option A — Drafting Table
6	
7	Every unit carries a small boxed lattice standing on end around its footprint, one thin tier per layer, brightest on the tier matching its own height. You read a unit's layer by which tier of its lattice glows, and the terrain behind it stays fully visible through the sparse lines.
8	
9	*You scan a line of units on a ridge; each one's lattice glows on a different rung, so you can tell at a glance who shares a layer before clicking anything. You box three, tap down; a hollow diamond appears low in each lattice, then fills as the descent starts. The bodies ease downward, rings swapping color only the instant each one lands. You tap the strip one layer up; everything off that layer dims just enough to let the units that matter jump back out.*
10	
11	**Stack at normal distance.** No floor plane anywhere — only the small lattices standing on each unit. A slope full of units reads as short lattices at different heights, like survey stakes.
12	
13	**A unit changing height.** The unit's own tier brightens first, the body eases upward over its transition time, and the ring swaps color only the instant the unit is actually standing on the new layer.
14	
15	**Grid, ring, waypoint.** The own tier holds near 50 percent strength, neighbors 10 to 20 percent, the far two 5 percent. A hollow diamond marks the target tier and fills in once the transfer starts.
16	
17	**HUD strip and focus.** A vertical five-slot strip, one swatch per layer; the focused slot is full strength, the rest — and every unit's off-focus tiers — dim to about 80 percent.
18	
19	**Pulse reveal and fade.** Every revealed unit's full lattice lights at full brightness for the pulse, then eases back to its normal falloff over about half a second rather than cutting off.
20	
21	**Vertical scale.** In the Settled Reach the tiers sit far apart, since open space needs the spacing itself to carry scale; on a land era before flight the tiers compress into hillside terraces a few meters apart.
22	
23	**Honors:** five layers; grid on the unit, never a plane; the falloff percentages; a waypoint icon; no fixed spacing; strip focus dims slightly. **Strains:** none beyond the shared tensions in Findings.
24	
25	**Prior art:** Unreal Engine's and AutoCAD's local translation gizmos and 3D navigation frames, which read an object's position without a full ground plane (VERIFIED — [Unreal](https://dev.epicgames.com/documentation/unreal-engine/transforming-actors-in-unreal-engine), [AutoCAD](https://www.autodesk.com/blogs/autocad/autocad-3d-navigation-and-visualization-tuesday-tips-with-frank/)); StarCraft 2's high-ground vision block (VERIFIED — [Liquipedia](https://liquipedia.net/starcraft2/High_Ground_and_Low_Ground)); the existing two-layer prototype's ring and smooth-not-snapped rise (VERIFIED, internal — `docs/northstar/research/mockups/layers/pass1/`).
26	
27	**Tradeoffs.** Legible and conventional; near a cluster the many small lattices can compete with each other for attention.
28	
29	Diagram: diagrams/option-a.svg
30	
31	## Option B — Terrace Reading
32	
33	Each unit's grid tiers are flat discs that tilt to match the real slope under that tier's height, so the unit's own disc sits flush with the ground and the other four rake in parallel above and below it. Same falloff idea as Option A, but the shape reports what the terrain is doing.
34	
35	*You walk a group up a switchback cut into a cliff. Each unit's disc-stack tilts more with every terrace crossed — you read the climb through the changing rake before the bodies even finish moving. Near the top you tap the strip; the lower notches fade toward the color of the stone itself rather than going flatly transparent, and the ground stays legible under everything you're not focused on.*
36	
37	**Stack at normal distance.** The tilted discs echo the terrace lines already cut into the terrain art instead of adding a second geometry on top of it.
38	
39	**A unit changing height.** The body climbs its own disc stack as in Option A; the disc's lean also visibly changes as it crosses from one terrace's slope to the next.
40	
41	**Grid, ring, waypoint.** Same 50/10–20/5 percent falloff. The waypoint is a small flag planted flat on the target disc, angled to that disc's own slope.
42	
43	**HUD strip and focus.** The strip is a small terrain cross-section with five notches, the focused one lit; focus fades the other discs toward the ground's own color, not to gray.
44	
45	**Pulse reveal and fade.** The pulse lights each unit's disc stack bottom to top in a quick sweep, then fades back down the same way, tier by tier.
46	
47	**Vertical scale.** Without real slope to hug, the Settled Reach's discs flatten toward a level lattice, spaced by deck; on land the tilt is the whole point, so spacing follows the mountain's own terrace height.
48	
49	**Honors:** the same core list as A; spacing here is read directly off the terrain. **Strains:** on flat ground or in space the tilt cue disappears and the option quietly degrades toward Option A.
50	
51	**Prior art:** the landscape phase's own terraced cliffs and elevation-first generator, which this option assumes (VERIFIED, internal — `docs/northstar/research/landscape_design/mockup/pass3/`); Halo Wars's camera holding constant height above sloped ground, per Westley's own account and general community description (REPORTED); Baldur's Gate 3's floor-peeling for multi-story buildings (REPORTED — [Steam discussion](https://steamcommunity.com/app/1086940/discussions/0/3819669231700210838/), no confirmed implementation detail found).
52	
53	**Tradeoffs.** Reads clearly where terrain has drama; on flat ground or in space the tilt cue vanishes, and two nearby units on uneven ground can show slightly different disc angles.
54	
55	Diagram: diagrams/option-b.svg
56	
57	## Option C — Sonar Bloom (wild)
58	
59	No static shape. Each layer height near a unit carries a soft ring that breathes outward on a slow rhythm, strongest and fastest at the unit's own height, fainter and slower at the layers nearby. You read a layer by which height's ring is brightest and quickest, not by comparing a fixed shape — no shipped strategy game reads layer membership this way.
60	
61	*You pan the front line and the whole picture seems to breathe — soft rings pulsing at different heights. You order a unit up a layer; a new ring starts weak at the target height while the old one slows and fades, the two ripples crossing as the body climbs between them. You trigger a pulse; for two seconds the hidden height wakes up bright and fast, then settles back to a slow quiet glow as the effect drains away.*
62	
63	**Stack at normal distance.** Dozens of soft, breathing rings at different heights read as a rhythm of light rather than a blueprint.
64	
65	**A unit changing height.** A new ring forms at the target height and grows stronger as the body climbs to meet it, while the old ring fades over the same span.
66	
67	**Grid, ring, waypoint.** The "grid" is brightness and rhythm: a fast full pulse at 50 percent on the own layer, a slow faint echo at 10 to 20 percent one layer off, a bare shimmer at 5 percent two off. 69	**HUD strip and focus.** Five small ring icons stacked vertically, each animating at its own tier's rhythm; the focused slot beats faster and brighter, the rest slow and soften slightly.
70	
71	**Pulse reveal and fade.** Every hidden layer's rings flash bright and fast for the pulse's duration, then the rhythm slows and brightness bleeds away over the fade window rather than cutting off.
72	
73	**Vertical scale.** Scale is how far a ring travels before fading. In the Settled Reach the rings travel far, matching huge deck gaps; on land they travel a short, tight distance between hillside terraces.
74	
75	**Honors:** grid-around-the-unit as a ring, never a plane; the falloff percentages as brightness and rhythm; the waypoint icon; per-era scale; slight dimming on focus. **Strains:** the brief's named register (AutoCAD, Unreal Engine, 3D visualization tools) is static lattices; a breathing ring keeps the falloff information but trades away the literal lattice look — the option's honest departure and the reason it is wild.
76	
77	**Prior art:** none shipped for layer legibility in this ring-and-rhythm form (none / AMBIGUOUS per the brief's own framing); the general sensor-sweep register appears in naval instrument displays and in strategy games rendering detection rings, such as Nebulous: Fleet Command (REPORTED, general genre knowledge, not independently verified this pass).
78	
79	**Tradeoffs.** Visually distinctive and close to the bible's "elegiac, alive" tone; constant animation across fifty units risks working against "visually quiet," and reads harder for a player who parses color faster than rhythm.
80	
81	Diagram: diagrams/option-c.svg
82	
83	## Option D — Floor Spindle (wild)
84	
85	Every unit plants a thin rod beside itself, threaded with five small discs stacked bottom to top like the five layers of the world. The disc at the unit's own height glows and sits slightly proud of the rod; the rest sit small and dim — a literal floor indicator, read the way a lift's call panel is read. No RTS attaches a persistent physical dial to every unit like this.
86	
87	*A line of units on a ridge looks like a row of tiny five-rung ladders, each with one lit rung at a different height — you read the pattern across the group before resolving any single unit. You toggle one down a layer; its target rung gets an outline and a chevron before anything moves, then the lit disc slides down the rod as the body descends beside it, locked together. You pulse a suspected position; a whole spindle blinks into being, then fades from its top rung down, last light landing on the true home disc.*
88	
89	**Stack at normal distance.** A ridge full of units looks like small five-rung ladders; the spindle is a thin line and five small discs, nothing more, so the terrain stays clear.
90	
91	**A unit changing height.** The lit disc slides up or down the rod to its new rung over the transition time while the body rises alongside it in lockstep.
92	
93	**Grid, ring, waypoint.** The "grid" is the discs' brightness ladder: home disc near 50 percent, neighbors 10 to 20 percent, far discs 5 percent. The waypoint is the target disc gaining an outline and a chevron the moment it's toggled, before it moves — grown out of the existing dial rather than added on top.
94	
95	**HUD strip and focus.** The same five-rung ladder drawn large at the screen edge, shared by the whole army; the focused rung is bright, the rest dim slightly, and clicking a rung is the same gesture as reading one on a unit.
96	
97	**Pulse reveal and fade.** Every hidden unit's spindle appears for the reveal window, then fades from the top rung down, last light landing on the home disc right before it disappears — the fade hints which layer the unit was on.
98	
99	**Vertical scale.** The rod's real height is the whole lever: tall in the Settled Reach so five discs read like an elevator shaft across a huge reach; knee-height on a land era with discs almost touching, since a tall rod on a hillside would read as a mistake.
100	
101	**Honors:** grid-around-the-unit as a literal instrument, never a plane; the waypoint icon grown from the same object; falloff as disc brightness; per-era scale via rod height; slight dimming on the strip. **Strains:** the brief's grid register implies a lattice or plane; a rod with five discs is far sparser than a "grid" — the option's honest departure and the reason it is wild.
102	
103	**Prior art:** no shipped RTS uses a per-unit physical floor indicator like this (none, per the brief's framing); the floor/elevator-panel convention is universal real-world signage, not a game citation (VERIFIED as a real-world convention).
104	
105	**Tradeoffs.** A single-glance read of "what layer, which way," borrowing a convention every player already knows; the extra geometry beside every unit adds real on-screen clutter in a large battle.
106	
107	Diagram: diagrams/option-d.svg
108	
109	## Findings
110	
111	Every fixed constraint in sections 4 and 8 of the brief is honorable by at least one option above; two tensions stay open rather than solved.
112	
113	First, S-010's demand that height "reads as height" assumes a camera oblique enough to show vertical offset, but E-16 R-103-03 fixes the launch camera as the top-down interim. The two-layer prototype already departed from strict top-down (a 60-degree pitch) to clear R-010-03's five-percent bar, and every diagram here assumes a similarly oblique view for the same reason. None of the four options resolves this; each assumes whatever pitch its height rule needs, and the actual answer belongs to the camera options pass (`../camera/`), not this one.
114	
115	Second, the brief's freedom on vertical scale ("large in space, small on land") pulls against "a grid around each unit, never a whole-layer plane." At a space era's largest candidate spacings a tier-to-tier gap can run into the thousands of world units, and a per-unit marker tall enough to visibly bridge that gap starts to look less like a personal instrument and more like a floor plane by sheer size. All four options answer this by sizing each marker to the unit itself rather than stretching it to fill the gap, so it states "here is my layer" without ever drawing the layer — a design choice, not a fully solved constraint: at very large spacing a lone marker can still read as an isolated mark with no visual link to its neighbors.
