# Active Layer Vision Mechanics

## What this brief is

Requested by Westley on 2026-10-01 with his sketch of a targeted ping (select units, choose the ping, press a layer number, click a place, get a very short burst of vision there; free scouts in eras without the technology). It reports what shipped games do. It makes no design recommendation. Feeds register flag `Q-005-03`.

Full report with every source link: `docs/research/reports/Active layer vision mechanics.md`. Gathering notes: `docs/research/research_notes/Active layer vision mechanics/` (three files). Tags: VERIFIED (read in a primary or authoritative source), REPORTED (secondary), ESTIMATED (the notes' own derivation), AMBIGUOUS (sources disagree).

One limit applies to everything below: there is no telemetry, experiment or developer postmortem in the material on whether forcing an action adds depth. Every judgment of depth is a reviewer's, player's or wiki author's opinion.

## 1. Paid reveals: common, exactly priced, thinly praised

- **StarCraft II Scanner Sweep.** 50 energy, any point on the map, radius 13, 12.3 seconds, reveals cloaked and burrowed units. The same 50 energy buys a MULE worth about 225 minerals, so a scan is paid for in income. [VERIFIED on a community wiki] Brood War's Comsat uses the same cost but stores up to four scans. [VERIFIED for cost; duration AMBIGUOUS]
- **Dota 2 Scan.** A team ability: 900 radius, 8 seconds, answers only "is any enemy hero here", no count and no identity, and the enemy is not told. Started on a 4.5 minute cooldown; now two charges at 210 seconds. [VERIFIED for the original; later values REPORTED]
- **Wards (Dota 2, League of Legends).** Placed, persistent vision (a Dota observer ward lasts 360 seconds) with a separate, rewarded game of finding and removing the enemy's. Riot scores both vision provided and vision denied. [VERIFIED]
- **Homeworld Remastered.** The nearest match to the sketch. A passive sensor array became select-and-press: a ping shows enemies for a few seconds. One player called it a downgrade from always-on; no developer reason was found. [REPORTED; numbers AMBIGUOUS]
- **Company of Heroes 2, World in Conflict.** Short recon sweeps bought with a scarce resource. A fan guide calls the CoH2 sweep "lackluster"; a fan summary calls World in Conflict's aerial recon "mostly regarded as a waste of points" because units that scout persistently see more for longer. [VERIFIED and REPORTED as community opinion]
- **Cheap scouts.** None is free in everything. The StarCraft II Changeling costs no minerals, gas or supply but needs an Overseer and its energy; its counter is the opponent noticing it. [REPORTED]

Pattern in the complaints, as the notes read it: a short reveal priced in a scarce resource loses to a persistent scout that does the same job. [ESTIMATED]

## 2. Sensing that gives the sensor away

- **The real rule.** An active sonar pulse reveals the emitter at about twice the range at which it can itself detect; a radar's echo falls with the fourth power of range while an interceptor hears the pulse falling with the square. "Twice" is a rule of thumb. [VERIFIED as stated by Wikipedia; ratio ESTIMATED]
- **Submarine games.** Going active trades secrecy for a fast fix. Cold Waters players: the pinged side gets a bearing line, and "the moment I go active they launch on me". [REPORTED]
- **Fleet games.** Nebulous: "It's either Stealth or detection"; radar off leaks nothing electronic and blinds some missile seekers. HighFleet: radar has graded modes (continuous, single sweep, sector, off) and passive receivers hear a radar at 1.4 to 2 times its range. [REPORTED]
- **Starsector's Active Sensor Burst.** The clearest short, player-triggered burst with a stated cost: a large jump in sensor strength and a larger jump in the fleet's own visibility, a one-day cooldown, the fleet slowed, and hostile fleets come to investigate. Players use it as bait. [VERIFIED on a community wiki]
- **EVE Online.** The free, constant scan does not warn the target; the precise probes are visible to it. [VERIFIED]
- **Supreme Commander, Beyond All Reason.** Intel is split into channels: vision identifies, radar gives unidentified blips that are inaccurate to shoot at, sonar sees underwater, stealth hides from radar and cloak hides from sight. Jammers cost upkeep. [VERIFIED for Beyond All Reason; Supreme Commander REPORTED]

How a scan warns its target differs in every game: a bearing line, a flag on the contact, a visible probe, or the enemy AI coming to look. [ESTIMATED]

## 3. Games with stacked layers

Layers that changed play each came with an explicit rule, a cost and a named counter:

- **The submarine thermal layer.** Which side of the layer you are on decides who can hear you: go below it to hide from a surface ship, above it to hide from a deep submarine. Depth costs noise at speed. Some sensors can be lowered across it. [VERIFIED as player statements; details AMBIGUOUS]
- **Supreme Commander and Beyond All Reason.** Five engine layers in Supreme Commander (seabed, submerged, water, land, air). Each weapon lists which layers it can hit from which layer. Counterplay comes from units that cross layers (torpedo bombers, amphibious tanks) and units that sit where most weapons cannot reach (hovercraft cannot be torpedoed). Sonar is rarer and shorter-ranged than sight. [REPORTED for Supreme Commander; VERIFIED for Beyond All Reason] The water layer went underused in Forged Alliance until it held resources worth fighting over. [VERIFIED, one review]
- **StarCraft II high ground.** Ground units cannot see up a cliff; a low-ground army "can be ambushed and cannot counterattack unless vision is gained" by a flyer, a scan, or a unit on the ledge; firing from above reveals the shooter. [REPORTED]
- **Wargame helicopters.** Three altitudes: high sees and shoots over cover but is easy to spot, low hides behind terrain. Players complain that helicopters drop altitude on their own. [REPORTED]
- **Planetary Annihilation's orbital layer.** Reviewers split between "the strongest system" and a forced layer with tedious transport. Units arriving in orbit cannot act for several seconds, which is the defender's window. [VERIFIED as opinions]

Reasons a layered or 3D battlefield was judged a gimmick [ESTIMATED from a handful of opinions]:

1. The camera and the unit AI absorb the extra axis (Homeworld 3: "it seldom comes up in actual gameplay").
2. Nothing strategic depends on it (Falling Frontier players: a flat map gives chokepoints to work with).
3. The game chooses the altitude for the player (Ancient Space).
4. Using the layer feels like a tax, or the layer holds nothing worth contesting.

Homeworld players disagree on whether the vertical axis matters: "by no means CRITICAL" against "a good player will slip a fleet above or below you". [AMBIGUOUS]

## Gaps

No game found with five stacked layers and a targeted per-layer vision burst, or with free scouts only in eras lacking the technology. No developer statement on any cited change. No case of a shipped game removing an active reveal for being busywork. Many wiki pages were blocked, so a share of the REPORTED items rest on search summaries. Not found: Halo Wars reveal powers, Harpoon altitude rules, usage data on how often players change layer in any game.

The same 50 energy buys a MULE worth about 225 minerals, so a scan is paid for in income. [VERIFIED on a community wiki] Brood War's Comsat uses the same cost but stores up to four scans. [VERIFIED for cost; duration AMBIGUOUS]
- **Dota 2 Scan.** A team ability: 900 radius, 8 seconds, answers only "is any enemy hero here", no count and no identity, and the enemy is not told. Started on a 4.5 minute cooldown; now two charges at 210 seconds. [VERIFIED for the original; later values REPORTED]
- **Wards (Dota 2, League of Legends).** Placed, persistent vision (a Dota observer ward lasts 360 seconds) with a separate, rewarded game of finding and removing the enemy's. Riot scores both vision provided and vision denied. [VERIFIED]
- **Homeworld Remastered.** The nearest match to the sketch. A passive sensor array became select-and-press: a ping shows enemies for a few seconds. One player called it a downgrade from always-on; no developer reason was found. [REPORTED; numbers AMBIGUOUS]
- **Company of Heroes 2, World in Conflict.** Short recon sweeps bought with a scarce resource. A fan guide calls the CoH2 sweep "lackluster"; a fan summary calls World in Conflict's aerial recon "mostly regarded as a waste of points" because units that scout persistently see more for longer. [VERIFIED and REPORTED as community opinion]
- **Cheap scouts.** None is free in everything. The StarCraft II Changeling costs no minerals, gas or supply but needs an Overseer and its energy; its counter is the opponent noticing it. [REPORTED]

Pattern in the complaints, as the notes read it: a short reveal priced in a scarce resource loses to a persistent scout that does the same job. [ESTIMATED]

## 2. Sensing that gives the sensor away

- **The real rule.** An active sonar pulse reveals the emitter at about twice the range at which it can itself detect; a radar's echo falls with the fourth power of range while an interceptor hears the pulse falling with the square. "Twice" is a rule of thumb. [VERIFIED as stated by Wikipedia; ratio ESTIMATED]
- **Submarine games.** Going active trades secrecy for a fast fix. Cold Waters players: the pinged side gets a bearing line, and "the moment I go active they launch on me". [REPORTED]
- **Fleet games.** Nebulous: "It's either Stealth or detection"; radar off leaks nothing electronic and blinds some missile seekers. HighFleet: radar has graded modes (continuous, single sweep, sector, off) and passive receivers hear a radar at 1.4 to 2 times its range. [REPORTED]
- **Starsector's Active Sensor Burst.** The clearest short, player-triggered burst with a stated cost: a large jump in sensor strength and a larger jump in the fleet's own visibility, a one-day cooldown, the fleet slowed, and hostile fleets come to investigate. Players use it as bait. [VERIFIED on a community wiki]
- **EVE Online.** The free, constant scan does not warn the target; the precise probes are visible to it. [VERIFIED]
- **Supreme Commander, Beyond All Reason.** Intel is split into channels: vision identifies, radar gives unidentified blips that are inaccurate to shoot at, sonar sees underwater, stealth hides from radar and cloak hides from sight. Jammers cost upkeep. [VERIFIED for Beyond All Reason; Supreme Commander REPORTED]

How a scan warns its target differs in every game: a bearing line, a flag on the contact, a visible probe, or the enemy AI coming to look. [ESTIMATED]

## 3. Games with stacked layers

Layers that changed play each came with an explicit rule, a cost and a named counter:

- **The submarine thermal layer.** Which side of the layer you are on decides who can hear you: go below it to hide from a surface ship, above it to hide from a deep submarine. Depth costs noise at speed. Some sensors can be lowered across it. [VERIFIED as player statements; details AMBIGUOUS]
- **Supreme Commander and Beyond All Reason.** Five engine layers in Supreme Commander (seabed, submerged, water, land, air). Each weapon lists which layers it can hit from which layer. Counterplay comes from units that cross layers (torpedo bombers, amphibious tanks) and units that sit where most weapons cannot reach (hovercraft cannot be torpedoed). Sonar is rarer and shorter-ranged than sight. [REPORTED for Supreme Commander; VERIFIED for Beyond All Reason] The water layer went underused in Forged Alliance until it held resources worth fighting over. [VERIFIED, one review]
- **StarCraft II high ground.** Ground units cannot see up a cliff; a low-ground army "can be ambushed and cannot counterattack unless vision is gained" by a flyer, a scan, or a unit on the ledge; firing from above reveals the shooter. [REPORTED]
- **Wargame helicopters.** Three altitudes: high sees and shoots over cover but is easy to spot, low hides behind terrain. Players complain that helicopters drop altitude on their own. [REPORTED]
- **Planetary Annihilation's orbital layer.** Reviewers split between "the strongest system" and a forced layer with tedious transport. Units arriving in orbit cannot act for several seconds, which is the defender's window. [VERIFIED as opinions]

Reasons a layered or 3D battlefield was judged a gimmick [ESTIMATED from a handful of opinions]:

1. The camera and the unit AI absorb the extra axis (Homeworld 3: "it seldom comes up in actual gameplay").
2. Nothing strategic depends on it (Falling Frontier players: a flat map gives chokepoints to work with).
3. The game chooses the altitude for the player (Ancient Space).
4. Using the layer feels like a tax, or the layer holds nothing worth contesting.

Homeworld players disagree on whether the vertical axis matters: "by no means CRITICAL" against "a good player will slip a fleet above or below you". [AMBIGUOUS]

## Gaps

No game found with five stacked layers and a targeted per-layer vision burst, or with free scouts only in eras lacking the technology. No developer statement on any cited change. No case of a shipped game removing an active reveal for being busywork. Many wiki pages were blocked, so a share of the REPORTED items rest on search summaries. Not found: Halo Wars reveal powers, Harpoon altitude rules, usage data on how often players change layer in any game.

content.text:
The research is done and pushed (`01b9e58`). The brief is at `docs/research/topics/active_layer_vision_mechanics.md`, and the three options are recorded on flag `Q-005-03` beside your ping.

One caveat first: nobody has measured whether forcing an action adds depth. Every judgment below is a reviewer's or player's opinion.

## What other games do

**Paid reveals are common, and the short ones are not well liked.**
- **StarCraft II's scan:** any point on the map, 12 seconds, paid for in income (the same energy buys about 225 minerals).
- **Dota 2's Scan:** 8 seconds, tells you only "is anyone here", with no count.
- **Homeworld Remastered:** the nearest match to your sketch. It turned an always-on sensor into select-and-ping for a few seconds. One player called it a downgrade.
- **Company of Heroes 2 and World in Conflict:** short recon sweeps, described by players as "lackluster" and a "waste of points".
- **The pattern in the complaints:** a short reveal that costs something scarce loses to a scout that just sits there and watches.

**In naval and fleet games, looking gives you away.**
- An active ping reveals the pinger at roughly twice the range it can see.
- Players choose between seeing and hiding: "It's either Stealth or detection."
- Starsector's sensor burst is used as bait, because it draws enemies to investigate.

**Layers mattered only when they had a rule, a cost and a counter.**
- **Submarine thermal layer:** which side of it you are on decides who can hear you.
- **Supreme Commander:** five layers, and each weapon can only hit certain ones. Units that cross layers are the counters.
- **StarCraft II high ground:** you can't see up a cliff without a spotter, and firing from above reveals you.

**Layers were called a gimmick for four reasons:**
1. The camera and unit AI absorb the extra axis.
2. Nothing strategic depends on it.
3. The game picks the altitude for you.
4. Using the layer feels like a chore.

## What this says about your ping

- **The seer could undercut it.** A persistent scout beating a short burst is exactly the pattern players complained about.
- **It could be click-heavy.** Four other layers times many places is a lot of pinging.
- **It has no counter yet.** In the games where sensing added tension, the target either learned it was being looked at or learned where the looker was.

## Three options beside the ping

**A. Going dark.** Each group chooses to emit or stay silent.
- Emitting: you see other layers at full range, but every layer sees you from far off.
- Silent: you see only your own layer and are hard to see from the others.
- The play is choosing who looks and when: bait with a loud group, ambush with a silent one.
- This also gives your ping a counter: pinging reveals the pinger.

**B. Layer pickets.** You place cheap, lasting sensors on a layer to watch a region, and the enemy hunts them down.
- Vision becomes something both sides fight over.
- Fewer clicks than pinging, and it matches what players preferred in other games.
- Risk: it can turn into a chore of placing and clearing.

**C. Reach by unit type.** Each unit type can only fire at certain layers: some only their own, some upward, some downward.
- The play is composing your army by layer and putting your up-shooters under their down-shooters.
- It covers two of your earlier points: a unit that is good at destroying units above it, and longer-range units being weak to something.
- It adds no new button, so it makes layers distinctive without a "specific action".

These are not exclusive. My lean is your ping plus A, so that looking carries a risk, with C as the answer to "long range should be weak to something". That is my opinion; the call is yours.

## One question your ping raises

Do units still see other layers passively (today's half range one layer away), or are other layers dark unless pinged? Your wording, "players have to actively ping specific layers to see vision on that layer", reads like dark unless pinged. That would replace the current vision rule, so I need you to confirm it.

input.message:
Heads-up from ouroboros-b1 (design chat) on a Westley decision that changes the layer skill (S3) in the lab; committed on main at b8d88c0. K0 and K1 are unaffected. Do not spend effort on the old layer play in K2.

Westley, 2026-10-01 (Q-005-03, closed): the layer system needs actions from the player. He chose three together, all costing no resource:
1. Targeted ping (E-01 S-162): selected units ping a chosen layer at a chosen place and get a very short burst of vision there, at a reach much longer than passive cross-layer vision. The pinged player is alerted and shown a sector of about 60 degrees toward where the ping came from.
2. Going dark (S-163): a force is set to emit or to silent. Emitting sees other layers further and is seen from every layer from further; silent is harder to see from other layers and gives up that extra sight.
3. Reach by unit type (S-164): each unit type fires only at certain layer offsets (own layer, so many up, so many down), in place of one range table for everyone. Longer reach is paid for with a weakness; at least one type fires upward well.
Passive cross-layer vision stays (symmetric), at a shorter range than the ping.

The numbers and edges are open as Q-005-04 with recommended starting values (cooldown as the only limit on the ping; any unit can ping; emit is per group and switches at once; passive factors start at today's 0.50 and 0.20; reach starts as own layer only for Line, one layer either way for Strike, downward only for Siege, plus one type that fires upward well; the S-006 pulse retired in favour of the ping). The lab tunes them.

What this means for the build:
- K2's baseline: run the four other skills (landscape, formation, enemy position, unit-type matchup) and their combinations as planned. Leave the layer slot at its naive default and say so in the profile; the LA/LB/LC tables can still be reported as a reference, but they are no longer the design.
- The engine needs three additions before S3 can be measured: a ping aimed at a layer and place (the scripted pulse_tick is unit-centred and all-layer, so it is not this); an emit or silent state per group that changes sight and visibility; a reach table per unit type. Propose where these go in your SPEC and in which rung (they pair naturally with the K4 order timeline, since a play has to choose when to ping and when to switch state), and report the proposal to Westley before building.
- The 60-degree alert matters to scripted plays only as a trigger ("pinged from that direction"); treat it as a possible K4 trigger, not a display.

Read: docs/bible/epics/E-01-layer-system.md S-162 to S-164; docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/README.md section 4 (the S3 row and the "Decided 2026-10-01" paragraph); research brief docs/research/topics/active_layer_vision_mechanics.md. No reply to me is needed; report to Westley in your chat.

content.text:
The three decisions are recorded and pushed (`b8d88c0`). I also sent the lab chat a heads-up, so it doesn't build the old layer play.

## What was recorded

- **`Q-005-03` is closed** with your words verbatim: the ping, going dark and reach by unit type, all three together, at no resource cost. Layer pickets were not chosen.
- **Three new stories in E-01**, with catalog rows:
  - **S-162, targeted ping:** a chosen layer at a chosen place, a very short burst, much longer reach than passive vision. The pinged player gets an alert and a sector of about 60 degrees toward the source.
  - **S-163, going dark:** a force is set to emit or stay silent. Looking further means being seen from further.
  - **S-164, reach by unit type:** each type fires only at certain layer offsets. Longer reach is paid for with a weakness, and at least one type fires upward well.
- **Passive vision stays**, symmetric, at a shorter range than the ping.
- **The lab's layer skill** is rewritten around the three actions.

## What I left open: `Q-005-04`

Your answer set the kind of each action but not the numbers. I flagged those with starting values for the lab to tune:
- **Ping:** radius, duration and reach. Because it is free, a cooldown is the only limit. Any unit can cast it.
- **Free scouts** for low-tech eras: small, fast, and can be shot.
- **The existing sensor pulse:** I recommended retiring it in favour of the ping. Say if you want both.

Here is the draft. A counter is what the larger side does to pull the skilled play's edge back toward even. Counters marked **later** need units to change orders mid-fight (rung K4).

## S1 Landscape

| Skilled play | Counter |
|---|---|
| Hold a choke | Go around or over it on another layer; or stand outside and outrange it |
| Hold the top of a slope | Take another way up, or fly; or shell the top from below with a type that fires upward |
| Fight from behind tall cover | Get sight first: ping behind the cover, or move to a layer above its height |

## S2 Formation

| Skilled play | Counter |
|---|---|
| Concave | Don't walk into it: stop at the edge of range, or throw the whole force at one horn of the arc |
| Spread to full width | Mass on one end and roll the line up |
| Long-range units behind a screen | Reach the back line from another layer, or send fast units around the screen |

## S3 Layers (the three actions)

| Skilled play | Counter |
|---|---|
| Ping before committing | Use the alert: move after being pinged so the picture is stale (**later**), or show a decoy to be pinged |
| Silent strike force with an emitting decoy | Ping the likely approaches; don't chase the emitter (**later**) |
| Place types where their reach covers the enemy and the enemy's doesn't | Change layer to get out of their reach and into yours; bring the type that fires upward |

## S4 Enemy position

| Skilled play | Counter |
|---|---|
| Scout with a seer | Kill the seer (it has no attack); go silent so it sees less |
| Take the route the enemy isn't watching | Watch more routes with pings; hold a reserve in the middle |
| Bait into a surround | Don't chase, or chase with a small detachment only (**later**) |
| Ambush, holding fire unseen | Ping ahead before advancing; send a vanguard first (**later**) |

## S5 Unit-type matchup

| Skilled play | Counter |
|---|---|
| Line each type up against the type it beats | Mix types evenly so there is no clean matchup; re-shuffle to mirror (**later**; this is your reactive idea) |
| Each type shoots the type it beats first | Keep the targeted type behind a screen |
| Keep the vulnerable type away from its counter | Reach it from another layer, or flank it |

## One pattern worth noticing

Almost every counter is another skill. Landscape is answered with layers, formation with layers or formation, scouting with going dark. That is the "counters have counters" principle from the hub, and it suggests the five skills form a web and not a ladder.

## What I need from you

1. **Corrections.** Which counters are wrong, missing, or too weak?
2. **Does refusing the fight count as a counter?** Against a choke with no way around, the honest answer may be "don't attack". In the lab the larger side is made to attack, so this never shows. In a real mission the objective and the clock would force it.
3. **Must every play have a counter on every map?** Or is it enough that a counter exists on most maps? A choke on a map with no second route has none except outranging it.

## "Mass on one end and roll the line up"

The defender (D) spreads into one wide line so every unit can fire forward. The attacker (A) doesn't meet it head-on. It puts its whole force at one end:

```
D  D  D  D  D  D  D  D  D  D     defender: one wide line of 10

                        A  A  A
                        A  A  A  attacker: everything at the right end
                        A  A
```

Only the two or three defenders at the right end are in range. The rest are too far to fire. The attacker destroys that end with everything it has, then works along the line, always fighting a few defenders at a time. It is the defeat-in-detail idea applied to a formation.

## Recorded (pushed, `5f4fd18`)

- **Plays and counters.** The full table is in the lab doc as §4.1a, marked accepted. I reworded the roll-up counter there so it explains itself.
- **The ping replaces the seer.** Your words are in the register. The earlier "seer as a roster unit" answer is rewritten as superseded. Whether the seer is dropped or kept at a very high cost is left for the lab to test (`Q-005-04`). I told the lab chat not to build the scouting play around the seer.
- **The travel-lanes idea.** It is in the bible as a deferred story, E-17 S-165 ("Later, perhaps: travel lanes"), with flag `Q-165-01`. It is marked as an idea and not a decision. It records lanes sprawling like a tree at 1.3× speed, slowdowns on key strategic ground such as high ground, and 1× everywhere else.

## Two counter questions you didn't answer

"Everything else looks good" may or may not have covered these, so I kept them open:

1. Does refusing the fight count as a counter? Against a choke with no way around, "don't attack" may be the honest answer.
2. Must every play have a counter on every map, or only on most?

## What's next in the plan

Still Stage 1. Remaining questions, in order:

1. **What "beats" means:** wiping the enemy out, or ending ahead by a margin.
2. **Cost or headcount** for the 3× multiple when unit types differ.
3. **Which map families count,** and in what proportion.
4. **Exact bands** for the conditions (the drafts are 1.2 to 1.4 per skill and 3 to 4 for all five).

After that:
- I cross-check the definition against your words and fold it into the bible.
- I write Stage 2, the assessment of the prototype and what the data must show.
- We read the baseline profile when the lab chat delivers it.

My leans on the first two, if you want to settle them quickly:
- **"Beats":** ending ahead by a clear margin, not a wipe-out, because a wipe-out rule rewards chasing down stragglers.
- **The multiple:** by cost, so that five heavy units and five light ones aren't counted as equal.

content.text:
Your four answers are recorded and pushed (`629594a`), and the lab chat has the two that affect its build.

## What was recorded

- **Refusing a fight is a counter.** Your words are in the doc: a skilled player only takes a battle they can win, and makes it so the opponent has no choice.
- **A counter is needed on most maps, not all.** A full surround or a closed trap may have none.
- **"Beats" means ending ahead by a margin,** not a wipe-out.
- **The multiple is by headcount.** To keep that fair, both sides field the same mix of unit types in the same proportions. Otherwise ten heavy units against ten light ones would count as even.

## Question 3, with context: which maps does the lab test on?

A rule set passes only if the skills work across many test maps, not one arena. So the kinds of map in the test set decide the verdict. If every test map is open space, the landscape skill can never show. If every map has a choke, landscape looks stronger than it is.

The lab can build these kinds:
- **Open:** nothing in the way.
- **Obstacles:** blocks and walls to go around or over.
- **Lanes:** a narrow passage between obstacles, which makes a choke.
- **Cover fields:** tall cover that blocks sight.
- **Ramps:** high ground with a slope up. This only matters for walking units.

Your launch era, the Settled Reach, is space, and every unit flies. Ramps and walking don't exist there.

So the question is what the test set should look like:
- **a. Space first.** Open, obstacles, lanes and cover only, tuned for the launch era.
- **b. Everything mixed,** ramps and walkers included.
- **c. Both, reported separately.** A rule set must pass on space maps; land maps are reported but don't block.

My lean is (c).

## Question 4, with context: the pass marks

These are the numbers a rule set has to hit. An example: ten skilled units holding a choke should beat 12 to 14 naive units and lose to 15 or more. That is a band of 1.2 to 1.4 for that skill.

The drafts, following from your "30% per skill":

| Mark | Draft | In plain terms |
|---|---|---|
| One skill alone | 1.2 to 1.4 | beats an army 20 to 40% bigger |
| All five together | 3 to 4 | beats an army three to four times bigger |

content.text:
Both answers are recorded and pushed (`74f2ed1`), and the lab chat has the build changes. Your Q4 answer changed how a rule set is judged, so I rewrote the conditions and need you to confirm them.

## Q3: maps

Recorded as (c), with your point about space:
- **Space maps must pass.** These are open space, obstacles, lanes between obstacles, cover fields, and the five free layers, which are the real terrain of a space fight.
- **Land maps are reported but don't block.** These have ramps and walking units.

## Q4: no fixed worth per skill

You're right that "each skill should be worth 1.3×" was too simple. A wide choke is worth little and a narrow one is worth a lot. The lab doc now says a skill has no fixed worth: a play is worth what it does to the firing count in that situation.

**What the lab tracks for every fight, per side:**
- how many units are able to fire, and for how long (unit-seconds of fire);
- that count through time, window by window.

The ratio between the two sides is the "quality of the choke", or of any other position.

**The two conditions that now carry the weight:**
1. **Skill wins the firing count.** Each skilled play gives its side more units firing, for longer, than the naive side gets.
2. **The result follows the firing count.** A position that lets three times as many units fire should hold about three times the force. If a damage multiplier or raw health decides the fight against the firing count, the rule set fails.

**The rest carry over,** restated in the same terms: skills stack, no skill dominates, no skill is dead, counters exist on most maps, results hold on most test maps, and fights stay readable.

**Your earlier numbers are kept as rough sizes, not pass marks:**
- about 30% more army for one skill in an ordinary situation;
- three times or more with everything used in the best situations. I kept this as a ceiling condition.

Two draft numbers remain: results must hold on 80% of test maps, and a win needs a margin of a few percent.

## What I told the lab chat

Every fight row now carries the firing figures per side. Each profile also gets a plot of result against firing advantage, with the points that fall off the line listed. Those are the cases where some other number decided the fight.

## Confirm before I move on

Does the restated version (conditions 1 and 2 above, with 30% and 3× as rough sizes only) match what you meant?

If yes, Stage 1 is defined. Next I cross-check it against your words, fold it into the bible, and write Stage 2.

input.content:
WESTLEY'S MESSAGES, 2026-10-01, VERBATIM FROM THE DESIGN CHAT (typos are his; do not correct)

[M0, on the lab's measure, before the re-plan]
meausring the margin works, but why does chaning the seed only change the positions and attack timing? My original intent was to shuffle *every* variable, vision, damange, range, literally everything, and find the configurations that lead to the forces winning that align with the pillars/principals we outlined from the beginning

[M1, the re-plan]
Let's re-write the plan correctly this time, but use what was built as a starting point. Stage 1: re-read the original prompt and clearly define the conditions we're looking for. It's something along the lines of "players with better understanding of the landscape, unit formation, layer awareness/intentionality, and the other players current position can defeat a much larger force". The goal is to create a game with significant strategic depth. We get to this goal by tuning all the variables we laid out such that that sentence becomes a reality. However long we need to clearly define that, and bring it down to specifications and think it through thoroughly, I'm ok with that, as I said this is the most important/distinctive part of the game Stage 2: assess the current prototype, clearly define what we're looking for in the data. Before I've just said "lines crossing", but clearly that was too abstract, we need to make it concrete.  stage 3:  modify the prototype accordingly.

[M2, answers to four multiple-choice questions]
Q: How should the lab represent "a player with better understanding"? A: Scripted plays (for each skill a skilled play and a naive play).
Q: What should "a much larger force" mean when a player uses every skill together? A: About 2x.
Q: When both sides play equally well, what should happen? A (typed by Westley): Larger force wins, but this is only if both players have exactly the same units, unit formation, vision, layer organization. Hypothetically this situation would *never* happen in the real game, given there are 5 different layers, different vision, the landscape will be autogenerated and not symmetrical.
Q: Should a single mastered skill be enough to beat a larger force, or should big upsets need skills in combination? A: Combinations (each skill alone gives a modest edge).

[M3]
S2 is not just about more units firing at once, it's also about the rock-paper-scissors, arranging their own rocks agains the enemies scissors, their own paper against the enemies rocks. Yes expand this to an S5, because it's bigger than just a subset of S2. (mark this in memory: after the prototype, if it's successful, I'd like to add a "reactive" aspect, have one team or both actively modify their formation to both try and put their own *rocks* against the enemies *scissors* (example)). - S4 not only shoots first, but induces traps, shoots on purpose with a lesser force to bring the enemies force into a trap (surround or somethign).

[M4, on the band arithmetic; option C was "keep singles at 30% or so and accept full mastery worth 3x or more"]
I like C, but this is abstract and not very functional, and I don't want to have too much of a hard time finding the place where the *lines cross*. I've just had an idea. What if we start the prototype with 2 variables, tune them until the expected behavior is exhibited, and then just keep iteratively adding and tuning until we get to the desired behavoir? I'm ok with implementing two prototypes, one all at once and the other with this strategy and see which one performs better for our goals. - we can move forward with the plan after that's documented

[M5, on the layer skill]
I'm thinking about the layers, and there's a flaw. If both units have the "same" compositions and the vision is constant, both units can just fire back at each other as soon as they see each other if they have the same range. And units with higher range will hypothetically have an advantage but they should be weaker to certain things, thus making the advantage temporary. I think we need to shift our methodology with regards to the layer system. I think that the layer system needs to be *utilized* somehow, not just static. I think we should create like a "rader pinging" system, and players have to actively ping specific layers to see vision on that layer. For eras that don't have technology, we could have them send out little scouts that cost nothing. The player would need to select specific units, select a "ping" ability, press a layer number and click where they want it to go, they'd then recieve a short burst of vision from that region for a very short time. Then the tuning would just become making sure that the *lines cross* when a player effectively uses the pings and swamps a smaller force. - Otherwise your list looks good, but I have a feeling that the layer system won't be distinctive without some specific action from the player. Research similar systems, come back with what other games/systems do, and come up with 2-3 other options other than radar for some way that players can utilize the system to introduce strategic depth.

[M6, after the research; the three options offered beside the ping were: going dark, layer pickets, reach by unit type]
I think we should give players all 3: going dark, reach by unit type, and the pinging. To avoid the dislike for the short scan for money, these options will be free, we want to induce strategic depth. - units will still see others passively, just a shorter range, the pinging can have a much longer range. I'd also like the player being pinged to get an alert that they were pinged, and a ~60 degree direction that they were pinged from (like the direction indicator skill from World of Warships). Record these as decicions, and what's next in the plan after that bunny trail

[M7, after the draft of counters]
"Mass on one end and roll the line up" idk what this means, I can't picture what the formation you're thinking of is. Use a simple text diagram. - I think that the pinging should replace the seer, or make the seer really expensive, the seer kinda makes pinging less useful. record that decision. - Everything else looks good. - I'd like you to mark a potential idea in the bible, not a decision but a potential gamemode. The biome generator creats "lanes" of travel, sprawling like a tree throughout the map. These lanes provide a 1.3x speed increase on troops moving through them. Also slowdowns in key strategic positions/layers like high ground, well thought out. everywhere else is 1x speed. Only an idea, not a decision. - What's next in the plan?

[M8; questions were: does refusing the fight count as a counter; must every play have a counter on every map; 1 what "beats" means; 2 cost or headcount; 3 which map families; 4 exact bands]
Yes refusing a fight counts as a counter, a skilled player only takes a battle that they can win, skilled players make it so that the opponent doesn't have a choice. - must have a counter only on most, some situations are unbeatable (like a full surround or a trap where the door gets closed). 1: ending ahead by a margin 2: headcount 3: I'm confused, not enough context 4: also confused, not enough context

[M9; Q3 option C was "both map sets, reported separately: a rule set must pass on space maps; land maps are reported but don't block"]
Q3: C, space doesn't have ramps but it does have very free layers that can be taken advantage of. Q4: Remember, it depends on the number of units that can get shots, not a basic ratio. We need to capture and track the number of units that are able to get shots off on each side, and compare the about of time and number for both. That will indicate the quality of the choke, not just that they should do *1.3x* better because it's not as simple as that.

[M10, asked whether the restated conditions (skill wins the firing count; the result follows the firing count; 30% and 3x as rough sizes only) match what he meant]
yes it matches, proceed

[42] ## 4. The target: understanding beats numbers (Stage 1, confirmed by Westley 2026-10-01)
[44] Westley, 2026-10-01, verbatim: "players with better understanding of the landscape, unit formation, layer awareness/intentionality, and the other players current position can defeat a much larger force. The goal is to create a game with significant strategic depth. We get to this goal by tuning all the variables we laid out such that that sentence becomes a reality."
[46] This section replaces the four test patterns the lab started with. It was defined with Westley in batches on 2026-10-01; his words are quoted where he ruled. Two numbers remain drafts: the share of maps in C8 and the winning margin. The plan it belongs to has three stages: define the conditions (this section), say concretely what the data must show (§6), then change the prototype (§7).
[58] The first prototype sets each side's arrangement once, by script. A reactive version, where a side re-forms during the fight to keep its rocks on the enemy's scissors, is wanted after the prototype if it succeeds (Westley, 2026-10-01); it is not in this build.
[62] - Every skill together beats a much larger force. First answer: about 2x. Then, on seeing that advantages multiply (five skills at 1.3x each combine to 3.7x), he chose to keep each skill at about 30 percent and accept full mastery worth 3x or more ("I like C").
[66] ### 4.1a Skilled plays and their counters (accepted by Westley, 2026-10-01)
[91] Almost every counter is another skill, which is hub principle 5 (counters have counters). The seer is no longer the scouting tool: the ping replaces it, or it stays only at a very high cost (Westley, 2026-10-01; `Q-005-04`).
[93] Settled 2026-10-01, verbatim: "Yes refusing a fight counts as a counter, a skilled player only takes a battle that they can win, skilled players make it so that the opponent doesn't have a choice. - must have a counter only on most, some situations are unbeatable (like a full surround or a trap where the door gets closed). 1: ending ahead by a margin 2: headcount" So: refusing the fight is a counter, and the mark of skill is leaving the opponent no choice; a play needs a counter on most maps, not all, and a closed 
[99] - **Beating.** The skilled side beats a force when it ends ahead by a margin, not when it wipes the enemy out (Westley, 2026-10-01). The size of the margin that counts is set with the bands.
[100] - **Premium.** Real maps are not symmetric, so a map can favour one start. R0 is the break-even of naive against naive on that map; a skill's premium is R\* / R0. The bands below are judged on the premium.
[102] - **An honest R\*.** A stalemate is not a win, and the larger, naive side always has to attack, or a side that never moves never loses. "Naive" is a ladder: a blob, a line abreast, and a line that holds still; the last isolates the "side that holds still wins" effect found in pass 1. Bands are judged against the line abreast.
[118] | C1 | Skill wins the firing count | each skilled play, where the map offers it, gives its side more units firing for longer than the naive side gets |
[119] | C2 | The result follows the firing count | R\* rises and falls with the firing advantage, situation by situation: a position that lets three times as many units fire holds about three times the force. A rule set where some other number (a damage multiplier, health, raw range) decides the fight against the firing count fails |
[124] | C7 | The ceiling is high | in the best situations, with every skill used, the skilled side beats three times its number or more (Westley's choice on the band arithmetic) |
[128] Rough sizes for orientation, not pass marks: a single skill in an ordinary situation is worth about 30 percent more army; the full set three times or more. Draft numbers still to confirm: the 80 percent in C8, and the winning margin (a few percent of starting strength).
[132] Westley, 2026-10-01, verbatim: "Q3: C, space doesn't have ramps but it does have very free layers that can be taken advantage of." The test set has two parts, reported separately. Space maps (the launch era: every unit flies, no ramps) are the ones a rule set must pass: open space, obstacles to go around or over, lanes between obstacles, cover fields, and above all the five free layers, which are the terrain of a space fight. Land maps (ramps, walking units, ground that exists only on some layers) are measured and 
[138] Settled 2026-10-01, the band arithmetic. Under the square law advantages multiply, so the size of one skill and the size of all five pin each other down. Offered: (a) small singles that multiply to 2x; (b) larger singles that saturate at 2x; (c) singles of about 30 percent and a higher ceiling. Westley: "I like C".
[140] The labels P1 to P4 in §5's tables are the earlier patterns: P1 (layer advantage) is now S3 and S4, P2 (the concave) is S2, P4 (the smaller force) is the target as a whole, and P3 (the protected fragile unit) waits until abilities are in scope.
[268] The first result is the **baseline profile**: the skill profile of today's default rules, under the base table and the three lever tables of §6.3. It says, before anything is tuned, whether each skilled play wins the firing count and whether results follow it. What the runs so far suggest (§8): the layer skill has no edge under vision alone; a concave is worth less than one unit; blindness is worth about one unit and a seer helps only above a sight threshold; the ramp goes from a win to a wipe-out between slope len
[280] What the passes so far say about the starting point, each to be re-measured as a firing advantage: a layer gives nothing under symmetric vision alone (pass 3); reach and damage penalties are steep, decisive within 20 percent (pass 3); a concave is worth less than one unit (pass 4); blindness is worth about one unit (pass 4); the ramp turns from a win to a wipe-out between slope lengths 150 and 200 (pass 4).
[290] | Method | Sample every knob together, measure each sampled rule set's full skill profile, keep the ones that pass, then refine around them | Start with two variables and one skill. Tune until that skill shows the expected behaviour. Add one variable or one skill, tune again, and re-measure everything tuned so far; if an earlier skill has left its band, re-tune the smallest set of knobs that restores it |
[298] The sections below are the record of how the lab got here. §6.1's firing-share measure is now the centre of the conditions (C1 and C2). §6.2's experiments E1 and E2 are confounded as written (the side that holds still wins) and E5 asks a probability question the lab cannot answer; all three are replaced by the skill profile. §6.3's rulings stand.
[416] - R\* by scan, not bisection. Margin is not always monotonic in enemy count, and one fluke win at a high count would inflate a "largest force beaten". The cross-check is done and its findings are fixed (pushed, `bd5c8e9`). The audit table is committed at `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/crosscheck_2026-10-01.md`.

## What the audit found

It compared everything written today against your messages as typed in this chat.

- **Your words (70 statements):** 45 landed cleanly, 11 were weakened, 5 were overstated, and 1 was missing.
- **The written text (118 claims):** 18 were overstated and 9 contradicted something else.
- **Verbatim quotes:** no words were changed, but one quote had been spliced and one was misdated.

## The fixes that matter

- **3× was written as a hard rule.** It appeared as a sacred principle, an acceptance bar and a pass condition. You confirmed it only as a rough size. It now reads "a much larger force; about three times is a rough size to aim at, not a pass mark" in all three places.
- **"Confirmed" and "settled" claimed too much.** You confirmed the restatement around units firing, not every line. Your "I like C" now carries its qualifier, "but this is abstract and not very functional".
- **Two suggestions were written as decisions.** The free scouts ("we could have them send out…") and the upward-firing unit are now marked as proposals.
- **The lab plan had no rung for the three layer actions.** I added one; where it sits is the lab chat's proposal to you.
- **I had a fact backwards.** I kept writing "the side that holds still wins". The run log shows it cuts both ways, and the doc now says so.
- **Your "take as long as it needs" sentence was missing.** It is now quoted with the target.
- **The roll-up diagram** is in the doc with the counters.

## One finding I resolved myself, for you to confirm

The audit pointed out a clash: the conditions judge everything by units firing, but unit-type matchup (your S5) works through damage per hit, not through how many units fire.

I resolved it with your own 2026-09-30 statement that type should be measured, "not just unit values but their type as well". The firing count is now weighted by type, so a unit firing at the type it beats counts for more. The type matchup is treated as the fifth skill, not as "a number overriding position".

Is that the right reading?

## Two items left open in the doc

- **How refusing a fight gets checked.** In the lab the larger side is forced to attack, so refusal can't be played there.
- **Whether abilities ever join the acceptance bar.** They are out for now, per your 2026-09-30 note.

Stages 1 and 2 are now written and audited. Stage 3 is with the lab chat; the next thing for you is its baseline.

content.text:
It is mostly defined, but there are two real gaps. The recording is specified. The reading is specified at three of four levels. What's missing is the pass marks for the conditions and the exact form of the final "lines crossing" picture.

## What gets recorded

| Level | One row per | What it holds |
|---|---|---|
| Fight | single fight | the rule settings, the map, each side's play and headcount, who won, the margin, and each side's unit-seconds of fire |
| Break-even | play × map × rule set | the headcount multiple where the fight is even, and the firing advantage beside it |
| Profile | rule set | the break-even and firing advantage for all 32 skill combinations, across all test maps |
| Search | many rule sets | which conditions each one passes or misses |

## How we read it

**1. One fight.** A replay, plus a chart of how many units each side had firing through time. This is where you judge by eye whether a play looks like skill.

**2. One play on one map.** A curve of margin against enemy headcount. It starts positive and falls as the enemy grows. Where it crosses zero is what that play is worth there.

**3. One rule set: the pillars.** A table with one row per skill, something like this (numbers invented for illustration):

| Skill | Firing advantage | Beats up to |
|---|---|---|
| Landscape (choke) | 1.8× | 1.7× |
| Formation (concave) | 1.1× | 1.1× |
| Layers (ping, dark, reach) | 1.4× | 1.5× |
| Enemy position | 1.3× | 1.2× |
| Unit-type matchup | 1.5× | 1.4× |
| All five | 3.4× | 3.1× |

It comes with one scatter plot: firing advantage across, result up. If the points sit on a line, position is deciding fights. A point far off the line is a fight where some other number decided, and those get listed.

**4. Many rule sets: the lines crossing.** For a pair of knobs, a map showing where each condition holds. Each condition's edge is a line. Where all the regions overlap is the crossing: the settings where every pillar works at once.

## The two gaps

**Gap 1: the conditions have no pass marks.** When you rejected fixed bands, the conditions became statements like "skill wins the firing count" and "the result follows it". They don't yet say by how much. Until they do, a computer can't mark a rule set pass or fail, so the level-4 picture can't be drawn. Missing:
- how much firing advantage counts as "wins" (any, or at least some amount);
- how close the result must sit to the firing line;
- how much a combination must beat its parts by;
- what "noticeably" means for a dead skill;
- how much a counter must take back.

**Gap 2: the final picture isn't specified.** The lab has dozens of knobs, and a map shows only two at a time. Nothing yet says which pairs get drawn or how the passing region is summarised.

A smaller one: "firing advantage" is recorded two ways (overall and window by window), and the doc doesn't pin which single figure goes on the scatter plot.

## Closing them

I can draft the pass marks and the report format for you to correct, the same way we did the plays. The marks would be about how closely results follow firing, not about fixed worth per skill, so they stay consistent with your ruling.

Shall I draft them?

content.text:
Base directory for this skill: /private/tmp/claude-501/bundled-skills/2.1.284/8cdc39a3fffe724f5d4b7eb21406f34e/dataviz

# Data Visualization

A chart is **read by people and executed by you**. This skill turns "make it look
good" into a procedure with checks, so the result is right by construction rather
than by taste.

**The method here is design-system-agnostic.** Nothing in the procedure, the form
heuristic, the six checks, or the mark specs is specific to one product. A design
system supplies a small set of *parameters* (its ramps, a categorical order, a
diverging pair, a status palette, a texture, its surfaces, its filter components);
the method consumes them unchanged. A **validated default palette** is the
reference instance, fully specified in `references/palette.md`. To target your
brand, read that file's structure and substitute its values - touch nothing else.

> The single most important habit: **the color part is computable, so compute it.**
> Never eyeball whether a palette is colorblind-safe - run `scripts/validate_palette.js`.

## The procedure - do these in order

Color comes LAST. Most bad charts pick colors first.

1. **Pick the form.** What is the data's job - magnitude, identity, polarity, a
   single headline, change-over-time? The job picks the chart type, and sometimes
   the answer is *not a chart* (a stat tile or hero number). -> `references/choosing-a-form.md`
2. **Assign color by the job it does.** Categorical (identity), sequential
   (magnitude), diverging (polarity), or status (state) - each has one rule.
   Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled. -> `references/color-formula.md`
3. **VALIDATE the palette - run the script, don't reason about Delta E.**
   `node scripts/validate_palette.js "<hex,hex,...>" --mode light` (relative to
   this skill's base directory - or load it as `<script type="module">` in the
   chart's own page, where it reads
   `data-palette` off `<body>` and logs a `console.table` report). It returns
   pass/fail on the lightness band, chroma floor, adjacent-pair CVD separation,
   the normal-vision floor, and contrast. Fix anything that FAILs before continuing. Re-run for
   `--mode dark` with that mode's surface.
4. **Apply mark specs & spacers.** Thin marks, 4px rounded data-ends anchored to
   the baseline, 2px lines, >=8px markers, a 2px surface gap between fills (stacked
   segments and adjacent bars alike) and a 2px surface ring on overlapping marks,
   selective direct labels. -> `references/marks-and-anatomy.md`
5. **Add the hover layer - by default.** An HTML/SVG chart *is* interactive; ship
   a crosshair+tooltip on line/area and a per-mark hover tooltip on bar/dot/cell.
   The only form that skips it is a bare stat tile with no plot. Hit targets bigger
   than the mark; filters in one row above the charts. -> `references/interaction.md`
6. **Final accessibility pass.** For >= 2 series a legend is always present and <= 4
   are also direct-labeled (a single series needs no legend box - the title names
   it), so identity is never color-alone; a table view exists; dark mode is **selected** - its own
   steps from the same ramps, validated against the dark surface, not an automatic
   flip; texture is available for the CVD/print/forced-colors case.
7. **Render it and look at it.** The validator checks color, not layout - open or
   screenshot the output and eyeball it for label collisions, geometry, and overflow
   before calling it done.

Then check the result against **`references/anti-patterns.md`** - it is the catalog
of what goes wrong. If your chart matches an entry, it's wrong.

## Non-negotiables (true in every design system)

- **Assign categorical hues in fixed order, never cycled.** A 9th series is never a
  generated hue - it folds into "Other," small multiples, or composite encoding.
- **One axis.** Never a dual-axis chart (two y-scales). Two measures of different
  scale -> two charts, small multiples, or indexed to a common base. *(This is the
  #1 chart mistake - see anti-patterns.)*
- **Color follows the entity, never its rank.** A filter that changes the series
  count must not repaint the survivors.
- **Sequential = one hue, light->dark. Diverging = two hues + a neutral gray
  midpoint.** Never a rainbow; never a hue at the diverging midpoint.
- **Run the validator before shipping any categorical palette.** CVD Delta E >= 8 is the
  target (OKLab ×100); 6-8 is a floor that is legal ONLY with secondary encoding. A
  normal-vision floor below 15 is a hard FAIL - full-color readers can't tell the
  pair apart; re-step it on the adjacent pairlist (secondary encoding does not excuse
  this one); under `--pairs all` cut series or facet instead - see check 4. A contrast WARN
  obligates visible labels or a table view - it is not dismissable.
- **Thin marks; a legend always present for >= 2 series (none for one), with
  selective direct labels (never a number on every point); recessive grid/axes.**
- **Text wears text tokens, never the series color** - values, labels, and legends
  stay in primary/secondary/muted ink; a colored mark beside them carries identity.
- **Status colors are reserved** (good/warning/serious/critical) and never reused
  for "series 4"; they ship with an icon + label, never color alone.

## Plugging in a design system

The method is invariant; only these parameters change per system. The reference
instance - every value filled in - is `references/palette.md`.

| Parameter | What the system provides |
|---|---|
| **Ramps** | the hue scales (named steps) the palette draws from |
| **Categorical theme** | the fixed hue order (a named theme); default + alternates |
| **Sequential hue** | the default single hue for magnitude |
| **Diverging pair** | two warm/cool poles + a neutral midpoint |
| **Status palette** | good / warning / serious / critical - steps distinct from categorical |
| **Texture fill** | one directional hand-drawn fill, used at 45° / 135° |
| **Surfaces** | light & dark chart-surface colors (the validator needs these) |
| **Filter controls** | date-range & dimension controls (behavioral spec in `interaction.md`) |

To onboard a new system: fill those rows, feed its ramps to the validator, and let
it snap each slot to the nearest passing step. Structure and rules stay as written.

## Reference files

| File | What it answers |
|------|-----------------|
| `references/choosing-a-form.md` | Which chart type / is it even a chart? |
| `references/color-formula.md` | The four jobs, the six checks, snap-to-passing |
| `references/marks-and-anatomy.md` | Mark specs, spacers, labels, figures, hero number |
| `references/interaction.md` | Tooltips & hover, filters & time ranges |
| `references/components.md` | The pieces a chart is made of - build each in plain HTML |
| `references/anti-patterns.md` | **What goes wrong - check every chart against this** |
| `references/palette.md` | **The reference palette instance** - every parameter, filled in; swap for your brand's |
| `scripts/validate_palette.js` | Runnable six-checks validator (run it; don't eyeball) |
