content.text:
## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font on an off-white ground, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it; always pin an exact version. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — don't build features on them (a screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection); file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers, so take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#key=value` state and never the query string — so deep-link to a tab or section with a bare token and keep all other state in the page.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may animate in, but from a visible resting state, never left at `opacity: 0` waiting for an observer. Size a hero to its content instead of to the viewport; a `100vh` opener pushes the rest of the page out of that first frame. A tool or app opens in a realistic working state: the user's real data where it exists, otherwise example rows, a loaded sample, or a plausibly filled form, clearly marked as examples and never presented as the user's own figures. The first view shows what the tool does; an empty shell waiting for input shows nothing. When those records live in the `db` capability, keep them out of the page source. Its first frame renders before the store answers, so make that frame a designed empty state that names what will appear and how to add the first entry, then fill it from the store. Seed the store through the `ArtifactData` tool (what type instructions call `write_db`) after the first publish: the user's real data, or marked examples for a tool only the user will use. For a store other people will fill with their own entries, seed only what the user gave you or asked for, never invented people or records.

**Avoid AI-generated design.** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. When the user specifies a visual direction, follow it exactly; their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. When nothing is specified, don't use that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly.** Watch for overlapping elements, cascade collisions, and silent font fallbacks. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, and respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. Give every form control a stable `id` (the platform preserves form values, focus, and scroll position across a republish). For generative or decorative graphics, use Canvas or WebGL instead of hand-writing long SVG path data.

**CSS rules.** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificity. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out, e.g. a type-based selector like `.section` and an element-based one like `.cta` both setting padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't undo your spacing unnoticed.

**Writing the copy.** Treat words as design material and never as decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen: name things by what people recognize instead of how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*; they don't manage *webhook config*). Use active voice; a control states exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it, without apologies or vagueness. Prefer specific to clever. Write plainly, the way a knowledgeable person would talk. Avoid mannered devices: asides set off by em-dashes, "not X, but Y" framing, colon-then-reveal sentences, scare quotes around invented labels, and stock phrases such as "worth noting" or "honest caveat". Prefer short, direct sentences over compressed or clever phrasing.

**Name the page like a product; don't caption it.** The `<title>` is the artifact's name in the gallery and the browser tab, and it gives the reader a first impression of the care taken. Give the page a real name: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific to the subject; or, for a page that exists to answer one question, that question itself, which then is the page's name. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Stop at the name; a title that adds its own explanation after a dash or colon reads as generated filler. The name must also identify the page among many: in the gallery it appears beside dozens of other artifacts, and a generic category label that could apply to any of them fails as a name just as an appended explanation does. When a candidate title combines the name with a generic word (a greeting, a category, a page-type label), keep the name; a trim that drops the identifying part and keeps the generic word produces a title that could apply to any page. This rule removes explanations and doesn't require brevity: a multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished, and shortening it further only makes it generic. Put the explanation in the one-sentence publish `description`; the gallery shows it directly under the title.

**Structure is information.** Structural devices (numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels) should encode something true about the content instead of decorating it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but those fit only if the content actually is a sequence, such as a real process or a typed timeline where the order is information the reader needs. Before adding numbered markers or similar devices, check that they actually make sense.

**When the page is a UI (dashboard, tool).** It is scanned and operated instead of read top to bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Put the summary before the detail. Encode state in form as well as in numbers (a pill, a chip, a severity stripe) so that whatever needs attention is visible at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. Interactive elements should look interactive.



## Process

Start from what the viewer should be able to do on the page, in addition to what they will read. If the page should take input, keep what people change for whoever opens it next, show live data, or ask Claude something, load the `artifact-capabilities` skill now and design around what it makes available to this user. A page that is only read doesn't need that.

Before writing the page, settle a short design plan (a compact token system) and write it into the file itself, as the `:root` block at the top of the page's `<style>`, rather than into your reply:
- **Color**: the palette as 4-6 named color tokens.
- **Type**: font tokens for 2+ roles: a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: the layout concept as a one-line comment above the tokens.

Then build the rest of the page from those tokens, deriving every color and type decision from them. The plan is working material, not part of the answer: unless the user asks about the design, one plain sentence on the direction is the most to say about it, with no hex values or font names.

**Write, check once, publish.** Before publishing you may look at the rendered page once, where this session offers a way: one `ArtifactCheck` preview (or the Artifact tool's own `action: "preview"` where there is no separate `ArtifactCheck` tool), or else one screenshot of the local file; if the session offers none of these, skip the look. The preview renders desktop and phone widths in light and dark and lists overflow, colors that ignore the theme, blocked loads and console errors, including a script that fails to parse, so nothing it covers needs a check of your own. The look is optional: if you take it, make one pass of edits for what it shows, without a second look; then publish. For a page that charts real numbers, take the look rather than skip it, and spend it on the chart. A page whose point is logic (dates, money, scoring, parsing) may get one more check before publishing: one run of a pure function on a sample input, or, where no preview ran, one syntax check of its script; nothing more. A page that declares `capabilities` takes the look rather than skipping it, then one functional pass after the first publish, because the preview cannot run that code: read back once what the page stores or serves (one read of its stored data or one read-only route call; where that read alone would prove nothing, as on an empty store, you may first write one probe document yourself and delete it after the read, passing the `version` the write returned as `if_version`; no other test writes unless the user wants one), tell the user in one line what you exercised and what you could not, and stop. None of this becomes a loop, because the user is waiting for a link: no second screenshot, no scripts that probe the DOM, no re-running a check that passed. Review happens on the live page, and further polish is for the user to request; if the user reports something visibly broken (a clipped column, unreadable text, a control that does nothing), fix that, take at most one more look if the session offers a way, and republish once. These checks are for code you wrote into this page, not for content you fill into an Artifact made from an Artifact type (a Slides deck, a Design canvas): there the type's own instructions say whether to check, and if they say nothing, don't.

**Open viewers.** You don't need to do anything for viewers who already have the page open: published changes are delivered to them automatically at their next quiet moment, with state preserved where possible. If your page has state a viewer would miss (a game, a long form), register `window.claude?.hot?.snapshot(...)` and boot through `window.claude?.hot?.ready ? window.claude.hot.ready(start) : start(window.claude?.hot?.data ?? {})`; `hot` is the viewer's own update hook, not a capability behind `claude.use()`, and is absent outside a viewer, hence the `?.`.

## When the request is editorial

The stance changes here: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated decisions, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part in the plan itself, without narrating the revision to the user. Write the code only after the plan is specific to this subject, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero states the thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world (headline, image, live demo, interactive moment). 
- Typography sets the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, avoiding the families you would use on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design instead of a neutral container for the content. 
- Use motion deliberately. Think about whether and where animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. One orchestrated moment is usually more effective than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation adds to the impression that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Put your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent clashes with the background, shift it toward an analogous hue or desaturate it instead of replacing it.

```css
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
```

This is the **reference instance** of the data-viz method: every parameter the
method needs, filled in with a validated default palette. The rest of the skill
is system-agnostic - **to target your brand, substitute this file's values** and

## How to use these values

Everything below is plain hex. In an HTML chart, **define the slots you use as
CSS custom properties in a local `<style>` block** at the top of the file, then
reference them by role throughout - so the light/dark values swap in one place,
and the chart body is written against roles rather than raw hex:

```css
.viz-root {
  color-scheme: light;
  --surface-1:      #fcfcfb;   /* chart surface */
  --text-primary:   #0b0b0b;
  --text-secondary: #52514e;
  --series-1:       #2a78d6;   /* categorical slot 1 */
  /* ...only the roles this chart uses */
}
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) {
  :root:where(:not([data-theme="light"])) .viz-root {
    color-scheme: dark;
    --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
    --text-primary:   #ffffff;
    --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
    --series-1:       #3987e5;
  }
}
:root[data-theme="dark"] .viz-root {
  color-scheme: dark;
  --surface-1:      #1a1a19;
  --text-primary:   #ffffff;
  --text-secondary: #c3c2b7;
  --series-1:       #3987e5;
}
```

content.text:
Charts work: I built a sample page from real lab fights and published it. It is private to you: https://claude.ai/artifact/WtQDNnNZTR8hqx6LpxBaJ2

I haven't seen it rendered. I only checked that its script parses, so tell me if anything looks off.

## How the charts can happen

- **Route:** the lab writes its data rows, a script turns them into one web page of charts, and the page is published as a private link you can open on any device. It works in light and dark, has hover values on every point, and has a table under each chart.
- **Per run:** each lab pass gets one page at a stable link that is updated in place.
- **What the sample shows:** three of the planned charts, from the lab's two control fights:
  - margin against enemy size;
  - units firing through one fight;
  - result against firing advantage.

## What the sample data says

- **Result is smaller than firing advantage.** With 20% more range at 16 units, that side had 1.22× the units firing per head and broke even at 1.09× the enemy. That is close to the square root, which is what the square law predicts. So "the result follows the firing count" should mean a consistent curve, not one-for-one.
- **There is a noise floor.** The mirror fight, which should read exactly 1.0, read between 0.88× and 1.17× on firing advantage. Pass marks have to clear that.

## Draft pass marks

These are about how closely results follow firing, not a fixed worth per skill.

| # | Condition | Draft mark |
|---|---|---|
| C0 | Control | mirrored fight breaks even between 0.9× and 1.1× |
| C1 | Skill wins the firing count | firing advantage of at least 1.2× (clear of the noise floor), on at least 80% of the maps that offer the play |
| C2 | Result follows the firing count | across all plays and maps, results rise with firing advantage (rank agreement of at least 0.8), and no more than 1 fight in 5 sits more than 25% off the trend |
| C3 | Skills stack | a combination beats its best part by at least 5% |
| C4 | No dominant skill | no single skill gives more than 60% of the full set's advantage |
| C5 | No dead skill | removing any one skill from the full set costs at least 10% |
| C6 | Counters | the counter takes back at least half the advantage, on at least 60% of maps |
| C7 | High ceiling | reported, not pass/fail: the best situations, against the rough size of 3× |
| C8 | Robust | C1 to C6 hold on 80% of space maps |
| C9 | Readable | reported, not pass/fail: fight length |
| — | A win | ahead by at least 5% of starting strength |

## Draft report, per rule set

1. **Pillars:** one row per skill, with firing advantage beside the size of enemy it beats, for space and land maps.
2. **Result against firing advantage:** every play and map as a point, with the trend drawn and the off-trend fights listed.
3. **Stacking:** how the advantage grows from one skill to five.
4. **Counters:** each play, bare and countered.
5. **Margin curves:** one small chart per skill.
6. **Exemplar fights:** the firing-through-time chart with a replay.

## Draft report, across rule sets (the lines crossing)

7. **Knob effects:** a grid showing which knob moves which skill.
8. **Pass maps:** two knobs at a time, for the three or four knobs that matter most, with each condition's edge drawn and the overlap shaded.
9. **Passing rule sets and near misses,** with the condition each one missed.

## What I need from you

- Does the sample page read well for you, and is that form what you want?
- Corrections to the pass marks. The ones I'm least sure of are the 1.2× in C1 and the 25% tolerance in C2.

input.prompt:
Research how game-balance and competitive-game data is visualized, in research papers and in industry practice.

Objective: Compile dense, sourced notes on the chart forms used to show (a) which side or unit or strategy beats which, (b) how much an advantage is worth, (c) how balance changes as a design parameter changes, and (d) how results of many automated playtest or simulation runs are presented to a game designer. For each form found, record: what is on each axis or in each cell, what a reader takes from it at a glance, where it was used (paper, talk, tool), and any stated reason the authors or designers chose it. Describe the figures in words precisely enough that someone could redraw them.

Key questions:
- Academic work on automated game balancing and simulation-based playtesting: Jaffe et al. "Evaluating Competitive Game Balance with Restricted Play" (AIIDE 2012); Volz, Rudolph, Naujoks "Demonstrating the Feasibility of Automatic Game Balancing" (GECCO 2016); Zook and Riedl on automatic playtesting; de Mesentier Silva et al. on evolving game heuristics / Hearthstone and Ticket to Ride balance; Holmgard et al. on procedural personas; Preuss et al. on RTS balancing; papers on StarCraft combat outcome prediction (Stanescu, Barriga, Buro; Uriarte and Ontanon) and AlphaStar's figures (payoff matrices, league exploitability, unit composition charts). What figures do they use and what does each show?
- Matchup tables and counter charts: fighting-game matchup charts, unit-versus-unit win-rate heat maps for RTS games (StarCraft II unit tester results, Age of Empires counter charts, Mechabellum or auto-battler matchup grids), rock-paper-scissors payoff matrices. How are they laid out and coloured?
- "How much is X worth" presentations in games: cost-efficiency curves, break-even army size plots, damage-per-second versus effective-health scatter plots, time-to-kill tables, resource-exchange charts used by designers or analysts (GDC talks by Blizzard, Riot, Relic, Uber/Planetary Annihilation; Game Developer articles; well-sourced community analyses with charts).
- Presentations of parameter sweeps to designers: any tool or paper that shows a designer how balance changes as one or two tuning knobs move (heat maps, contour plots, "balance landscapes", slider-linked charts).
- Any stated lessons on what makes such charts readable or unreadable to designers who are not statisticians.

Suggested sources:
- AAAI/AIIDE, IEEE CoG/CIG, FDG, GECCO proceedings; arXiv; DeepMind's AlphaStar Nature paper and blog figures
- GDC Vault talks and their slide decks, Game Developer (gamedeveloper.com), official dev blogs (Riot, Blizzard), Liquipedia and well-known community analysis sites only where they show the chart form
- You cannot see images directly in most cases: rely on figure captions, surrounding text, and descriptions, and say when a description is inferred from a caption

Constraints:
- This feeds the design of a report for a game designer who found a first attempt (a line chart of "margin" against "enemy size as a multiple", and a scatter of "break-even" against "firing advantage") hard to read: he "had to stare at it to figure out what it meant". The data: a deterministic combat simulator; for each scripted "skilled play" and map, the size of enemy force it can beat, and how many units on each side were able to fire over time; later, how those change across many rule settings. input.prompt:
Research how military operations research and combat-simulation studies visualize their results, especially studies that run many small simulated engagements while varying inputs.

Objective: Compile dense, sourced notes on the chart forms used to present combat-model output: who wins, by how much, where the break-even lies, and how that depends on force size, position, sensing and other factors. For each form, record what is on each axis or in each cell, what a reader takes from it at a glance, where it is used, and any stated reason for the choice. Describe figures in words precisely enough to redraw them.

Key questions:
- Lanchester models: the phase-plane or state-space plot (one side's strength on each axis, trajectories of battles, the separatrix or "parity line" dividing who wins); strength-versus-time curves for both sides; force-ratio versus outcome plots; how textbooks and lecture notes (Washburn, Mesterton-Gibbons, Taylor, MacKay, Kress) draw them and what they annotate.
- "Data farming" and agent-based combat simulation (Project Albert, the Naval Postgraduate School SEED Center; Sanchez and Lucas, "Exploring the world of agent-based simulations: simple models, complex analyses" (WSC 2002); Horne and Meyer on data farming; MANA, Pythagoras, ISAAC/EINSTein by Ilachinski): what plots do they use to explore many runs over many factors: main-effects and interaction plots, regression or classification trees, contour and response-surface plots, "fitness landscapes", parallel coordinates, scatterplot matrices, box plots per design point. What do the authors say each is good for, and which do they recommend for briefing decision makers?
- Loss-exchange-ratio and force-exchange-ratio charts; casualty curves; "winning probability versus force ratio" curves (for example the Dupuy Institute's force-ratio tables and charts); break-even or parity curves in two parameters (for example range advantage against numbers).

- Any guidance in this literature on presenting simulation results so that a commander or designer can read them without statistical training.

- Winter Simulation Conference proceedings (informs-sim.org), Naval Postgraduate School Calhoun archive and SEED Center pages (harvest.nps.edu), Military Operations Research journal, MORS publications, RAND reports, DTIC

- The Dupuy Institute blog (dupuyinstitute.org) for force-ratio charts
- You often cannot see images: rely on captions, surrounding text and descriptions, and say when a description is inferred

input.prompt:
Research what the visualization literature says makes a chart readable at a glance for a non-specialist, and which chart forms are recommended for (a) comparing a handful of options on one or two measures and (b) showing how an outcome depends on several tunable parameters, including the region where a set of pass/fail conditions all hold.

Objective: Compile dense, sourced notes that a report designer can apply directly: findings on graphical perception, on explanatory versus exploratory charts, on annotation and titling, and on specific chart forms for parameter studies. For each recommendation, give the source and what evidence backs it (experiment, expert guidance, or convention).

Key questions:
- Graphical perception: Cleveland and McGill (1984) ranking of elementary perceptual tasks (position on a common scale, length, angle, area, colour); Heer and Bostock (2010) crowdsourced replication; what this implies for choosing bars, dots, lines, heat maps. Include accuracy rankings as stated.
- Explanatory versus exploratory graphics; "the title should state the finding" / assertion-evidence; annotation on the chart instead of in a caption; direct labelling instead of legends; plain-language axis labels and concrete units instead of ratios or indices. Sources: Tufte, Few, Cairo, Knaflic ("Storytelling with Data"), Schwabish ("Better Data Visualizations"), Kosara, Borkin et al. (2013, 2016) on memorable and comprehensible visualizations, Hullman on annotation, the Financial Times Visual Vocabulary, Datawrapper's and the UK ONS / Government Analysis Function guidance.
- Evidence on which forms lay readers misread or find hard: scatter plots, log scales, dual axes, ratio axes, heat maps without numbers, box plots, radar charts, small multiples. Include any studies of chart literacy (for example Lee, Kim and Kwon's Visualization Literacy Assessment Test; Boerner et al. on data visualization literacy; Pew Research on scatter plot comprehension).
- Chart forms for "A versus B" comparisons that readers find easy: dot plots, dumbbell / connected dot plots, slope charts, bar charts with a reference line, icon arrays / unit charts (showing counts as rows of icons, used in risk communication: Galesic, Garcia-Retamero, Gigerenzer; Spiegelhalter), bullet graphs (Few).
- Chart forms for parameter studies and sensitivity analysis: tornado diagrams, one-at-a-time sensitivity plots, heat maps and contour plots of two parameters, small multiples for a third, partial dependence and ICE plots, parallel coordinates, Sobol index bar charts, "feasible region" or "viability" plots where several constraints are overlaid and the region satisfying all is shaded (as in engineering design-space or operating-envelope charts, linear programming feasible-region diagrams, phase diagrams). What is said about how readable each is for non-experts?
- Showing time series of two competing quantities (for example two sides' strength over time): line charts with direct labels, difference shading between two lines, stacked or mirrored area ("population pyramid over time", stream of two), and when animation or replay helps or hurts (Tversky, Morrison and Betrancourt 2002 "Animation: can it facilitate?"; Robertson et al. 2008 on animated trend visualization).
- Guidance on using concrete examples, pictures of the situation, or "natural frequencies" alongside abstract numbers so that a reader grasps what a number means.

Suggested sources:
- The original papers (JASA 1984; CHI 2010; IEEE TVCG / InfoVis), books and the authors' own sites and blogs, Datawrapper Academy, FT Visual Vocabulary, UK Government Analysis Function charts guidance, Pew Research
- Sensitivity-analysis and design-of-experiments texts (Saltelli et al.), engineering design-space literature

Constraints:
- This feeds the redesign of a report for a game designer who found a first attempt hard to read: a line chart of "margin" (a signed share, -1 to 1) against "enemy size as a multiple of this side's headcount", a two-line chart of "units able to fire" per five-second window, and a scatter of "break-even multiple" against "firing advantage" with a dashed diagonal. He "had to stare at it to figure out what it meant". The underlying facts are simple statements such as "ten units holding this choke beat thirteen attackers but lose to fourteen" and "they had about twice as many units firing". Report facts and what sources say; do NOT design the report.
- Every claim carries a source (URL or full citation) and one confidence tag: VERIFIED (read in the source), REPORTED (secondary), ESTIMATED (your inference), AMBIGUOUS.

The notes are not a full literature sweep: the web-search tool hit its cap partway through, and many papers were read as abstracts only.

**Findings**
- **Perception:** Heer & Bostock (CHI 2010) text read in full.
  - Their replication preserved the Cleveland–McGill ranking: position beat length significantly.
  - Angle was not worse than length, despite theory predicting it.
  - Rectangular and circular area judgments were about equally accurate.
- **Titles and annotation:**
  - Borkin 2016: description quality 1.90 with titles vs 1.30 without. Observational, and confounded by source type.
  - Ajani 2022: finding-headline plus highlighted data plus annotation gave better recall of the highlighted pattern. Memory tasks only.
  - Kong 2018: title slant changes the message readers take away.
  - UK Analysis Function, Datawrapper and Few: direct labels, plain words, no dual axes. Expert guidance, not experiments.
- **Chart literacy:**
  - Pew 2015 scatterplot item: 63% correct overall, about 50% for high school or less.
  - Galesic 2011: about one third of adults had low graph literacy and low numeracy.
  - VLAT items ranged from 0.15 to 1.0 difficulty.
  - Verma & Fan 2025 (N=503): stacked bars hardest (0.40), histograms easiest (0.83), but chart type explains little of the variation.
  - Romano 2020: log scales reduced understanding.
- **A vs B forms:**
  - Icon array evidence is mixed: Galesic 2009 positive; Ruiz 2013 randomised trial found inferior short-term recall.
  - Few's bullet graph is a documented design with no lay test found.
- **Natural frequencies:** Gigerenzer & Hoffrage 1995, read in full: 46% and 50% Bayesian responses with frequencies vs 16% and 28% with probabilities. Replicated in managers (Hoffrage 2015).
- **Animation:** Robertson 2008: animation was fastest for presentation but error-prone, and the least effective for analysis. Small multiples were more accurate than animation.

**Gaps**
- No lay-reader evidence found for feasible-region, tornado, contour, ICE or Sobol plots.

- Cleveland & McGill's full 1984 ordering was not read. It is quoted from the standard citation and tagged REPORTED; only the position, length, angle and area parts are verified through Heer & Bostock.
- Tversky 2002 could not be retrieved, so I did not cite it from memory.
- Not retrieved: Knaflic, Schwabish, Tufte (original), Cairo (original), Kosara, Saltelli and Spiegelhalter.

**Source-quality warnings**
- Tornado, OAT, Sobol, parallel coordinates, radar and small-multiples entries rest on Wikipedia and are tagged REPORTED.
- Isenberg 2011 "dual-scale charts" is not about dual y-axes. The notes flag that it must not be cited for that.

The notes also contain a few ESTIMATED inferences linking the findings to the three original charts. They do not design the report.</result>

---
name: Charts for Combat Simulation Data
description: How game-balance research, combat-simulation studies and the visualization literature present "who beats whom, by how much, and under which settings", and what is known about charts a non-specialist can read at a glance. Gathered after the first layer lab sample charts proved hard to read.
type: topic_brief
captured_at: 2026-10-01
contributor: Research Lane, queue Q79; three gathering sub-agents, brief written by the main chat from their notes (no separate synthesized report)
---

# Charts for Combat Simulation Data

## What this brief is

Westley, 2026-10-01, on the first sample charts from the layer lab: "it doesn't read well, I had to stare at it to figure out what it meant, research similar data sets and find out how they visualize it, research/scientific papers might be a good source." This brief reports what the sources show. It makes no design recommendation. Notes, with every source link: `docs/research/research_notes/Charts for combat simulation data/` (three files). Tags: VERIFIED (read in the source), REPORTED (secondary), ESTIMATED (inferred, for example from a caption), AMBIGUOUS. The gatherers could not see images; figure descriptions come from captions and surrounding text.

## 1. What makes a chart readable at a glance

- **Counts beat ratios.** Stating a problem in natural frequencies ("10 out of 1,000") instead of probabilities raised correct answers from 16 to 28 percent up to 46 to 50 percent. [VERIFIED, Gigerenzer and Hoffrage 1995; replicated in managers, Hoffrage 2015]
- **Position on a common scale is read most accurately**, ahead of length; angle and area are worse. [VERIFIED via Heer and Bostock 2010, replicating Cleveland and McGill 1984]
- **A title that states the finding helps.** Descriptions of charts were better with titles than without (1.90 against 1.30), though the study was observational. A finding as headline, the relevant data highlighted, and a note on the chart improved recall of the pattern. A title's slant changes what readers take away. [VERIFIED, Borkin 2016; Ajani 2022; Kong 2018]
- **Direct labels, plain words, no dual axes** are expert guidance (UK Analysis Function, Datawrapper, Few), not experiment. [VERIFIED as guidance]
- **Scatter plots and log scales lose readers.** 63 percent of US adults read a scatter plot correctly, about half of those with high school or less. About a third of adults have low graph literacy. Log scales reduced understanding. [VERIFIED, Pew 2015; Galesic 2011; Romano 2020]
- **Small multiples are read more accurately than animation**; animation is quick for presentation and error-prone for analysis. [VERIFIED, Robertson 2008]
- **Icon arrays have mixed evidence.** [VERIFIED, Galesic 2009 positive; Ruiz 2013 negative]
- No lay-reader evidence was found for tornado, contour, feasible-region, ratio-axis or signed-share-axis charts.

## 2. How combat-simulation studies present results

- **Strength against time, one curve per side**, is the standard Lanchester picture. [VERIFIED, Washburn's notes]
- **The phase plane:** one side's strength on each axis, each battle a path, and a straight line (the separatrix) dividing the starts from which each side wins. [VERIFIED by caption, Kress et al.]
- **A map of who wins by two inputs.** Mesterton-Gibbons plots numbers ratio against fighting-ability ratio and shades the regions where each side wins. Sanchez and Lucas plot initial Red size against initial Blue size for a deterministic model and colour by winner; the winner flips back and forth along some lines, non-monotone in 5 of 9 slices, which they trace to chaotic battle paths. [VERIFIED]
- **A decision tree with green, yellow and red leaves** is what the Naval Postgraduate School data-farming group calls "useful for succinctly presenting results to decision-makers"; the briefing version strips the statistics. [VERIFIED, Cioppa, Lucas and Sanchez 2004]
- **Also used by that group:** grids of small interaction plots; contour plots of two factors with a plain-English reading; trellis plots conditioned on a third factor; a table of factors marked significant or not. Their advice: gridded designs are the easiest to explain to non-statisticians, and single runs or sparse samples mislead. [VERIFIED]
- **Force-ratio tables** with a verbal result per band (Dupuy Institute). [REPORTED]

## 3. How game-balance work presents results

- **A table with an "Interpretation" column** beside each row of numbers. [VERIFIED, Jaffe et al. 2012]
- **The same number can mislead in one form and inform in another.** A bar chart of average kills per character would have led designers to weaken the wrong character; the same quantity drawn against player skill fixed it. [VERIFIED, Jaffe dissertation 2013]
- **A band of acceptable balance (45 to 55 percent) drawn on a plane, repeated for three values of one design parameter**, is the closest form found to "how balance moves as a knob moves". [VERIFIED, Jaffe 2013]
- **Matchup grids:** rows against columns, each cell a win rate, coloured on a diverging scale with a neutral middle, rows sorted by strength. Used for skill against skill (Sorochan et al.), for agents (AlphaStar's payoff matrix), and for characters or units (fighting-game and auto-battler community charts, the latter using letter grades for how much health the winner keeps). [VERIFIED and REPORTED]
- The StarCraft combat-prediction papers show accuracy curves and tables only; no break-even or army-size plots were found, and no tool that shows a designer a balance landscape with sliders.

## Gaps

No study tests whether game designers understand any of these forms. Search limits cut all three threads short: the Hughes and Armstrong salvo presentations, GDC balance talks from the large studios, and several standard visualization books were not reached. Several entries on chart types rest on encyclopedia summaries and are tagged REPORTED in the notes.

# Charts for Combat Simulation Data

## What this brief is

Westley, 2026-10-01, on the first sample charts from the layer lab: "it doesn't read well, I had to stare at it to figure out what it meant, research similar data sets and find out how they visualize it, research/scientific papers might be a good source." This brief reports what the sources show. It makes no design recommendation. Notes, with every source link: `docs/research/research_notes/Charts for combat simulation data/` (three files). Tags: VERIFIED (read in the source), REPORTED (secondary), ESTIMATED (inferred, for example from a caption), AMBIGUOUS. The gatherers could not see images; figure descriptions come from captions and surrounding text.

## 1. What makes a chart readable at a glance

- **Counts beat ratios.** Stating a problem in natural frequencies ("10 out of 1,000") instead of probabilities raised correct answers from 16 to 28 percent up to 46 to 50 percent. [VERIFIED, Gigerenzer and Hoffrage 1995; replicated in managers, Hoffrage 2015]
- **Position on a common scale is read most accurately**, ahead of length; angle and area are worse. [VERIFIED via Heer and Bostock 2010, replicating Cleveland and McGill 1984]
- **A title that states the finding helps.** Descriptions of charts were better with titles than without (1.90 against 1.30), though the study was observational. A finding as headline, the relevant data highlighted, and a note on the chart improved recall of the pattern. A title's slant changes what readers take away. [VERIFIED, Borkin 2016; Ajani 2022; Kong 2018]
- **Direct labels, plain words, no dual axes** are expert guidance (UK Analysis Function, Datawrapper, Few), not experiment. [VERIFIED as guidance]
- **Scatter plots and log scales lose readers.** 63 percent of US adults read a scatter plot correctly, about half of those with high school or less. About a third of adults have low graph literacy. Log scales reduced understanding. [VERIFIED, Pew 2015; Galesic 2011; Romano 2020]
- **Small multiples are read more accurately than animation**; animation is quick for presentation and error-prone for analysis. [VERIFIED, Robertson 2008]
- **Icon arrays have mixed evidence.** [VERIFIED, Galesic 2009 positive; Ruiz 2013 negative]
- No lay-reader evidence was found for tornado, contour, feasible-region, ratio-axis or signed-share-axis charts.

## 2. How combat-simulation studies present results

- **Strength against time, one curve per side**, is the standard Lanchester picture. [VERIFIED, Washburn's notes]
- **The phase plane:** one side's strength on each axis, each battle a path, and a straight line (the separatrix) dividing the starts from which each side wins. [VERIFIED by caption, Kress et al.]
- **A map of who wins by two inputs.** Mesterton-Gibbons plots numbers ratio against fighting-ability ratio and shades the regions where each side wins. Sanchez and Lucas plot initial Red size against initial Blue size for a deterministic model and colour by winner; the winner flips back and forth along some lines, non-monotone in 5 of 9 slices, which they trace to chaotic battle paths. [VERIFIED]
- **A decision tree with green, yellow and red leaves** is what the Naval Postgraduate School data-farming group calls "useful for succinctly presenting results to decision-makers"; the briefing version strips the statistics. [VERIFIED, Cioppa, Lucas and Sanchez 2004]
- **Also used by that group:** grids of small interaction plots; contour plots of two factors with a plain-English reading; trellis plots conditioned on a third factor; a table of factors marked significant or not. Their advice: gridded designs are the easiest to explain to non-statisticians, and single runs or sparse samples mislead. [VERIFIED]
- **Force-ratio tables** with a verbal result per band (Dupuy Institute). [REPORTED]

## 3. How game-balance work presents results

- **A table with an "Interpretation" column** beside each row of numbers. [VERIFIED, Jaffe et al. 2012]
- **The same number can mislead in one form and inform in another.** A bar chart of average kills per character would have led designers to weaken the wrong character; the same quantity drawn against player skill fixed it. [VERIFIED, Jaffe dissertation 2013]
- **A band of acceptable balance (45 to 55 percent) drawn on a plane, repeated for three values of one design parameter**, is the closest form found to "how balance moves as a knob moves". [VERIFIED, Jaffe 2013]
- **Matchup grids:** rows against columns, each cell a win rate, coloured on a diverging scale with a neutral middle, rows sorted by strength. Used for skill against skill (Sorochan et al.), for agents (AlphaStar's payoff matrix), and for characters or units (fighting-game and auto-battler community charts, the latter using letter grades for how much health the winner keeps). [VERIFIED and REPORTED]
- The StarCraft combat-prediction papers show accuracy curves and tables only; no break-even or army-size plots were found, and no tool that shows a designer a balance landscape with sliders.

## Gaps

No study tests whether game designers understand any of these forms. Search limits cut all three threads short: the Hughes and Armstrong salvo presentations, GDC balance talks from the large studios, and several standard visualization books were not reached. Several entries on chart types rest on encyclopedia summaries and are tagged REPORTED in the notes.

content.text:
The research is in, and I redrew the sample from it. It is at the same link: https://claude.ai/artifact/WtQDNnNZTR8hqx6LpxBaJ2

As before, I haven't seen it rendered; I only checked that its script parses.

## What the research says

**On reading at a glance:**
- **Counts beat ratios.** In experiments, stating a problem as counts instead of rates roughly doubled or tripled correct answers. "16 units beat 17" reads better than "1.09×".
- **A heading that states the finding helps.** So does putting the note on the chart itself.
- **Scatter plots lose people.** About 63% of adults read one correctly.
- **Position along one shared line is the easiest thing to read.**
- **Small side-by-side charts are read more accurately than animation.**

**How combat-simulation studies show this kind of data:**
- **Strength over time,** one line per side. This is the standard picture.
- **A map of who wins,** with two inputs along the sides and each cell coloured by winner. One study of a deterministic model found the winner flipping back and forth along a line. That is the same trap the lab hit earlier.
- **A decision tree with green, amber and red endings.** The analysts who do "data farming", which is close to your method, recommend it for briefing decision makers.

**How game-balance work shows it:**
- **A table with a plain-words "interpretation" column** beside the numbers.
- **Matchup grids:** rows against columns, coloured blue for win and red for loss, with a neutral middle.
- **A band of acceptable balance drawn on a chart, repeated for three values of a knob.** This is the nearest published form to your "lines crossing".

Nobody has tested whether designers understand any of these forms; that gap is in the brief.

## What I changed in the sample

- **Headings state the finding in soldiers:** "With longer range, 16 units beat 17. Identical sides beat 15."
- **The first chart is now a line of fights.** Each dot is one fight at an enemy size, blue for won and orange for lost. You read along until the colour changes.
- **The firing chart labels each line on the chart** and shades the gap between them.
- **The scatter plot is gone.** It is now a table with a plain-words column.

## What this means for the full report

The same rules would apply throughout: findings in soldiers, labels on the chart, a plain-words column. The "lines crossing" view would be a coloured map of two knobs showing where every condition holds, with small side-by-side maps for a third knob and a short decision-tree summary in words.

The brief is at `docs/research/topics/charts_for_combat_simulation_data.md` (pushed, `18c4ea3`).

Does the second draft read at a glance? If not, tell me which part you still had to stare at.

"""Small batch (design chat, 2026-10-01): a control first, then ONE skill on ONE map family at ONE size, read in soldiers.
Usage: python3 experiments/small_batch.py"""
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from layerlab.skill import controls, plays
from layerlab.skill.rstar import rstar, rstar_windows
from layerlab.skill.situation import sample_situations


def show(title, rs, size):
    print(f"\n{title}")
    print("  enemy heads | skilled margin | skilled firing/head | naive firing/head | firing advantage")
    for p in rs.points:
        print(f"  {round(p['ratio'] * size):>11d} | {p['value']:>+14.3f} | {p['skilled_firing_per_head']:>19.1f} | "
              f"{p['naive_firing_per_head']:>17.1f} | {p['firing_adv'] if p['firing_adv'] is None else round(p['firing_adv'], 2)}")
    if rs.value is not None:
        print(f"  break-even: {size} skilled heads beat {size * rs.last_win:.0f} and lose to {size * rs.first_loss:.0f}"
              f" (R* {rs.value:.3f}, cost ratio {rs.value_cost:.3f}); firing advantage at break-even {rs.firing_adv_at_rstar},"
              f" at equal heads {rs.firing_adv_equal}; valid={rs.valid} label_gap={rs.label_gap:.3f}")
    else:
        print(f"  no break-even: above_scan={rs.above_scan} below_scan={rs.below_scan} short_scan={rs.short_scan} valid={rs.valid}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    size = 8
    m = controls.mirror_control(size, processes=4)
    show(f"CONTROL mirror, {size} v {size} identical raiders, flat: expect break-even 1.0", m, size)
    sit = [s for s in sample_situations(14, 1) if s.family == "flat"][0]
    print(f"\nsituation: family={sit.family} mix={sit.mix} approach={sit.approach_distance:.0f} refusable={sit.refusable}")
    for combo, name in ((frozenset(), "naive vs naive (R0)"), (frozenset({"S2"}), "S2 formation (concave) vs naive")):
        build = plays.build_scenario(sit, combo, size)
        rs = rstar(build, seeds=(0, 1, 2), processes=4)
        show(f"{name}", rs, size)

content.text:
The lab chat sent its small-batch report, and I checked it by re-running its script. The numbers reproduce exactly.

## What it ran

It stopped the big baseline at 32 of 112 tasks, as you told it to. It then ran about 330 fights:
- the mirror control;
- one skill (formation: a concave against a plain line) on one flat map, at 8 units, with long-range units.

## What it found

- **The control passes.** Over 40 fights of 8 identical units against 8, one side won 19 and the other 21. There is no side bias.
- **Noise is about one soldier at this size.** A single fight swings by roughly a quarter of a force on spawn jitter alone.
- **Formation did nothing on this map.** Eight units in a concave beat 7 and lost to 8. The replay shows why: with range-350 units on open ground, all 8 fire in either formation, so the concave can't get more units firing.
- **The earlier 2,933 invalid cells were not a rules problem.** It had rebuilt the library while the run was going.

## Two corrections from my check

- **"The concave is worse than the line" overstates it.** The difference between the two is well inside the noise. The honest reading is "no measurable effect on this map".
- **The "beats N, loses to N+1" line is not reliable yet.** Its scan uses fractional sizes that round to the same headcount. The table shows a loss at 8 or 9 enemy units while the summary says "beat 8 and lose to 10". It found the cause itself: scanning in whole units fixes this.

I sent it both notes.

## What this says about the design

The formation result fits your principle. A concave only matters when range is short compared with the width of the line, so that a straight line leaves some units out of reach. With long-range units in the open, everyone fires anyway.

## Its proposed next step

It proposes three things, in order:
1. Scan in whole units, with 10 or more seeds.
2. Repeat the formation test with short-range units on the same map.
3. Then test landscape on a lane.

That is small and sensible. It is waiting for your approval in its chat.

One housekeeping item: its small-batch script isn't committed yet, and the old baseline data file shows as deleted in its working tree.

"""R*: the enemy-to-skilled headcount ratio at which the skilled side's margin crosses the win margin (SPEC.md
sections 14.1 and 14.5)."""
from dataclasses import dataclass

from ..run import run
from .cost import force_cost
from .fight import run_fights
from .margin import effective_margin

RATIOS = (0.5, 0.7, 0.85, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.7, 2.0, 2.4, 2.9, 3.5, 4.2, 5.0, 6.0, 8.0)
_RERUN_SHIFT = 1000
_TARGET_SCAN = 3.0


@dataclass
def _measure(build, ratios, seeds, processes, lib):
    """Run both labels and every seed at each ratio; a ratio `build` rejects is skipped."""
    jobs, slots, skipped, cost_ratio = [], [], [], {}
    for r in ratios:
        try:
            scns = (build(r, False), build(r, True))
        except ValueError:
            skipped.append(r)
            continue
        cost_ratio[r] = _mean([force_cost(scn, 1 - sk) / force_cost(scn, sk)
                               for sk, scn in zip((0, 1), scns)])
        for swap, scn in zip((False, True), scns):
            for seed in seeds:
                jobs.append((scn, seed))
                slots.append((r, swap))
    results = run_fights(jobs, processes=processes, lib=lib) if jobs else []
    by_ratio = {}
    for (r, swap), fr in zip(slots, results):
        if fr.outcome == "error":
            raise ValueError("fight at ratio %g failed: %s" % (r, fr.error))
        by_ratio.setdefault(r, []).append((swap, fr))
    points = []
    for r, rows in by_ratio.items():
        a = [fr.margin for swap, fr in rows if not swap]
        b = [fr.margin for swap, fr in rows if swap]
        sk_fire = _mean([fr.firing_per_head(int(swap)) for swap, fr in rows])
        nv_fire = _mean([fr.firing_per_head(1 - int(swap)) for swap, fr in rows])
        points.append({
            "ratio": r, "value": (_mean(a) - _mean(b)) / 2.0,
            "margin_A_label": _mean(a), "margin_B_label": _mean(b),
            "n_stalemate": sum(fr.outcome == "stalemate" for _, fr in rows),
            "n_no_contact": sum(not fr.contact for _, fr in rows),
            "cost_ratio": cost_ratio[r],
            "skilled_firing_per_head": sk_fire, "naive_firing_per_head": nv_fire,
            "skilled_alive_ticks": _mean([fr.alive_ticks[int(swap)] for swap, fr in rows]),
            "naive_alive_ticks": _mean([fr.alive_ticks[1 - int(swap)] for swap, fr in rows]),
            "firing_adv": sk_fire / nv_fire if nv_fire else None,
        })
    return points, skipped, len(jobs)


def _solve(build, ratios, seeds, refine, processes, lib, viol_tol, win_margin):

"""Design chat (b1): one skill, one map, one size, whole heads, read in soldiers.
Usage: python3 experiments/b1_scan.py <unit> <skills: - or S2 or S1+S2> <size> <enemy from> <enemy to> [seeds=10] [family=flat]"""
import sys, dataclasses
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
from layerlab.skill import plays
from layerlab.skill.fight import run_fights
from layerlab.skill.situation import sample_situations

def pick(family, unit):
    sit = [s for s in sample_situations(14, 1) if s.family == family][0]
    return dataclasses.replace(sit, mix={unit: 1.0})

def scan(sit, skills, size, heads, seeds, processes=8, config=None, ladder="line"):
    build = plays.build_scenario(sit, skills, size, ladder=ladder, config=config)
    jobs, slots = [], []
    for n in heads:
        for swap in (False, True):
            scn = build(n / size, swap)
            for seed in range(seeds):
                jobs.append((scn, seed)); slots.append((n, swap))
    rows = {}
    for (n, swap), fr in zip(slots, run_fights(jobs, processes=processes)):
        sk = int(swap)
        m = -fr.margin if swap else fr.margin
        rows.setdefault(n, []).append((m, fr.firing_ticks[sk] / max(fr.ticks, 1), fr.firing_ticks[1 - sk] / max(fr.ticks, 1), fr.outcome, fr.ticks))
    return rows

def report(title, size, rows, win=0.05):
    print(f"\n{title}")
    print(f"  {'enemy':>5} | {'won':>7} | {'margin':>7} | avg firing: ours | theirs | {'secs':>5} | stalemates")
    beat = None
    for n in sorted(rows):
        r = rows[n]; k = len(r)
        won = sum(1 for x in r if x[0] > win)
        mm = sum(x[0] for x in r) / k
        print(f"  {n:>5} | {won:>3}/{k:<3} | {mm:>+7.2f} | {sum(x[1] for x in r)/k:>16.1f} | {sum(x[2] for x in r)/k:>6.1f} | {sum(x[4] for x in r)/k/20:>5.0f} | {sum(1 for x in r if x[3]=='stalemate')}")
        if won * 2 > k:
            beat = n
    lose = min((n for n in rows if n > (beat or 0) and sum(1 for x in rows[n] if x[0] > win) * 2 <= len(rows[n])), default=None)
    print(f"  => {size} units beat {beat} and lose to {lose}" if beat else f"  => {size} units beat nothing in this range")
    return beat

if __name__ == "__main__":
    unit, sk, size, lo, hi = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2], int(sys.argv[3]), int(sys.argv[4]), int(sys.argv[5])
    seeds = int(sys.argv[6]) if len(sys.argv) > 6 else 10
    family = sys.argv[7] if len(sys.argv) > 7 else "flat"
    skills = frozenset() if sk == "-" else frozenset(sk.split("+"))
    sit = pick(family, unit)
    report(f"{unit}, {family}, {size} units, play: {'naive line' if not skills else '+'.join(sorted(skills))}", size, scan(sit, skills, size, range(lo, hi + 1), seeds))

content.text:
I've taken over the testing and run the first batch: 1,300 fights in six small steps. The scripts and a run-log entry are pushed.

## What I did

- **Looked at the scripted concave before measuring it.** The lab's "concave" is a wide arc placed halfway to the enemy that then walks in. It is not a curve around the point where the enemy arrives.
- **Switched to short-range units.** The earlier "formation does nothing" result used range-350 units, and at that range every unit fires in any formation.
- **Measured in whole soldiers.** Each cell is 20 fights. A side "beats N" when it wins more than half of them.

## Results: 16 short-range units, open ground, one layer

| Our 16 | Enemy | Beats | Loses to | Units firing at 16 against 16 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| blob | blob | 15 | 16 | 4 against 5 |
| line | line | 15 | 16 | 9 against 9 |
| line | blob | 18 | 19 | 10 against 6 |
| concave | blob | 18 | 19 | 12 against 8 |
| concave | line | 16 | 17 | 8 against 7 |

## What it means

- **Formation is real: worth 3 units in 16 against a blob.** In a blob only about 5 of 16 units fire; in a line about 10 do.
- **Your principle held in every pairing.** The side with more units firing won.
- **The gain comes from being wide, not from being curved.** A plain line does as well as the concave against a blob, and the concave is worth only one unit against a line.
- **There is a reason for that.** With the same unit type on both sides, if my unit can reach yours, yours can reach mine. A curve can't put more of my units in the fight than yours unless your force is deep.
- **So the "naive" line abreast already has most of the formation skill.** That makes the naive play too smart. The real naive player moves in a blob.

## Decisions for you

1. **Should the naive play be the blob, not the line?** I think yes: an unskilled player right-clicks and gets a clump.
2. **What does a concave buy in your game that a line doesn't?** In StarCraft it matters because of focus fire and because the enemy arrives through a gap. On open ground with equal units, the lab says it buys almost nothing. That may be correct and not a bug.

## Things to know

- **One odd reading to chase:** line against line, 16 against 20 and 21 enemies, where the margin steps the wrong way.
- **The lab chat has an unpushed commit** of new tests on this machine. I pushed only my own work.
- **`project.godot` has an uncommitted one-line change** (Godot version 4.7 to 4.6). It blocks pulls on this checkout. I left it alone and pushed around it.

## Next small step

Landscape on a lane: 16 units holding a choke against a larger force, with firing counts. That is the test of your "3× the units that can shoot" statement. I'll run it unless you want one of the two decisions settled first.
