28	Pattern in the complaints, as the notes read it: a short reveal priced in a scarce resource loses to a persistent scout that does the same job. [ESTIMATED]
29	
30	## 2. Sensing that gives the sensor away
31	
32	- **The real rule.** An active sonar pulse reveals the emitter at about twice the range at which it can itself detect; a radar's echo falls with the fourth power of range while an interceptor hears the pulse falling with the square. "Twice" is a rule of thumb. [VERIFIED as stated by Wikipedia; ratio ESTIMATED]
33	- **Submarine games.** Going active trades secrecy for a fast fix. Cold Waters players: the pinged side gets a bearing line, and "the moment I go active they launch on me". [REPORTED]
34	- **Fleet games.** Nebulous: "It's either Stealth or detection"; radar off leaks nothing electronic and blinds some missile seekers. HighFleet: radar has graded modes (continuous, single sweep, sector, off) and passive receivers hear a radar at 1.4 to 2 times its range. [REPORTED]
35	- **Starsector's Active Sensor Burst.** The clearest short, player-triggered burst with a stated cost: a large jump in sensor strength and a larger jump in the fleet's own visibility, a one-day cooldown, the fleet slowed, and hostile fleets come to investigate. Players use it as bait. [VERIFIED on a community wiki]
36	- **EVE Online.** The free, constant scan does not warn the target; the precise probes are visible to it. [VERIFIED]
37	- **Supreme Commander, Beyond All Reason.** Intel is split into channels: vision identifies, radar gives unidentified blips that are inaccurate to shoot at, sonar sees underwater, stealth hides from radar and cloak hides from sight. Jammers cost upkeep. [VERIFIED for Beyond All Reason; Supreme Commander REPORTED]
38	
39	How a scan warns its target differs in every game: a bearing line, a flag on the contact, a visible probe, or the enemy AI coming to look. [ESTIMATED]
40	
41	## 3. Games with stacked layers
42	
43	Layers that changed play each came with an explicit rule, a cost and a named counter:
44	
45	- **The submarine thermal layer.** Which side of the layer you are on decides who can hear you: go below it to hide from a surface ship, above it to hide from a deep submarine. Depth costs noise at speed. Some sensors can be lowered across it. [VERIFIED as player statements; details AMBIGUOUS]
46	- **Supreme Commander and Beyond All Reason.** Five engine layers in Supreme Commander (seabed, submerged, water, land, air). Each weapon lists which layers it can hit from which layer. Counterplay comes from units that cross layers (torpedo bombers, amphibious tanks) and units that sit where most weapons cannot reach (hovercraft cannot be torpedoed). Sonar is rarer and shorter-ranged than sight. [REPORTED for Supreme Commander; VERIFIED for Beyond All Reason] The water layer went underused in Forged Alliance until it held resources worth fighting over. [VERIFIED, one review]
47	- **StarCraft II high ground.** Ground units cannot see up a cliff; a low-ground army "can be ambushed and cannot counterattack unless vision is gained" by a flyer, a scan, or a unit on the ledge; firing from above reveals the shooter. [REPORTED]
48	- **Wargame helicopters.** Three altitudes: high sees and shoots over cover but is easy to spot, low hides behind terrain. Players complain that helicopters drop altitude on their own. [REPORTED]
49	- **Planetary Annihilation's orbital layer.** Reviewers split between "the strongest system" and a forced layer with tedious transport. Units arriving in orbit cannot act for several seconds, which is the defender's window. [VERIFIED as opinions]
50	
51	Reasons a layered or 3D battlefield was judged a gimmick [ESTIMATED from a handful of opinions]:
52	
53	1. The camera and the unit AI absorb the extra axis (Homeworld 3: "it seldom comes up in actual gameplay").
54	2. Nothing strategic depends on it (Falling Frontier players: a flat map gives chokepoints to work with).
55	3. The game chooses the altitude for the player (Ancient Space).
56	4. Using the layer feels like a tax, or the layer holds nothing worth contesting.
57	
58	Homeworld players disagree on whether the vertical axis matters: "by no means CRITICAL" against "a good player will slip a fleet above or below you". [AMBIGUOUS]
59	
60	## Gaps
61	
62	No game found with five stacked layers and a targeted per-layer vision burst, or with free scouts only in eras lacking the technology. No developer statement on any cited change. No case of a shipped game removing an active reveal for being busywork. Many wiki pages were blocked, so a share of the REPORTED items rest on search summaries. Not found: Halo Wars reveal powers, Harpoon altitude rules, usage data on how often players change layer in any game.
63	
</system-reminder>

# Skill lab on the real engine: record the decisions, then measure in small batches

## Context

Two days of work on the layer system produced a toy simulator, three research briefs and many rulings, and ended with a change of instrument. The toy's unit behaviour is not the game's, and results kept turning on that difference (overlapping units in pass 2; held units that never step forward and chasing units that run through a choke in pass 7). On 2026-10-01 the real C sim was compiled on this machine and driven headless: a 16 v 16 fight takes 3 ms, the same as the toy, with the real movement engine and unit rules.

Westley, 2026-10-01: "yes to the real engine, so long as we can accomplish the original goal from the original plan. ... We're looking to tune the different knobs to see the expected result, but not just 'one'. The *lines* can cross in multiple locations, there may be configurations where health/range/vision/ping distance is much higher/lower but the expected behavior is exhibited. This new 'simulator' will do small batches of tests, that produce output that both of us can read (using the visual artifact style you produced and more if the type of data we're looking at changes). Use TDD, manager-mode methods. This is a big conversation with several revlelations and big decisions, we need to condense the main points into the plan and record them to the repo so that they persist for future chats."

So this plan has two jobs: (1) condense what was decided and write it where a future chat will find it; (2) rebuild the measuring instrument on the real engine without losing the goal.

## Part 1. What was decided (the record to persist)

### The goal

"players with better understanding of the landscape, unit formation, layer awareness/intentionality, and the other players current position can defeat a much larger force." (Westley, 2026-10-01.) Reached by tuning every variable until that sentence is true. The original 2026-09-30 prompt asked for a simulator that varies everything an RTS varies, documents how the variables relate, and finds where the "lines cross".

### The principle

- **What decides a fight is how many units on each side can get shots off, and for how long.** ("the differentiator is **can your unit get shots off**", 2026-09-30.) Consistent advantage over the whole fight, not only the opening. Equal numbers firing means an even exchange; the side with more in reserve then outlasts the other.
- **A skill has no fixed worth.** A play is worth what it does to the firing count in that situation ("it's not as simple as that", on a flat 1.3x). About 30 percent for one skill and about 3x for all five are rough sizes, not pass marks.
- **Unit type is the one other factor**: it weights each shot. A number that decides a fight against the firing count (a layer damage multiplier, raw health) is "a number that's off".
- **Lines cross in more than one place.** There may be several different configurations (health, range, vision, ping distance much higher or lower) under which the expected behaviour appears. The search must find and describe each such region, not stop at the first.

### Five skills, their plays and counters

S1 landscape, S2 formation, S3 layers, S4 enemy position (scouting and baiting into traps), S5 unit-type matchup (your rocks on their scissors). Skill is represented by scripted plays, a skilled one and a naive one. The accepted table of plays and counters is in the lab README §4.1a. Refusing a fight is a counter; a play needs a counter on most maps, not all; a sprung trap or full surround may have none. After the prototype, if it works: a reactive version where sides re-form mid-fight.

### The measure

- **Margin**, a signed share of strength left, replaces win rate (combat has no dice).
- **Break-even in whole units**: "16 beat 17 and lose to 18". By headcount, both sides fielding the same unit mix. Beating means ending ahead by a margin, not a wipe-out.
- **Units firing per side through time**, recorded for every fight, and the firing advantage beside every result.
- **Conditions C0 to C9** (README §4.3): control; skill wins the firing count; the result follows the firing count; skills stack; none dominant; none dead; counters on most maps; a high ceiling; robust across maps; fights readable. Draft pass marks exist and are not yet confirmed.
- **Maps**: space maps (every unit flies, five free layers) must pass; land maps (ramps, walkers) are reported.

### How results are read

Small batches, read together, then the next step. Charts in the form approved on 2026-10-01 (sample: https://claude.ai/artifact/WtQDNnNZTR8hqx6LpxBaJ2): the heading states the finding in soldiers; a line of fights by enemy size with won and lost dots and the break-even marked; units firing through the fight with each line labelled; a table with a plain-words column in place of scatter plots. "Lines crossing" is shown as a map of two knobs, shaded where every condition holds.

### Layer rulings (E-01 and the register)

Five layers always. Vision symmetric by layer distance; passive cross-layer vision stays short and the ping reaches far. Three free layer actions: the targeted ping (the pinged side gets an alert and a 60-degree sector), going dark, reach by unit type (S-162 to S-164). The ping replaces the seer, or the seer stays only at a very high cost. No blind fire. Shortest route across layers. Walking and flying units. Slopes: progress is position, cross-over at the midline, a unit is on the layer on its side of it. Abilities out of scope for now. No faster descent in space eras. Deferred ideas: travel lanes (S-165), reactive formations.

### What the toy showed, and why it is being left

- A layer alone gives nothing under symmetric vision; reach and damage penalties are steep.
- Width matters, curvature barely: a line or a concave is worth three units in sixteen against a blob; a concave is worth one against a line.
- Holding a choke gave nothing, for three reasons: walls did not block sight, there was no stance between "never move" and "chase anywhere", and reach is only four unit-widths.
- Results kept depending on the toy's own movement. The real engine has the game's unit rules (E-11 R-087, E-13 R-096) and is as fast.

### Research on file

`docs/research/topics/lanchester_and_combat_theory.md` (square and linear laws; a choke switches between them; defeat in detail; the hidden side's edge is bounded; first strike and staying power; height as initiative), `active_layer_vision_mechanics.md`, `charts_for_combat_simulation_data.md`.

### Lessons about method

Check written text against Westley's actual words. Look at what a scripted play does before measuring it. One skill, one map, one size, then widen. A surprising result is first a question about the instrument.

### Open

Register: `Q-001-05`, `Q-005-04`, `Q-008-02`, `Q-008-03`, `Q-009-02`, `Q-165-01`. Not yet ruled: the draft pass marks; how refusing a fight is checked; whether abilities join the bar. Ruled while planning: every skill is measured against both a blob and a line abreast.

Decisions taken while planning (AskUserQuestion, 2026-10-01): build the engine's gaps into the real engine, in order, measuring as each lands; accept the recommended starting values on `Q-005-04` and `Q-001-05` as provisional so the E-01 stories can be built; discard the stray `project.godot` change; measure every skill against both a blob and a line abreast, side by side; and the work must be portable between this Mac and the Linux machine, which is working on the same repo in parallel.

## Part 2. What the real engine can and cannot do today (inventory, 2026-10-01)

Can: headless fights through the public API (`om_world_new`, `om_unit_spawn`, `om_command_attack_move`, `om_command_group_move`, `om_tactical_step`), the game's own unit rules (acquire, anchor, 200 leash, return fire, flinch), group moves that keep shape, hard collision, unit stats changed at run time through `om_roster_register_custom_unit`, abilities switched off with `om_tactical_disable_abilities`. Fully deterministic. 3 ms for 16 v 16.

Cannot, each a gap against its own bible:

| Gap | Bible rule it misses | Blocks |
|---|---|---|
| No routing: units walk straight; obstacles do not block movement | E-13 R-097-01 | S1 landscape (no choke can exist) |
| Targeting ignores fog and line of sight | E-12 R-093-02, E-01 R-008-04 | S4 enemy position, all vision work |
| No layer changes, slopes, ping, going dark, reach by type; same-layer fire only | E-01 S-002, S-004, S-162 to S-164 | S3 layers |
| Rule numbers are compile-time `#define`s generated from `algorithms.md`; no `-D` override | (none; a tooling gap) | sweeping any knob other than unit stats |
| No hold order; no "can fire" counter; attack cooldown not exposed | (harness works around these) | nothing, with care |
| The first-spawned faction shoots first; no randomness between seeds | (property of the engine) | honest measurement, unless the harness swaps sides and varies positions |
| Root `Makefile` passes `-msse2 -mfpmath=sse` with no architecture check, so it fails on this arm64 Mac | determinism contract names macOS | building here |

So today the real engine supports open-ground, same-layer fights: formation (S2), unit-type matchup (S5) and unit-stat knobs.

## Part 3. The instrument: `scripts/skilllab/` (no engine edits)

A Python package that only calls the production library, beside the existing precedent `scripts/bench_tactical_pipe.py`. Tests in `tests/skilllab/` (outside the fenced `tests/csim/`).

- `engine.py`: builds the library into a scratch directory with flags chosen by architecture (until G0 lands), loads it with ctypes, binds the two dozen calls it needs.
- `fight.py`: `fight(setup, seed) -> FightResult`. Steps the tactical tick; every few ticks reads positions, targets, hp; computes per side the units able to fire (enemy on its layer within its range and `om_combat_can_shoot`), since the engine has no such counter. Returns margin, survivors, the firing series, unit-seconds of fire.
- Honesty built in: every cell runs with the spawn order swapped (the engine gives first shot to the first-spawned side) and with small seeded shifts of position as replicates (the engine has no randomness of its own).
- Reused from the toy, engine-independent, copied not imported: the whole-unit scan and non-increasing fit (`toys/layerlab/layerlab/skill/rstar.py`), headcount shares (`skill/cost.py`), formation geometry (`layerlab/formations.py`), grid and random sampling (`layerlab/sample.py`), CSV rows (`layerlab/batch.py`), the choke arithmetic from pass 7.
- `plays.py`: the naive ladder (blob, line abreast), then skilled plays per skill as the engine comes to support them. Every skill reported against both naive plays.
- `knobs.py`: unit stats through custom roster types (reach, health, damage, interval, speed, sensor); rule numbers through runtime config once G1 lands.
- `report.py`: one HTML page per batch in the approved chart form, published as a private artifact, plus a short run file in the repo.
- Tests first (TDD): the mirror is even after the side swap; twice the numbers wins; a planted reach advantage beats a known number more; the firing count is right on a hand-built case; the same inputs give the same rows; a committed set of result hashes matches on both machines.

Built with the manager-mode-lite method (Westley, 2026-10-01): Sonnet sub-agents for everything, including the shard test writers and the auditors. I write the spec, the contract (`fight`'s types) and a failing umbrella test; a separate Sonnet test-writer writes the per-part failing tests; a Sonnet auditor reviews them before any code; Sonnet implementers write only code; each part is admitted by gates. The model is named on every spawn, as CLAUDE.md requires.

## Part 4. One controls batch, before the engine work

Only the controls run on today's engine: the mirror, twice the numbers, a planted reach advantage. A few hundred fights, one page of charts, one run file. Two purposes: prove the harness reads correctly while the engine is still unchanged, and keep a before-picture to compare against once the engine cascade lands. No skill batches yet; routing, fog-gated targeting and tunable rule numbers would change them all, so they wait (Westley, 2026-10-01).

## Part 5. The engine gaps, built in one cascade (tests first, manager-mode-lite)

One cascade covers G0 to G7 (Westley, 2026-10-01), all Sonnet sub-agents, with shard test writers and auditors. Inside it the steps are waves in dependency order: the header and config contract first, then G2 and G3, then the layer steps G4 to G7. The files it touches are registered in `docs/northstar/plans/push/pieces.toml` first, so the Linux side does not edit them at the same time. If the decomposition comes out above the method's limit of 16 parts in one wave, it is split into waves, not into separate cascades.

| Step | What is built | Stories | Unlocks |
|---|---|---|---|
| G0 | `Makefile` chooses SSE flags only on x86; `.gdignore` in `toys/` and lab result folders | determinism contract | building on both machines |
| G1 | Rule numbers readable and settable at run time (vision factors, leash, collision size, type matrix, later the layer tables), defaults from `om_constants.h` | tooling | every knob sweep beyond unit stats |
| G2 | Solid terrain that blocks movement, sight and fire, and routing around it | E-13 S-097, E-01 S-001 | S1 landscape: chokes |
| G3 | Units acquire and fire only on what they can see | E-12 R-093-02, E-01 R-008-04 | S4 by vision; ambush |
| G4 | Layer changes: the timed transfer, the cross-over rule, shortest route across layers | E-01 S-002, S-004, R-001-05 | S3 begins |
| G5 | Reach by unit type and the cross-layer fire tables | E-01 S-164, S-008 | S3 |
| G6 | Going dark | E-01 S-163 | S3, S4 |
| G7 | The targeted ping and the alert to the pinged side | E-01 S-162 | S3, S4 |

Before G4: close `Q-005-04` and `Q-001-05` with the recommended starting values, marked provisional, every number a runtime setting (Westley's decision above); run the E-01 gate for the stories involved. G2 and G4 are the large ones. Land eras (walkers, slopes) follow the space set.

The toy (`toys/layerlab/`) is frozen as a reference for the layer-action rules it already has. The lab chat is told to stop; the sight-blocking request to it is withdrawn.

## Part 5b. Small batches, on the finished engine

After the cascade lands and the controls batch is re-run against its before-picture. Each batch is a few hundred to a few thousand fights, one page of charts, one run file, read with Westley before the next. One skill, one map, one size, then widen.

1. Formation (S2): blob, line, concave, each against the blob and the line, at 8 and 16 units.
2. Unit-type matchup (S5): lined up against mixed.
3. Landscape (S1): a choke held properly, against the pass 7 arithmetic.
4. Enemy position (S4): sight first, ambush.
5. Layers (S3): reach by type, going dark, the ping.
6. Knobs, one at a time and then in pairs: reach against spacing (the pass 7 question), health against damage (staying power), speed, vision and ping distance. For each skill, record **every** region of settings where it wins the firing count and the result follows, not only the first.
7. Combinations of skills, and the counters.

## Part 6. The search, once the skills can be measured

Both tracks from the lab README: all at once (sample every knob together) and incremental (two variables, tune, add, re-tune). Output: each distinct region of settings where conditions C0 to C9 hold, described in plain words and shown as shaded maps of two knobs at a time; what each near-miss fails. Numbers that survive go to `algorithms.md`, the S-008 rules gain values, `Q-008-02` and `Q-008-03` close.

## Part 7. Two machines, one repo

- **No machine paths.** The harness finds the repo root from its own file; nothing under `/Users/` or `/home/`.
- **Build by architecture.** Until G0, the harness compiles its own copy with the right flags; after G0, plain `make` works on both.
- **Same numbers on both.** A small committed file of result hashes for the control fights; a test compares against it on each machine. A mismatch between arm64 and x86 is a determinism finding to escalate, not to tolerate.
- **Processes.** macOS starts worker processes fresh and Linux forks; every script uses a `__main__` guard and passes plain data to workers (the stdin crash seen on 2026-10-01).
- **Git.** Work lands on `main` in small units. Merge, never rebase. Pull before editing a shared file. Cascade branches and worktrees (`swarm/...`) stay local and are removed when a cascade ends; only the result is pushed.
- **Fewer shared files.** Each lab pass gets its own file under `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/runs/` in place of one long shared log, and the register is edited one row at a time, to keep merges with the Linux side small.
- **Nothing generated is committed**: libraries, result CSVs and pictures, Godot `.import` and `.uid` files.
- **Stale worktrees.** 34 agent worktrees from the toy build sit under `.claude/worktrees/`; removing them is asked of Westley, not done silently.

## Part 0. First: write the record into the repo

1. `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/README.md` becomes a short "start here": Part 1 of this plan, the inventory of Part 2, where everything is. The present long file moves to `history_2026-09-30_to_10-01.md` beside it, with the run log split into `runs/`.
2. E-01 S-008 and the register rows `Q-008-02`, `Q-008-03`, `Q-005-04` and queue row Q76 stop naming the toy as the instrument and name the skill lab on the real engine. `Q-005-04` and `Q-001-05` closed as provisional.
3. Memory: rewrite `project_layer_lab.md` (what the lab is now, where the record is, the two-machine rules); keep the reactive follow-up note.
4. `CLAUDE.md`, "Where things are": one line for the skill lab and its record.
5. Message the lab chat: toy frozen, sight request withdrawn.
6. A cross-check of the new README against Westley's words, as before.

## Order of work

1. Part 0: write the record into the repo.
2. Part 3: build the harness (it compiles its own copy of the library, so it does not wait for G0).
3. Part 4: the one controls batch, read with Westley.
4. Part 5: the engine cascade, G0 to G7 in one.
5. Re-run the controls; then Part 5b, the small batches, Westley reading each.
6. Part 6: the search.

Westley runs once, since the guard blocks me from discarding files: `git restore project.godot`.

## Files

- New: `scripts/skilllab/{engine,fight,plays,knobs,scan,sample,report}.py`, `tests/skilllab/`, `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/runs/`, `history_2026-09-30_to_10-01.md`.
- Rewritten: `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/README.md`; memory `project_layer_lab.md`.
- Edited: `docs/bible/epics/E-01-layer-system.md`, `docs/northstar/ambiguity_register.md`, `docs/research_lane_queue.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/northstar/plans/push/pieces.toml`, `Makefile` (G0).
- Engine, per step G1 to G7: `csrc/ouroboros_sim.h` and `docs/northstar/spec_factory/signatures.toml` (contract pieces), `csrc/unit.c`, `csrc/tactical_move.c`, `csrc/fog.c`, `csrc/tactical_mapgen.c`, new tests under `tests/csim/`.

## Verification

- Part 0: a fresh chat given only the new README and memory can state the goal, the principle, the measure and the next step; the cross-check finds no unsourced claims.
- Harness: its tests pass on the Mac and on Linux with the same result hashes; the mirror control is even after the side swap; a 16 v 16 scan of twenty enemy sizes runs in seconds.
- Each batch: a published page Westley can read at a glance, and a run file.
- Each engine step: its tests were red before and are green after; the existing `tests/csim` suite does not regress; O0 and O2 builds agree; the lab batch it unlocks runs.

The ping replaces the seer, or the seer stays only at a very high cost. No blind fire. Shortest route across layers. Walking and flying units. Slopes: progress is position, cross-over at the midline, a unit is on the layer on its side of it. Abilities out of scope for now. No faster descent in space eras. Deferred ideas: travel lanes (S-165), reactive formations.

### What the toy showed, and why it is being left

- A layer alone gives nothing under symmetric vision; reach and damage penalties are steep.
- Width matters, curvature barely: a line or a concave is worth three units in sixteen against a blob; a concave is worth one against a line.
- Holding a choke gave nothing, for three reasons: walls did not block sight, there was no stance between "never move" and "chase anywhere", and reach is only four unit-widths.
- Results kept depending on the toy's own movement. The real engine has the game's unit rules (E-11 R-087, E-13 R-096) and is as fast.

### Research on file

`docs/research/topics/lanchester_and_combat_theory.md` (square and linear laws; a choke switches between them; defeat in detail; the hidden side's edge is bounded; first strike and staying power; height as initiative), `active_layer_vision_mechanics.md`, `charts_for_combat_simulation_data.md`.

### Lessons about method

Check written text against Westley's actual words. Look at what a scripted play does before measuring it. One skill, one map, one size, then widen. A surprising result is first a question about the instrument.

### Open

Register: `Q-001-05`, `Q-005-04`, `Q-008-02`, `Q-008-03`, `Q-009-02`, `Q-165-01`. Not yet ruled: the draft pass marks; how refusing a fight is checked; whether abilities join the bar. Ruled while planning: every skill is measured against both a blob and a line abreast.

Decisions taken while planning (AskUserQuestion, 2026-10-01): build the engine's gaps into the real engine, in order, measuring as each lands; accept the recommended starting values on `Q-005-04` and `Q-001-05` as provisional so the E-01 stories can be built; discard the stray `project.godot` change; measure every skill against both a blob and a line abreast, side by side; and the work must be portable between this Mac and the Linux machine, which is working on the same repo in parallel.

## Part 2. What the real engine can and cannot do today (inventory, 2026-10-01)

Can: headless fights through the public API (`om_world_new`, `om_unit_spawn`, `om_command_attack_move`, `om_command_group_move`, `om_tactical_step`), the game's own unit rules (acquire, anchor, 200 leash, return fire, flinch), group moves that keep shape, hard collision, unit stats changed at run time through `om_roster_register_custom_unit`, abilities switched off with `om_tactical_disable_abilities`. Fully deterministic. 3 ms for 16 v 16.

Cannot, each a gap against its own bible:

| Gap | Bible rule it misses | Blocks |
|---|---|---|
| No routing: units walk straight; obstacles do not block movement | E-13 R-097-01 | S1 landscape (no choke can exist) |
| Targeting ignores fog and line of sight | E-12 R-093-02, E-01 R-008-04 | S4 enemy position, all vision work |
| No layer changes, slopes, ping, going dark, reach by type; same-layer fire only | E-01 S-002, S-004, S-162 to S-164 | S3 layers |
| Rule numbers are compile-time `#define`s generated from `algorithms.md`; no `-D` override | (none; a tooling gap) | sweeping any knob other than unit stats |
| No hold order; no "can fire" counter; attack cooldown not exposed | (harness works around these) | nothing, with care |
| The first-spawned faction shoots first; no randomness between seeds | (property of the engine) | honest measurement, unless the harness swaps sides and varies positions |
| Root `Makefile` passes `-msse2 -mfpmath=sse` with no architecture check, so it fails on this arm64 Mac | determinism contract names macOS | building here |

So today the real engine supports open-ground, same-layer fights: formation (S2), unit-type matchup (S5) and unit-stat knobs.

## Part 3. The instrument: `scripts/skilllab/` (no engine edits)

A Python package that only calls the production library, beside the existing precedent `scripts/bench_tactical_pipe.py`. Tests in `tests/skilllab/` (outside the fenced `tests/csim/`).

- `engine.py`: builds the library into a scratch directory with flags chosen by architecture (until G0 lands), loads it with ctypes, binds the two dozen calls it needs.
- `fight.py`: `fight(setup, seed) -> FightResult`. Steps the tactical tick; every few ticks reads positions, targets, hp; computes per side the units able to fire (enemy on its layer within its range and `om_combat_can_shoot`), since the engine has no such counter. Returns margin, survivors, the firing series, unit-seconds of fire.
- Honesty built in: every cell runs with the spawn order swapped (the engine gives first shot to the first-spawned side) and with small seeded shifts of position as replicates (the engine has no randomness of its own).
- Reused from the toy, engine-independent, copied not imported: the whole-unit scan and non-increasing fit (`toys/layerlab/layerlab/skill/rstar.py`), headcount shares (`skill/cost.py`), formation geometry (`layerlab/formations.py`), grid and random sampling (`layerlab/sample.py`), CSV rows (`layerlab/batch.py`), the choke arithmetic from pass 7.
- `plays.py`: the naive ladder (blob, line abreast), then skilled plays per skill as the engine comes to support them. Every skill reported against both naive plays.
- `knobs.py`: unit stats through custom roster types (reach, health, damage, interval, speed, sensor); rule numbers through runtime config once G1 lands.
- `report.py`: one HTML page per batch in the approved chart form, published as a private artifact, plus a short run file in the repo.
- Tests first (TDD): the mirror is even after the side swap; twice the numbers wins; a planted reach advantage beats a known number more; the firing count is right on a hand-built case; the same inputs give the same rows; a committed set of result hashes matches on both machines.

Built with the manager-mode-lite method (Westley, 2026-10-01): Sonnet sub-agents for everything, including the shard test writers and the auditors. I write the spec, the contract (`fight`'s types) and a failing umbrella test; a separate Sonnet test-writer writes the per-part failing tests; a Sonnet auditor reviews them before any code; Sonnet implementers write only code; each part is admitted by gates. The model is named on every spawn, as CLAUDE.md requires.

## Part 4. One controls batch, before the engine work

Only the controls run on today's engine: the mirror, twice the numbers, a planted reach advantage. A few hundred fights, one page of charts, one run file. Two purposes: prove the harness reads correctly while the engine is still unchanged, and keep a before-picture to compare against once the engine cascade lands. No skill batches yet; routing, fog-gated targeting and tunable rule numbers would change them all, so they wait (Westley, 2026-10-01).

## Part 5. The engine gaps, built in one cascade (tests first, manager-mode-lite)

One cascade covers G0 to G7 (Westley, 2026-10-01), all Sonnet sub-agents, with shard test writers and auditors. Inside it the steps are waves in dependency order: the header and config contract first, then G2 and G3, then the layer steps G4 to G7. The files it touches are registered in `docs/northstar/plans/push/pieces.toml` first, so the Linux side does not edit them at the same time. If the decomposition comes out above the method's limit of 16 parts in one wave, it is split into waves, not into separate cascades.

| Step | What is built | Stories | Unlocks |
|---|---|---|---|
| G0 | `Makefile` chooses SSE flags only on x86; `.gdignore` in `toys/` and lab result folders | determinism contract | building on both machines |
| G1 | Rule numbers readable and settable at run time (vision factors, leash, collision size, type matrix, later the layer tables), defaults from `om_constants.h` | tooling | every knob sweep beyond unit stats |
| G2 | Solid terrain that blocks movement, sight and fire, and routing around it | E-13 S-097, E-01 S-001 | S1 landscape: chokes |
| G3 | Units acquire and fire only on what they can see | E-12 R-093-02, E-01 R-008-04 | S4 by vision; ambush |
| G4 | Layer changes: the timed transfer, the cross-over rule, shortest route across layers | E-01 S-002, S-004, R-001-05 | S3 begins |
| G5 | Reach by unit type and the cross-layer fire tables | E-01 S-164, S-008 | S3 |
| G6 | Going dark | E-01 S-163 | S3, S4 |
| G7 | The targeted ping and the alert to the pinged side | E-01 S-162 | S3, S4 |

Before G4: close `Q-005-04` and `Q-001-05` with the recommended starting values, marked provisional, every number a runtime setting (Westley's decision above); run the E-01 gate for the stories involved. G2 and G4 are the large ones. Land eras (walkers, slopes) follow the space set.

The toy (`toys/layerlab/`) is frozen as a reference for the layer-action rules it already has. The lab chat is told to stop; the sight-blocking request to it is withdrawn.

## Part 5b. Small batches, on the finished engine

After the cascade lands and the controls batch is re-run against its before-picture. Each batch is a few hundred to a few thousand fights, one page of charts, one run file, read with Westley before the next. One skill, one map, one size, then widen.

1. Formation (S2): blob, line, concave, each against the blob and the line, at 8 and 16 units.
2. Unit-type matchup (S5): lined up against mixed.
3. Landscape (S1): a choke held properly, against the pass 7 arithmetic.
4. Enemy position (S4): sight first, ambush.
5. Layers (S3): reach by type, going dark, the ping.
6. Knobs, one at a time and then in pairs: reach against spacing (the pass 7 question), health against damage (staying power), speed, vision and ping distance. For each skill, record **every** region of settings where it wins the firing count and the result follows, not only the first.
7. Combinations of skills, and the counters.

## Part 6. The search, once the skills can be measured

Both tracks from the lab README: all at once (sample every knob together) and incremental (two variables, tune, add, re-tune). Output: each distinct region of settings where conditions C0 to C9 hold, described in plain words and shown as shaded maps of two knobs at a time; what each near-miss fails. Numbers that survive go to `algorithms.md`, the S-008 rules gain values, `Q-008-02` and `Q-008-03` close.

## Part 7. Two machines, one repo

- **No machine paths.** The harness finds the repo root from its own file; nothing under `/Users/` or `/home/`.
- **Build by architecture.** Until G0, the harness compiles its own copy with the right flags; after G0, plain `make` works on both.
- **Same numbers on both.** A small committed file of result hashes for the control fights; a test compares against it on each machine. A mismatch between arm64 and x86 is a determinism finding to escalate, not to tolerate.
- **Processes.** macOS starts worker processes fresh and Linux forks; every script uses a `__main__` guard and passes plain data to workers (the stdin crash seen on 2026-10-01).
- **Git.** Work lands on `main` in small units. Merge, never rebase. Pull before editing a shared file. Cascade branches and worktrees (`swarm/...`) stay local and are removed when a cascade ends; only the result is pushed.
- **Fewer shared files.** Each lab pass gets its own file under `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/runs/` in place of one long shared log, and the register is edited one row at a time, to keep merges with the Linux side small.
- **Nothing generated is committed**: libraries, result CSVs and pictures, Godot `.import` and `.uid` files.
- **Stale worktrees.** 34 agent worktrees from the toy build sit under `.claude/worktrees/`; removing them is asked of Westley, not done silently.

## Part 0. First: write the record into the repo

1. `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/README.md` becomes a short "start here": Part 1 of this plan, the inventory of Part 2, where everything is. The present long file moves to `history_2026-09-30_to_10-01.md` beside it, with the run log split into `runs/`.
2. E-01 S-008 and the register rows `Q-008-02`, `Q-008-03`, `Q-005-04` and queue row Q76 stop naming the toy as the instrument and name the skill lab on the real engine. `Q-005-04` and `Q-001-05` closed as provisional.
3. Memory: rewrite `project_layer_lab.md` (what the lab is now, where the record is, the two-machine rules); keep the reactive follow-up note.
4. `CLAUDE.md`, "Where things are": one line for the skill lab and its record.
5. Message the lab chat: toy frozen, sight request withdrawn.
6. A cross-check of the new README against Westley's words, as before.

## Order of work

1. Part 0: write the record into the repo.
2. Part 3: build the harness (it compiles its own copy of the library, so it does not wait for G0).
3. Part 4: the one controls batch, read with Westley.
4. Part 5: the engine cascade, G0 to G7 in one.
5. Re-run the controls; then Part 5b, the small batches, Westley reading each.
6. Part 6: the search.

Westley runs once, since the guard blocks me from discarding files: `git restore project.godot`.

## Files

- New: `scripts/skilllab/{engine,fight,plays,knobs,scan,sample,report}.py`, `tests/skilllab/`, `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/runs/`, `history_2026-09-30_to_10-01.md`.
- Rewritten: `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/README.md`; memory `project_layer_lab.md`.
- Edited: `docs/bible/epics/E-01-layer-system.md`, `docs/northstar/ambiguity_register.md`, `docs/research_lane_queue.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `docs/northstar/plans/push/pieces.toml`, `Makefile` (G0).
- Engine, per step G1 to G7: `csrc/ouroboros_sim.h` and `docs/northstar/spec_factory/signatures.toml` (contract pieces), `csrc/unit.c`, `csrc/tactical_move.c`, `csrc/fog.c`, `csrc/tactical_mapgen.c`, new tests under `tests/csim/`.

## Verification

- Part 0: a fresh chat given only the new README and memory can state the goal, the principle, the measure and the next step; the cross-check finds no unsourced claims.
- Harness: its tests pass on the Mac and on Linux with the same result hashes; the mirror control is even after the side swap; a 16 v 16 scan of twenty enemy sizes runs in seconds.
- Each batch: a published page Westley can read at a glance, and a run file.
- Each engine step: its tests were red before and are green after; the existing `tests/csim` suite does not regress; O0 and O2 builds agree; the lab batch it unlocks runs.


If this plan is relevant to the current work and not already complete, continue working on it.
</system-reminder>

skills.name: artifact-design
skills.content:
## Page contract — read before your first publish

These are the Artifact tool's own rules for the file you publish; the design guidance below builds on them.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Skeleton**: The file is wrapped in a `<!doctype html>…<head>…</head><body>` skeleton at publish time, so write the page content directly — no `<!DOCTYPE>`, `<html>`, `<head>`, or `<body>` tags of your own. Its head carries only a charset and viewport meta (with `viewport-fit=cover`) plus a small reset — light `color-scheme`, `:root` padded top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets, zero body margin with a 14px system font on an off-white ground, `img{max-width:100%}`, and `[hidden]{display:none!important}` (toggle visibility with `el.hidden`, not `style.display`) — so put your own `<title>` and `<style>` at the top of the file. Keep the `:root` padding: a bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding, and a sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)`, not `0`.

**Title**: Put a `<title>` at the top of the HTML; only the first 8KB of the file is scanned for it. It is the artifact's name in the browser tab and the gallery, so write a name, not a summary: a short noun phrase, typically two to four words, specific enough to pick this page out among many, the way an app or a document is named. When the user already has a specific name for the thing, use that name for the title rather than coining a new one. Never use a generic category label alone, and never append an explainer after a dash or colon. If you shorten a title that pairs the name with a generic word, keep the name, not the generic word. A multi-word title that already reads as one specific name is finished; do not shorten it further. The explanation goes in the one-sentence `description` parameter, which becomes the gallery card's subtitle. The `title` parameter fills in only when an HTML file has no `<title>` tag (Markdown pages keep their filename). Keep the title stable across redeploys.

**External resources — CDN allowlist (CSP-enforced)**: external scripts load ONLY from https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, https://unpkg.com, https://cdn.tailwindcss.com (Tailwind's play-CDN script) and https://code.jquery.com; external stylesheets ONLY from https://fonts.googleapis.com, with the font files they pull from https://fonts.gstatic.com (give every face a real fallback stack). Everything else is blocked, with no visible error: every other host (esm.sh included) and, even on those CDNs, anything but a script — stylesheets, images, media, fetch/XHR/WebSocket, a library's runtime fetches. So inline all other CSS and JS and embed assets as data: URIs. **How to load a library**: `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/<lib>/<exact version>/<file>">` — pick the UMD build, which defines a global (e.g. react/18.3.1/umd/react.production.min.js, then react-dom) — placed BEFORE any inline `<script>` that uses it; always pin an exact version. The viewer's sandbox also blocks any download the page starts itself — `<a download>` links (data:/blob: hrefs included) and script-driven saves are inert for viewers — so never offer a file through a plain link. Links to other websites (`https://…`) open in a new tab, but email, phone and app links (`mailto:`, `tel:`, `sms:`, other custom schemes) are unreliable inside an artifact: for many viewers (for example anyone outside the user's organization, or anyone viewing through a public link) following one, by link or by script, often does not work, and the page cannot tell whether it did. So show the address or number itself as selectable text (a copy button helps), treat such a link as a convenience that may do nothing, and never tell the viewer a message was sent or a call placed because the viewer tapped one. Artifacts render mermaid diagrams natively — markdown via ```mermaid fences, HTML via `<pre class="mermaid">` blocks — no library needed, don't load one. The viewer never shows `alert()`, `confirm()` or `prompt()` dialogs — `confirm()` returns false and `prompt()` returns null immediately — so build any confirmation step into the page itself.

**What the viewer's frame allows**: The page runs in a locked-down frame; what it refuses below, it refuses for every viewer (anonymous, signed-in, embedded, desktop and mobile apps), so build around these limits instead of detecting them. The page cannot open the print dialog — `window.print()` does nothing — so never offer a Print or "Save as PDF" button. Forms work as page UI (inputs, validation, submit events), but a real submission has nowhere to go: handle `submit` in script with `preventDefault()` and never point `action` at another site or a mailto: address. Copy buttons work when `navigator.clipboard.writeText` is called inside the click handler — catch its rejection (older desktop apps and some app views refuse it) and fall back to selecting the text; reading the clipboard never works, though the viewer's own Paste (the `paste` event) does. Camera, microphone, screen capture, location, Web Share and similar device APIs are refused without a prompt — don't build features on them (a screen wake lock may be granted while the page is visible: request it and tolerate rejection); file inputs, drag-and-drop of files and `FileReader` work in browsers, so take photos, audio and data as uploaded files instead. Fullscreen and pointer lock work from a click in desktop browsers; treat both as optional (handle the rejection) since phones and some app views lack them. Sound plays only after the viewer interacts (muted autoplay is fine), so start audio from a button. Other sites cannot be embedded — no YouTube, map or form iframes, and no `<object>`/`<embed>`; link out instead: links open outside the artifact, normally in a new tab, while `window.open` works only for some signed-in viewers in the artifact's own organization and returns null for everyone else, so use real `<a href>` links. Web Workers work from your own files or `blob:` URLs; service workers and WebRTC do not. `fetch()` of files published alongside the page works with relative URLs; images from your own files, `data:` or `blob:` URLs draw to canvas and export cleanly. Only a plain `#anchor` (letters, digits, `.` `_` `~` `-`) from the artifact's link reaches `location.hash` — never `#key=value` state and never the query string — so deep-link to a tab or section with a bare token and keep all other state in the page.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Responsive**: The page must also work at phone width (about 400px), and the page body must never scroll horizontally. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, and give that element its vertical padding with `padding-block`, never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Use relative units. Let flex and grid rows wrap or stack to one column when narrow, and give any flex or grid child that holds running text, code or a table `min-width: 0`, so long content wraps or scrolls inside it instead of pushing the page wider. Put `max-width: 100%` on images and on any `aspect-ratio` box, and give nothing a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only tables, diagrams and code blocks may be wider, each inside its own `overflow-x: auto` container.

**Theme-aware**: The page renders in the viewer's theme, which has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets nothing, so for most viewers only `prefers-color-scheme` tells light from dark. Define every color as a token, in this shape (token names and count are the design's own):
```css
:root { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: … }  /* every token, light values */
@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark) { :root:not([data-theme="light"]) { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark } }
:root[data-theme="dark"] { --bg: …; --fg: …; --accent: …; color-scheme: dark }  /* same dark values, so the toggle wins both ways */
body { background: var(--bg); color: var(--fg) }
```
Every token gets its first definition on bare `:root`; the two dark blocks only redefine tokens, and their `color-scheme: dark` makes form controls and scrollbars follow. No color has its only definition inside a media or `[data-theme]` block, and no component rule uses a literal color that reads in one theme only. `body` keeps that explicit token background: the viewer paints its own ground behind the page, so a transparent body shows the host's theme instead. A dark-first design mirrors the whole shape, selectors included: dark values and `color-scheme: dark` on bare `:root` (the skeleton pins `light` there), light values and `color-scheme: light` under `(prefers-color-scheme: light)` guarded `:root:not([data-theme="dark"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="light"]`. A design that deliberately commits to a single look may drop the two dark blocks but still sets the background and every color explicitly, plus `color-scheme: dark` on `:root` if that look is dark.

**Icon** (on every first publish): Pass one short generic word as `icon` (e.g. `"chart"`, `"calendar"`, `"recipe"`) for the artifact's browser-tab icon — a plain signifier for what the page is, never a product or brand name, and never an emoji or markup. It stays the **same** for the life of an artifact, so on a redeploy (the same file path this session, or `url`) omit `icon` and the artifact keeps the one it has; pass a different one only when the user asks.

Work the way the design lead at a small, versatile studio would: give each client a visual identity at the level of treatment the task calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Decide the treatment; designing is a given. A doc gets the same craft as a landing page; only the treatment differs. Format is a separate matter: author HTML, and publish Markdown only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. A Markdown publish keeps its filename as its title, uses almost none of the craft below, and is never a way to save time.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished, with real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages don't need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

If unsure: a well-composed page is always acceptable; an over-designed visual identity sometimes isn't.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. Follow the editorial process after them only when that reading calls for it.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Respect what already exists.** Look for an existing design system first: CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, define it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. Distinctive choices come from the subject's own world: its materials, instruments, and vernacular. Whatever the treatment, include at least one detail only this subject would have (its real units and scales, its document conventions, its terms of art) as content rather than ornament; it costs nothing even on a plain page. Use real content throughout and never lorem ipsum.

**Pair typefaces.** Typography determines how the page reads even when the page isn't about typography. Google Fonts is the only font host the Artifact CSP allows; link it directly (`<link rel="stylesheet" href="https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=...&display=swap">`). A face from anywhere else must be inlined as a @font-face data URI, or the browser silently uses a fallback. In both cases, declare a real fallback stack. Keep running text near 65 characters wide. Set a type scale and keep to it. Give headings `text-wrap: balance`, give body text comfortable spacing, and give uppercase labels a little letter-spacing.

**Load libraries instead of inlining them.** When the page really needs a library (React, a charting or highlighting package), load its UMD build from cdnjs with one pinned `<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/...">` placed before the inline script that uses its global; don't inline the library's source or hand-write a substitute. Only the script loads this way; a library's stylesheet still has to be inlined, and the page contract above lists the few other script hosts the CSP admits. The page's own CSS and JS, its images, and its data ship with the page. Most pages don't need any library; use one only when it does substantial work for the page.

**Choose neutrals deliberately.** A pure mid-grey looks unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent looks intentional. Pure white and near-black are fine backgrounds when they suit the subject, as long as you chose the neutral deliberately instead of inheriting a default.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme, and the viewer has three states: an explicit choice sets `data-theme="dark"` or `data-theme="light"` on the root element, and the default "system" setting sets *nothing*. Most viewers see the document with no `data-theme` attribute, where only `prefers-color-scheme` distinguishes light from dark. Structure the CSS at the token level for all three. The bare `:root` block defines the complete light palette (for a deliberately dark-first design, swap light and dark consistently through this whole pattern); `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` redefines only the tokens, guarded as `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` so an explicit light choice overrides a dark OS setting; `:root[data-theme="dark"]` redefines them again so the toggle also overrides in the other direction; wherever the dark palette applies - both dark blocks, or bare `:root` in a dark-first or single-dark design - also set `color-scheme: dark` (the skeleton pins `light` on `:root`), so native form controls and scrollbars follow the palette. Style components through the tokens, never directly inside a media or `[data-theme]` block: a color defined only inside `[data-theme]` never applies when no `data-theme` attribute is set, and the page then shows one theme's text on the other theme's background. Two more rules keep each theme consistent. First, the artifact is composited over a background the viewer paints in *its own* theme, so `body` must set an explicit `background` from a token; a transparent body shows the host's background with no warning. Second, every element that sets a color takes it from the same token set as the surface behind it, never from a literal that works in only one theme. Declare every token in the bare `:root` block before any media or `[data-theme]` block redefines it; a color that exists only inside one of those blocks is the classic unreadable-artifact bug. Give the second theme the same care as the first: don't simply invert it; keep contrast legible and keep the accent working on both backgrounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme: then omit the media query and `[data-theme]` blocks entirely but still set the background and every color explicitly, so the page looks right on either host background; do this by choice, never by omission.

**Use layout for spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap` instead of per-element margins, which collapse or double without warning. Keep a side gutter of at least 16px at every width: set it once as side padding on `body` or one outer wrapper, whose vertical padding uses `padding-block` and never a `padding` shorthand that zeroes the sides. Let rows wrap or stack to one column at phone width (about 400px). Give images and any `aspect-ratio` box `max-width: 100%`, and don't give anything a `min-width` wider than the screen. Only wide tables, code, and diagrams may exceed it; give each `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. The publish skeleton pads `:root` top and bottom by the phone's safe-area insets (zero everywhere except a phone app) so the page runs edge to edge while its content stays clear of the system bars; keep that padding. A bar fixed to the top or bottom stays at `0` and adds `env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` or `env(safe-area-inset-bottom, 0px)` to its own padding. A sticky page header uses `top: env(safe-area-inset-top, 0px)` and never `0`. Size a one-screen app with `height: 100%` on `html` and `body` instead of `100vh`, so it fits inside that padding. A page that includes its own viewport meta gets this padding only when that meta declares `viewport-fit=cover`. Use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Make repeated elements consistent.** For cards in a row, label/value pairs down a list, or badges on sibling items, use the same edges, baselines, and inner padding on each, and put any recurring element in the same place on each. Let content set a container's height and pick a column count the items fill, so nothing stretches over empty space or sits alone in a row. Make text that can outgrow its track wrap or scroll in its own container; clipped text is a bug.

**Use card styling selectively.** Border, fill, radius, and shadow each mark an element as a separate object. Apply them by role, to set off the one element that needs it; applying the same radius and shadow to every block flattens the hierarchy. Open with big-number tiles only when those figures are the point of the page.

**Draw charts to scale.** Place marks, ticks, and labels with one scale, and make every label name a value the chart actually reaches. Color chart text from the theme tokens so it is readable in both themes. Keep marks, labels, and edges clear of one another and inside the drawing's bounds; in SVG, leave room in the viewBox for the outermost labels and give every drawn shape an explicit fill.

**Make the page complete at rest.** Everything meant to be read is visible once the page has loaded, with no scrolling to trigger it; that first still frame is what a thumbnail, a shared link, and a skimming reader all see. A section may
