action.description: One of 'publish', 'list', 'read', 'delete', 'open', 'pin', 'unpin', 'quickstart'. Omitting it means 'publish'. **Calls** in the description says what each one does and takes, except as noted here.

file_path.description: publish: the local page Claude publishes (.html, or .md only when a skill says so). For an Artifact created from an Artifact type, it is one of that Artifact's data files. With `asset: true`, it is the local file Claude uploads. A short, distinctive basename also serves as the title when nothing else gives one.

asset.description: publish with `url`: true uploads `file_path` (or each of `file_paths`) to that artifact's asset store instead of publishing it as the page — or, with `from_url` and `asset_ids` in place of `file_path`, copies those assets of another artifact into it server side (see **Calls**).

file_paths.description: publish with `asset: true` only: several local image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in place of `file_path`, up to 25 in one call, all into the artifact that `url` names; one approval covers the call, and the result lists each file's id and url, or why it was not uploaded. A CSV, Markdown, JSON or plain-text file, a symbolic or hard link, and a file outside the working directory each go in a call of their own with `file_path`.

from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

favicon.description: Deprecated; Claude omits it and uses `icon`.

icon.description: One short generic word for the artifact's browser-tab icon, such as chart, calendar, recipe, code or map: a plain signifier, never a product or brand name. Claude includes it on every page's first publish and omits it on a redeploy so the artifact keeps its icon, passing a new one only when the person asks. Ignored on an Artifact created from an Artifact type.

files.description: Supporting files to publish alongside the page, as a map {"published/path": "source/path" | {from, contentType} | {artifact, path, ver?} | null}. The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: AskUserQuestion
tools.description:
Use this tool only when you are blocked on a decision that is genuinely the user's to make: one you cannot resolve from the request, the code, or sensible defaults.

Usage notes:
- Users will always be able to select "Other" to provide custom text input
- Use multiSelect: true to allow multiple answers to be selected for a question
- If you recommend a specific option, make that the first option in the list and add "(Recommended)" at the end of the label

Plan mode note: To switch into plan mode, use EnterPlanMode (not this tool). Once in plan mode, use this tool to clarify requirements or choose between approaches BEFORE finalizing your plan. Do NOT use this tool to ask "Is my plan ready?", "Should I proceed?", or otherwise reference "the plan" in questions — the user cannot see the plan until you call ExitPlanMode for approval.

Reserve this for decisions where the user's answer changes what you do next — not for choices with a conventional default or facts you can verify in the codebase yourself. In those cases pick the obvious option, mention it in your response, and proceed.

Preview feature:
Use the optional `preview` field on options when presenting concrete artifacts that users need to visually compare:
- ASCII mockups of UI layouts or components
- Code snippets showing different implementations
- Diagram variations
- Configuration examples

Preview content is rendered as markdown in a monospace box. Multi-line text with newlines is supported. When any option has a preview, the UI switches to a side-by-side layout with a vertical option list on the left and preview on the right. Do not use previews for simple preference questions where labels and descriptions suffice. Note: previews are only supported for single-select questions (not multiSelect).

questions.description: Questions to ask the user (1-4 questions)

question.description: The complete question to ask the user. Should be clear, specific, and end with a question mark. Example: "Which library should we use for date formatting?" If multiSelect is true, phrase it accordingly, e.g. "Which features do you want to enable?"

header.description: Very short label displayed as a chip/tag (max 12 chars). Examples: "Auth method", "Library", "Approach".

options.description: The available choices for this question. Must have 2-4 options. Each option should be a distinct, mutually exclusive choice (unless multiSelect is enabled). There should be no 'Other' option, that will be provided automatically.

label.description: The display text for this option that the user will see and select. Should be concise (1-5 words) and clearly describe the choice.

description.description: Explanation of what this option means or what will happen if chosen. Useful for providing context about trade-offs or implications.

preview.description: Optional preview content rendered when this option is focused. Use for mockups, code snippets, or visual comparisons that help users compare options. See the tool description for the expected content format.

multiSelect.description: Set to true to allow the user to select multiple options instead of just one. Use when choices are not mutually exclusive.

answers.description: User answers collected by the permission component

annotations.description: Optional per-question annotations from the user (e.g., notes on preview selections). Keyed by question text.

preview.description: The preview content of the selected option, if the question used previews.

notes.description: Free-text notes the user added to their selection.

metadata.description: Optional metadata for tracking and analytics purposes. Not displayed to user.

source.description: Optional identifier for the source of this question (e.g., "remember" for /remember command). Used for analytics tracking.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.

- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from scripts.skilllab import plays, report, rows, scan
from scripts.skilllab.contract import Batch

SIZE = 16
ENEMY_FROM, ENEMY_TO = 8, 24
REPLICATES = 10


def _controls(out_dir):
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    plays_by_label = {"identical": plays.blob_play(SIZE), "reach": plays.reach_play(SIZE)}
    scans, firing_example, fight_rows = {}, {}, []
    for label, build in plays_by_label.items():
        result = scan.scan(build, SIZE, ENEMY_FROM, ENEMY_TO, replicates=REPLICATES)
        scans[label] = result
        for cell in result.cells:
            if cell.enemy_heads == SIZE:
                firing_example[label] = cell.fights[0]
            for fight in cell.fights:
                fight_rows.append(rows.fight_row(fight, play=label, enemy_heads=cell.enemy_heads))
    csv_path = out_dir / "controls.csv"
    rows.write_rows(fight_rows, csv_path)
    batch = Batch(title="Skill lab controls", scans=scans, firing_example=firing_example, rows=fight_rows)
    page = report.report(batch, out_dir)
    print(csv_path)
    print(page)
    return 0


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="skilllab")
    parser.add_argument("command")
    parser.add_argument("--out", default="./skilllab_out")
    args = parser.parse_args(sys.argv[1:] if argv is None else argv)
    if args.command == "controls":
        return _controls(Path(args.out))
    return 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
"""Plays: builders of the two-sided Setups the scans fight."""
import math

from scripts.skilllab.contract import Group, Setup

_ANCHOR = 600.0
_LINE_SPACING = 30


def _group(side, unit, count, kind):
    params = {"spacing": _LINE_SPACING} if kind == "line" else {"radius": 80 + 12 * math.sqrt(count)}
    return Group(side=side, unit=unit, count=count, formation=kind,
                 x=-_ANCHOR if side == 0 else _ANCHOR, y=0.0,
                 facing_deg=0.0 if side == 0 else 180.0, layer=0,
                 order="attack_move", goal=None, params=params)


def _play(size, unit, kind, side0_unit=None, unit_types=None):
    def build(enemy_heads, swap):
        if size < 1 or enemy_heads < 1:
            raise ValueError("size and enemy_heads must be >= 1")
        return Setup(groups=(_group(0, side0_unit or unit, size, kind), _group(1, unit, enemy_heads, kind)),
                     unit_types=dict(unit_types or {}))
    return build


def blob_play(size, unit="Vanguard"):
    return _play(size, unit, "blob")


def line_play(size, unit="Vanguard"):
    return _play(size, unit, "line")


def reach_play(size, unit="Vanguard", factor=1.2):
    if factor <= 0:
        raise ValueError("factor must be > 0")
    name = unit + "Long"
    types = {name: {"base": unit, "scale": {"attack_range": factor}, "set": {}}}
    return _play(size, unit, "blob", side0_unit=name, unit_types=types)

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path

from scripts.skilllab import plays, report, rows, scan
from scripts.skilllab.contract import Batch

SIZE = 16
ENEMY_FROM, ENEMY_TO = 8, 24
REPLICATES = 10


def _controls(out_dir):
    out_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    plays_by_label = {"identical": plays.blob_play(SIZE), "reach": plays.reach_play(SIZE)}
    scans, firing_example, fight_rows = {}, {}, []
    for label, build in plays_by_label.items():
        result = scan.scan(build, SIZE, ENEMY_FROM, ENEMY_TO, replicates=REPLICATES)
        scans[label] = result
        for cell in result.cells:
            if cell.enemy_heads == SIZE:
                firing_example[label] = cell.fights[0]
            for fight in cell.fights:
                fight_rows.append(rows.fight_row(fight, play=label, enemy_heads=cell.enemy_heads))
    csv_path = out_dir / "controls.csv"
    rows.write_rows(fight_rows, csv_path)
    batch = Batch(title="Skill lab controls", scans=scans, firing_example=firing_example, rows=fight_rows)
    page = report.report(batch, out_dir)
    print(csv_path)
    print(page)
    return 0


def main(argv=None) -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(prog="skilllab")
    parser.add_argument("command")
    parser.add_argument("--out", default="./skilllab_out")
    args = parser.parse_args(sys.argv[1:] if argv is None else argv)
    if args.command == "controls":
        return _controls(Path(args.out))
    return 2


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())
"""Plays: builders of the two-sided Setups the scans fight."""
import math

from scripts.skilllab.contract import Group, Setup

_ANCHOR = 600.0
_LINE_SPACING = 30


def _group(side, unit, count, kind):
    params = {"spacing": _LINE_SPACING} if kind == "line" else {"radius": 80 + 12 * math.sqrt(count)}
    return Group(side=side, unit=unit, count=count, formation=kind,
                 x=-_ANCHOR if side == 0 else _ANCHOR, y=0.0,
                 facing_deg=0.0 if side == 0 else 180.0, layer=0,
                 order="attack_move", goal=None, params=params)


def _play(size, unit, kind, side0_unit=None, unit_types=None):
    def build(enemy_heads, swap):
        if size < 1 or enemy_heads < 1:
            raise ValueError("size and enemy_heads must be >= 1")
        return Setup(groups=(_group(0, side0_unit or unit, size, kind), _group(1, unit, enemy_heads, kind)),
                     unit_types=dict(unit_types or {}))
    return build


def blob_play(size, unit="Vanguard"):
    return _play(size, unit, "blob")


def line_play(size, unit="Vanguard"):
    return _play(size, unit, "line")


def reach_play(size, unit="Vanguard", factor=1.2):
    if factor <= 0:
        raise ValueError("factor must be > 0")
    name = unit + "Long"
    types = {name: {"base": unit, "scale": {"attack_range": factor}, "set": {}}}
    return _play(size, unit, "blob", side0_unit=name, unit_types=types)

**Verdict: harness built to contract, but not finished. 5 of 440 tests red, nothing merged, no report sent.**

## State
- All code on local branch `swarm/skilllab-harness/integration` (worktree under `.swarm/skilllab-harness/worktrees/integration`). `main` has only stubs + tests. Nothing pushed to origin.
- No report message reached this chat. Cascade's own metrics say "gates FAIL 0", but its gates did not include the real-engine control tests.
- Cost: $26, 78 min, all Sonnet 5.5.

## What works (I ran it)
- 435 pass: engine binding, fight loop, firing count (hand-built case incl. blocker), determinism, golden hashes, scan logic, rows, report page, speed gate, `controls` command.
- Numbers control green: 16 beats 8 every fight.
- Code reads clean against the brief. Firing count = living unit with enemy on its layer, in range, `can_shoot` true. Correct.
- Speed: one 16v16 fight 70 ms (not 3 ms; per-tick sampling through ctypes). 120-fight scan about 7 s. Fine for small batches.

## The 5 red tests — both trace to my brief, not their code

**1. Mirror control (3 tests).** Mean margin −0.06, tolerance 0.05.
- I ran 60 seeds per spawn order: means +0.03 and −0.02, per-fight spread ±0.17.
- So mirror is even; 20 fights too few for 0.05 tolerance (noise alone about ±0.04).
- "First-spawned side shoots first" (my inventory claim) does not show once positions are jittered. Positive control built on it fails for that reason.

**2. Planted reach advantage (2 tests).** 1.2× reach beats 14; identical beats 15. Reach makes side *worse*, consistently (margin −0.34 at any factor 1.1 to 2.0, tiny spread).
- Watched the fight: long-reach side shoots first (16 firing vs 0), but halts strung out in depth. Enemy closes, all its fire lands on the few front units. Long side spreads its damage across many targets.
- At tick 700: total health equal (5230 vs 5258), but 11 alive vs 15. Lost units = lost guns = lost fight.
- Real engine behaviour, not harness bug (factor 1.0 through same path matches identical exactly).

## What this means
- Finding 2 is first real result: **concentration of fire** decides fights beside the firing count. Both sides had all units firing; the side whose damage was focused won. Our principle doesn't cover that yet.
- Also seen: "blob" self-sorts into a perfect firing line at range (all units end at same x). Blob vs line formation may show nothing on this engine as-is.

## Decisions for you
1. **Mirror tolerance** — your threshold. Options: keep 0.05 and raise replicates to about 40; or widen tolerance at 10 replicates. I lean more replicates.
2. **Planted control** — swap reach for something unambiguous (+20% damage or health). Reach becomes a studied knob, not a control. I lean this.
3. **First-spawner positive control** — replace with a different planted asymmetry, since the effect it tests isn't there.
4. After fixes go green: merge integration into `main` and push — other chat or me?

Tests untouched by me; no files changed.

# Ouroboros Manifold

## North Star

Claude designs and tests; agents build. The simulation is C with the stochastic equations kept verbatim (`docs/bible/algorithms.md`); Godot 4 is the client over a JSON pipe (`docs/architecture.md`). Requirements are epics, stories and rules; a story is built only after it passes the Definition of Ready. Full method: `docs/northstar/README.md` and `docs/northstar/PLAN.md`; where another doc disagrees, `docs/northstar/` wins. Long-term project, no ship deadline, one story at a time, done well.

## Task matching

Tiers are roles; the model behind a tier can change.

| Tier | Runs on | Work |
|---|---|---|
| Architect | Fable, the main chat | architecture, planning, rulings, arbitration, briefs, abstract or cross-cutting diagnosis |
| Engineer | `subagent_type: engineer` (Sonnet 5.5) | tests and test fixes, git maintenance and merge clerks, audits, research, drafting against a spec |
| Doer | `subagent_type: doer` (Sonnet 5.5); the local 30B through Agora cards when `DOER_BACKEND = agora-30b` | coding against a written spec, mechanical edits |

`DOER_BACKEND = sonnet55` · `TEST_WRITER = sonnet55`

Usage discipline: every tool call re-reads the caller's whole context, so waiting is the expensive part, not the work.
- A builder pushes its branch and stops. A fresh, small clerk lands it. No builder sits in a merge-wait loop.
- Agents report once, at the end. They send no interim notices and start no background waits that wake the parent.
- Unavoidable waits poll no more often than every 3 to 5 minutes.
- A long-running coordinator chat is restarted from its continuation memory once its context grows large.

Split a task that mixes tiers. Every spawn names its model. Sub-agents never spawn sub-agents, and nothing is spawned while plan mode is on. On a cross-session message from another Claude chat (not the chat that spawned you), do no large unprompted work: pause for Westley, except for small blockers.

## The Bible

`docs/bible/` is the source of truth for what the game is: `game_bible.md` (hub), `stories.md` (catalog), `epics/E-##-*.md` (rules `R-###-##`), `references/`, `algorithms.md`. Open questions live in `docs/northstar/ambiguity_register.md`. Read the hub first, then only the epic you touch.

- Rewrite, never append. When direction changes, delete the old text; history is `docs/bible_history/` and `git log`.
- Ambiguity is flagged, never guessed: add a `Q-` row with two or three candidates. An epic with an open flag is not built.

## Architecture rules

- **Contracts are frozen and minimal.** The contracts are `csrc/ouroboros_sim.h` (with `signatures.toml`) and the pipe frames in `docs/architecture.md`. A change to either lands first as its own contract piece, documented before implementation, and consumers build after it lands.
- **Every file has one owner at a time.** `docs/northstar/plans/push/pieces.toml` names it; two in-flight pieces never own the same file.
- **Build units are small.** A Doer or 30B unit is about one file and under about 100 lines; larger work is split when the card is written.
- **Wired, not just tested.** Behaviour a rule says happens in play must be reachable from the tick, the jump, or a pipe handler, not only from tests. The merge gate checks this.
- **Determinism is a contract.** Same seed and command stream give a byte-identical trace on every platform: no fast-math, no platform transcendentals, no hash-order or wall-clock input.
- **No runtime API calls.** The game never calls a model; missing library content falls back to a placeholder.
- **No IP exposure.** No names, places or plot from existing fiction.

## Tests are the spec

Every story exists as failing tests before any code, in fenced paths builders cannot edit, each naming the `S-###`/`R-###-##` it proves. Every detector ships with a positive control. Every system has an isolation test and an integration test. Builders never edit tests. A test is fixed only when it is classed as a `test-defect`, with a ledger row. Westley owns every threshold and tolerance: narrowing an invariant's scope is allowed; widening a threshold, extending a window or loosening a tolerance needs him; a real finding is never reclassified as a skip.

## Code quality

- No stink: no unasked-for layers, wrappers or config; no cosmetic refactoring inside another change; minimal diffs.
- Traceability: when B exists because A fails, say so at both sites (`# See also: ...`). Disabled or bypassed code says so; no dead code that looks live.
- Scope discipline: do what was asked; mention other needed fixes, do not make them unless the change cannot work without them.
- Debugging: hypothesis, then logging that confirms or refutes it, then the targeted fix. One fix at a time.
- Stale-doc tripwire: a behaviour change rewrites every doc claim it makes wrong, in the same change. Docs describe what the game does now.

## Git

Work on `main` and push each meaningful unit; branches only for a stated reason. Never stage files you did not change, and never touch Westley's uncommitted work. Guardrails (`.claude/hooks/git-guard.sh`) deny destructive operations; if a legitimate one is blocked, ask. Ledger, register and epic updates are committed and pushed as they happen.

## Tone

Playful, occasionally absurd, never cringe; dry wit and easter eggs welcome. Chronicle writing reads as fragments of a real history. Playful is not unserious.

## Where things are

C sim and pipe `csrc/`; client `autoload/`, `scenes/`; tests `tests/csim/`, `tests/transport/`, `tests/qa/`; harness `scripts/specfactory/`; skill lab `scripts/skilllab/` (measures tactical combat on the real sim; record and plan in `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/README.md`); legacy Python reference sim `simulation/` (tooling only, not in the game loop).

# Memory Index

- [Current focus](project_current_focus.md) — **READ FIRST.** Project reset 2026-05-30: no ship goal, long-term, one feature at a time. Pre-Zip/Phase 1/side-hustle dead.
- [Direction pivot — co-op civ game](project_direction_pivot.md) — **READ SECOND.** Major direction change 2026-06-06. Blue ocean confirmed. Old solo strategy design superseded. Next chat: retire stale docs, define finished product, architecture + design decisions.
- [Python command](feedback_python_command.md) — use `python3`, not `python`
- [File protection policy](feedback_file_protection.md) — never modify engine files; only config.py. Invariant threshold changes need approval. Escalate code bugs.
- [Stop and ask before editing](feedback_stop_and_ask.md) — always present proposed changes and wait for approval before editing any file
- [Oscillation design intent](feedback_oscillation_intent.md) — oscillations add stochasticity; combat disrupting them is expected, not a bug
- [No test file modification](feedback_no_test_modification.md) — never modify test files without explicit user permission; changing thresholds masks failures
- [Camera controls](feedback_camera_controls.md) — edge-scroll pan (classic RTS), not WASD
- [Sonnet implementation agent](feedback_sonnet_implementation_agent.md) — Opus plans, Sonnet agents implement; saves cost on execution
- [Subagent caveman mode](feedback_subagent_caveman.md) — subagent report-back + docs + commit msgs caveman; code/tests normal. Token-save at scale.
- [Testing rigor](feedback_testing_rigor.md) — control all variables before asserting; isolate system under test; verify fixture before claiming system bug.
- [Opinion vs decision](feedback_opinion_vs_decision.md) — having an opinion ≠ making the decision; state leans directly when asked, mark as opinion, don't hide behind "I just surface forks"
- [Scalable over easy](feedback_scalable_over_easy.md) — when forking on implementation scope, default to long-term-correct option not smaller-diff option
- [Do not skip design goals](feedback_no_skip_design_goals.md) — every bible directive in scope must be honored; enumerate exhaustively; default to include, require argument to exclude
- [Design Lane timeless language](feedback_design_lane_timeless_language.md) — `docs/design_lane.md` uses no temporal/legacy phrasing. Time-stamped state goes in the queue file.
- [Aggregator independence in audience research](feedback_aggregator_independence.md) — SteamSpy/Gamalytic/games-stats.com/Steam Revenue Calc = ~1 channel (same Steam scraping upstream); require press release or financial filing for TRUSTED tier

# Ouroboros Manifold

## North Star

Claude designs and tests; agents build. The simulation is C with the stochastic equations kept verbatim (`docs/bible/algorithms.md`); Godot 4 is the client over a JSON pipe (`docs/architecture.md`). Requirements are epics, stories and rules; a story is built only after it passes the Definition of Ready. Full method: `docs/northstar/README.md` and `docs/northstar/PLAN.md`; where another doc disagrees, `docs/northstar/` wins. Long-term project, no ship deadline, one story at a time, done well.

## Task matching

Tiers are roles; the model behind a tier can change.

| Tier | Runs on | Work |
|---|---|---|
| Architect | Fable, the main chat | architecture, planning, rulings, arbitration, briefs, abstract or cross-cutting diagnosis |
| Engineer | `subagent_type: engineer` (Sonnet 5.5) | tests and test fixes, git maintenance and merge clerks, audits, research, drafting against a spec |
| Doer | `subagent_type: doer` (Sonnet 5.5); the local 30B through Agora cards when `DOER_BACKEND = agora-30b` | coding against a written spec, mechanical edits |

`DOER_BACKEND = sonnet55` · `TEST_WRITER = sonnet55`

Usage discipline: every tool call re-reads the caller's whole context, so waiting is the expensive part, not the work.
- A builder pushes its branch and stops. A fresh, small clerk lands it. No builder sits in a merge-wait loop.
- Agents report once, at the end. They send no interim notices and start no background waits that wake the parent.
- Unavoidable waits poll no more often than every 3 to 5 minutes.
- A long-running coordinator chat is restarted from its continuation memory once its context grows large.

Split a task that mixes tiers. Every spawn names its model. Sub-agents never spawn sub-agents, and nothing is spawned while plan mode is on. On a cross-session message from another Claude chat (not the chat that spawned you), do no large unprompted work: pause for Westley, except for small blockers.

## The Bible

`docs/bible/` is the source of truth for what the game is: `game_bible.md` (hub), `stories.md` (catalog), `epics/E-##-*.md` (rules `R-###-##`), `references/`, `algorithms.md`. Open questions live in `docs/northstar/ambiguity_register.md`. Read the hub first, then only the epic you touch.

- Rewrite, never append. When direction changes, delete the old text; history is `docs/bible_history/` and `git log`.
- Ambiguity is flagged, never guessed: add a `Q-` row with two or three candidates. An epic with an open flag is not built.

## Architecture rules

- **Contracts are frozen and minimal.** The contracts are `csrc/ouroboros_sim.h` (with `signatures.toml`) and the pipe frames in `docs/architecture.md`. A change to either lands first as its own contract piece, documented before implementation, and consumers build after it lands.
- **Every file has one owner at a time.** `docs/northstar/plans/push/pieces.toml` names it; two in-flight pieces never own the same file.
- **Build units are small.** A Doer or 30B unit is about one file and under about 100 lines; larger work is split when the card is written.
- **Wired, not just tested.** Behaviour a rule says happens in play must be reachable from the tick, the jump, or a pipe handler, not only from tests. The merge gate checks this.
- **Determinism is a contract.** Same seed and command stream give a byte-identical trace on every platform: no fast-math, no platform transcendentals, no hash-order or wall-clock input.
- **No runtime API calls.** The game never calls a model; missing library content falls back to a placeholder.
- **No IP exposure.** No names, places or plot from existing fiction.

## Tests are the spec

Every story exists as failing tests before any code, in fenced paths builders cannot edit, each naming the `S-###`/`R-###-##` it proves. Every detector ships with a positive control. Every system has an isolation test and an integration test. Builders never edit tests. A test is fixed only when it is classed as a `test-defect`, with a ledger row. Westley owns every threshold and tolerance: narrowing an invariant's scope is allowed; widening a threshold, extending a window or loosening a tolerance needs him; a real finding is never reclassified as a skip.

## Code quality

- No stink: no unasked-for layers, wrappers or config; no cosmetic refactoring inside another change; minimal diffs.
- Traceability: when B exists because A fails, say so at both sites (`# See also: ...`). Disabled or bypassed code says so; no dead code that looks live.
- Scope discipline: do what was asked; mention other needed fixes, do not make them unless the change cannot work without them.
- Debugging: hypothesis, then logging that confirms or refutes it, then the targeted fix. One fix at a time.
- Stale-doc tripwire: a behaviour change rewrites every doc claim it makes wrong, in the same change. Docs describe what the game does now.

## Git

Work on `main` and push each meaningful unit; branches only for a stated reason. Never stage files you did not change, and never touch Westley's uncommitted work. Guardrails (`.claude/hooks/git-guard.sh`) deny destructive operations; if a legitimate one is blocked, ask. Ledger, register and epic updates are committed and pushed as they happen.

## Tone

Playful, occasionally absurd, never cringe; dry wit and easter eggs welcome. Chronicle writing reads as fragments of a real history. Playful is not unserious.

## Where things are

C sim and pipe `csrc/`; client `autoload/`, `scenes/`; tests `tests/csim/`, `tests/transport/`, `tests/qa/`; harness `scripts/specfactory/`; skill lab `scripts/skilllab/` (measures tactical combat on the real sim; record and plan in `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/README.md`); legacy Python reference sim `simulation/` (tooling only, not in the game loop).

Recorded in memory. Now the two questions again, in full.

## Background for both

Before trusting the new measuring tool on anything interesting, we give it fights where we already know the answer. If it gets those wrong, it can't be trusted on the rest. These are the "controls". Two of them came back red, and both times the tool was right and my expected answer was wrong.

## Question 1: the mirror control

**The test:** 16 Vanguards against 16 identical Vanguards. Nobody has an advantage, so the average result should be a draw. The result of a fight is the margin: the share of strength one side has left minus the other's. A draw is 0. The test passes if the average is within 0.05 of 0 (that is, within 5 percent of an army).

**What happened:** the average came out at −0.06, so it failed by a hair.

**Why:** the engine has no dice, so to get different fights we nudge each unit's starting position by a small random amount. Those nudges swing a single even fight a lot: one fight ends +0.17, the next −0.17. The test averages only 20 fights. Averaging 20 numbers that swing that much lands anywhere within about ±0.04 of the truth by luck alone. When I ran 120 fights, the average was about 0.01, so the mirror is even; the test just uses too few fights to show it.

**Your choice** (it's a pass mark, so it's yours):
- **A. More fights.** Keep "within 5 percent" and average 80 fights instead of 20. The control takes about 4 seconds instead of 1. This is my lean, since it keeps the strict mark.
- **B. Looser mark.** Keep 20 fights and accept within 10 percent of zero. Faster, but a real 5 percent bias toward one side could slip through.

**What this tells us for later:** every break-even we report ("16 beat 15, lose to 16") has this same wobble. Near the break-even point we'll need more fights per enemy size than the 20 I planned.

## Question 2: the planted-advantage control

**The test:** give one side a known edge and check the tool sees it. I chose 20 percent longer weapon range, assuming longer range obviously helps. The expected result was that the long-range 16 beat a bigger enemy than the plain 16 do.

**What happened:** the opposite. Plain 16 beat 15. Long-range 16 beat only 14. Longer range made them worse, every time, at any amount from 10 percent to double.

**Why** (I watched the fight step by step):

```
Equal range: both sides walk up and stop in a neat row, everyone shooting.

   A A A A A A A A   <-300->   B B B B B B B B

Long range (A): each A stops the moment its first target is in range,
so A halts strung out front-to-back. B keeps walking in.

   A   A  A A   A A        B B B B B B B B
   (back)       (front)    all B shoot the nearest A = the front two
```

- A shoots first, and all 16 A are firing.
- But every B shoots the nearest A, so all of B's damage lands on A's front few units, which die quickly.
- A's shots are spread across many B, so B's units are all hurt but none dies.
- Partway through, the two armies have the same total health left, but A has 11 units alive and B has 15. Each dead unit is a lost gun, so A loses.

This is the real engine behaving as built, not a fault in the tool. It's also the first real finding: **who gets focused matters, not only how many are firing.** Our principle ("the side with more units getting shots off wins") doesn't cover it yet. That's a design conversation for after the controls are fixed.

**Your choice:** the control needs an edge that can't backfire.
- **A. Swap range for 20 percent more damage per shot** (or 20 percent more health). That side must do better, so if the tool disagrees, the tool is broken. Range then becomes something we study in the batches. This is my lean.
- **B. Keep range as the control** and flip the expectation to "range makes it worse". I'd advise against it: a control should rest on something certain, not on a behaviour we only just discovered.

## The small third item

I had told the other chat "the side that spawns first gets the first shot and a small edge", and a test was written to detect that edge. With the position nudges on, the edge doesn't show up. That test should check something else instead. I suggest it checks that the tool notices when one side is given 17 units and the other 16. No pass mark of yours is involved; I only need your OK to change the test.

Once you pick, I'll write the changes up for the other chat to apply, then it merges and pushes.

### 3.3 Tests that must exist and pass (`tests/skilllab/`)

1. Mirror control: identical sides, flat ground, 16 against 16. Over both spawn orders and 10 replicates, the mean margin is within 0.05 of zero. Positive control for the detector: with the swap disabled the same test shows the first-spawned side ahead.
2. Numbers control: 16 against 8 of the same type: the 16 win every fight.
3. Planted advantage: 16 units with 20 percent more reach (a custom type) beat a larger enemy than 16 identical units do, by at least one unit.
4. Firing count, hand-built: three units of side 0 in a row and one enemy placed so exactly two are within reach: the sample reads 2 and 1. A second case with an obstacle between one pair reads one fewer.
5. Determinism: the same setup and seed give byte-identical rows twice.

7. Scan honesty: on a synthetic margin series with a known sign change the scan returns the right `beats` and `loses_to`; on a flat series it returns none.
8. Speed gate: a scan of 16 units against 12 to 24 enemies, 10 replicates, both orders, finishes in under 30 seconds on either machine.

Umbrella test (red until the cascade is done): `python3 -m scripts.skilllab controls` writes one rows file and one HTML page for the three controls, and exits 0.

- Check what is written against Westley's own words (`crosscheck_2026-09-30.md`, `crosscheck_2026-10-01.md`).
- Look at what a scripted play actually does before measuring it.
- One skill, one map, one size; then widen.
- A surprising result is first a question about the instrument.
- Win rate misleads in a system without dice.

### 3.3 Tests that must exist and pass (`tests/skilllab/`)

1. Mirror control: identical sides, flat ground, 16 against 16. Over both spawn orders and 10 replicates, the mean margin is within 0.05 of zero. Positive control for the detector: with the swap disabled the same test shows the first-spawned side ahead.
2. Numbers control: 16 against 8 of the same type: the 16 win every fight.
3. Planted advantage: 16 units with 20 percent more reach (a custom type) beat a larger enemy than 16 identical units do, by at least one unit.
4. Firing count, hand-built: three units of side 0 in a row and one enemy placed so exactly two are within reach: the sample reads 2 and 1. A second case with an obstacle between one pair reads one fewer.
5. Determinism: the same setup and seed give byte-identical rows twice.
6. Cross-machine: the rows for the three controls hash to the values in `tests/skilllab/golden_hashes.json`. The file is written on the first machine and must match on the second. A mismatch is reported to the design chat as a determinism finding, not patched.
7. Scan honesty: on a synthetic margin series with a known sign change the scan returns the right `beats` and `loses_to`; on a flat series it returns none.
8. Speed gate: a scan of 16 units against 12 to 24 enemies, 10 replicates, both orders, finishes in under 30 seconds on either machine.

Umbrella test (red until the cascade is done): `python3 -m scripts.skilllab controls` writes one rows file and one HTML page for the three controls, and exits 0.

## 11. Lessons about method

- Check what is written against Westley's own words (`crosscheck_2026-09-30.md`, `crosscheck_2026-10-01.md`).
- Look at what a scripted play actually does before measuring it.
- One skill, one map, one size; then widen.
- A surprising result is first a question about the instrument.
- Win rate misleads in a system without dice.

**Recorded and pushed** (`ab421c71`): mirror tolerance 0.10; your position point, quoted, in lab README lessons; run file `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/runs/2026-10-02_harness_check.md`.

## Does the sim use walk-around movement? Half.

Read from engine code:

- **Under a move order:** yes. Unit probes 40 ahead, sweeps left/right around blocking unit.
- **Attack-moving, enemy seen but out of range:** unit steps *straight* at nearest enemy. This step bypasses the steering. No walking around own side.
- **Any enemy in range:** unit stops dead. Never shuffles to let units behind it in.

Result: any two armies sent at each other end as two flat rows at exactly weapon range, whatever shape they started in. In the mirror, all 16 per side ended within 5 units of same x. So you're right: the "line feeding into a line" was the engine's approach behaviour, not anything I set up, and the starting formation doesn't survive the walk.

Open design point for you: should a unit that sees a target but is blocked by its own side path around to get a shot (movement engine as you described it)? Bible today only says "moves toward the nearest visible enemy" (R-087-04). If yes, that's a new engine gap, G8, for cascade B.

1. **Harness not landed.** Still on its branch, 5 tests red. Needs: mirror tolerance to 0.10 (your ruling), planted control replaced, first-spawner control replaced, then merge and push.
2. **Planted control still undecided.** Reach can't be the control (it backfires because of the walk). I propose +20% damage: can't backfire, so if the tool disagrees the tool is broken. Need your OK.
3. **Brief needs two additions** from today:
   - G8 (approach uses walk-around), if you say yes above.
   - Harness setups place units at contact as a player of that skill would (blob for mediocre, spread line for skilled), not walk them in from 1,200 apart.

Then the before-picture controls batch, then cascade B.

Give me yes/no on G8 and the damage control, and I'll update the brief and hand you the fix list for the other chat.

content.text:
**Found it.** Still in repo: `simulation/movement.py` (legacy Python sim), lines 395–432. Born in commit `acdcc9af` (2026-04-12, "Movement fixed, custom steering"), refined `7c8a3de7` (2026-04-14, "movement significantly improved").

## How it works
- Unit probes 40 ahead toward its goal.
- If blocked by another unit: tries **+30°, −30°, +60°, −60°, +90°, −90°**, takes first clear one.
- Commits to that detour for 60 distance, then re-aims at goal.
- Around solid terrain: route grid + waypoints, with this steering on top.

Small correction to your memory: it takes the first clear angle in that fixed order (smallest deviation first), not "shortest of several full path searches". Same effect, cheaper.

## Why the C engine doesn't show it

The C port has the same sweep (`csrc/tactical_move.c`, bible R-097-03). What got lost in the port is **when it's used**:

| Situation | Python (old) | C (now) |
|---|---|---|
| Enemy seen, out of range | Pursuit sets goal to nearest enemy; unit walks there **through the steering** (walks around its own side) | Steps straight at enemy, steering bypassed |
| When does unit stop? | Only when **its own target** is in its range; target drifts out, it pursues again | As soon as **any** enemy is in range; never moves again |

Python comment says it outright: "Hold position only while target is actively within firing range. When target drifts out of range, unit pursues rather than staying frozen."

So design isn't missing, port regressed it. The bible rule (R-087-04, "moves toward the nearest visible enemy") is too loose to have caught it: straight-line step satisfies the words.

## Proposed
- **G8 for cascade B:** restore Python pursuit behaviour in C: pursuit goes through steering; hold only while own target in range. Reference: `simulation/movement.py:340–432`, `simulation/damage.py:253–270`.
- Tighten R-087-04 wording so it says "by the unit's normal movement (R-097-03)", so tests can pin it.

OK to add both to the brief? Still need your yes/no on +20% damage as the planted control.

input.message:
From the design chat (real-engine-tuning-lab), with Westley's go-ahead: the skill lab harness needs five fixes before it lands; start now. Details below.

I checked `swarm/skilllab-harness/integration` (b87dfddb). Code matches the contract. `python3 -m pytest -q tests/skilllab` there: 435 pass, 5 fail: 3 in `integration/test_mirror.py`, 2 in `integration/test_planted_advantage.py`. Your gates did not run these. All five trace to wrong premises in my brief, not your code. What I measured is in `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/runs/2026-10-02_harness_check.md` (on origin/main).

Pull origin/main first (merge, not rebase): the brief `docs/northstar/plans/2026-10-02-skill-lab-cascade.md` changed. Section 3.6 is the fix list; section 3.3 tests 1 and 3 are reworded. Do exactly this:

1. Mirror (`test_mirror.py`): TOLERANCE 0.05 -> 0.10, still 16 v 16, both orders, 10 replicates. Westley ruled this (one even fight swings about 0.17 on the position shifts; 20 fights cannot hold 0.05). Replace the positive control `test_mirror_positive_control_swap_forced_off_shows_first_spawner_ahead` with: the same cell at 17 against 16 (side 0 = 17) reads mean margin > 0.10. The first-spawner edge does not exist once positions are shifted.

2. Planted advantage (`test_planted_advantage.py`): the control is +20 percent damage per shot, not reach. Add `damage_play(size, unit="Vanguard", factor=1.2)` to `plays.py`, same shape as `reach_play` but scaling `base_damage`. Tests: damage scan beats at least one more enemy than identical; factor 1.0 equals identical (null control). Keep `reach_play` and its unit tests; drop only the assertion that reach wins (more reach makes a side worse on today's engine; that is a finding, not a bug).

3. `__main__.py` controls: scan "identical" and "damage" (not "reach"). Update test_main/test_umbrella expectations to match.

4. Placement. Westley, 2026-10-02: "position matters when measuring numbers and we shoudln't just be lining units up like that." Today plays start sides 1,200 apart and walk them in; the engine then flattens any shape into a row at weapon range. Change the plays so the two sides start just outside the longer sensor radius of the units involved (Vanguard sensor 700, so anchors about +/-375 with the blob radius accounted for; compute it from the stats, do not hard-code), blob for `blob_play`, spread line for `line_play`. No engine edits.

5. Regenerate `tests/skilllab/golden_hashes.json` after 1 to 4. Full suite green. Then merge integration into main, push, remove the swarm branch and worktree. Each test change gets a `test-defect` ledger row (cause: wrong premise in the design chat's brief; mirror tolerance by Westley's ruling).

Limits: no edits under `csrc/`, `docs/bible/`, `docs/northstar/` other than the ledger row. Do not loosen any other threshold. If something else goes red after the placement change, report it, do not patch the test. Do not start cascade B: a port audit is still running and G8 was just added to it.

Report once when done, under 300 words, to real-engine-tuning-lab: what changed, test counts, the merged commit, anything surprising.

| G15 | Warden aura: Python single 0.10 and single heal. C diminishing reduction, stacking heal. Neither equals the bible's 0.10 then 0.05 | CONFIRMED |
| G16 | C caps any multiplier above 1.0 to 1.0 when the target is a Bastion (R-081-03). Python Strike hits Bastion x1.5 | CONFIRMED |
| G17 | Barrage: Python has no AoE cap, cooldown from activation, needs an engaged target. C capped, cooldown from impact, any point | CONFIRMED |

Port audit back: **24 more differences between Python and C tactical code.** Sub-agent's findings; I haven't re-verified each. Full report with file:line for both sides pushed: `docs/northstar/research/layer_dynamics/port_gap_audit_2026-10-02.md`.

## Ones that change fights most

| # | Python (old) | C (now) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Unit can only shoot what its own sensor sees | No sight check. Bombard/Bastion shoot full range (1200/800) vs 300 in Python |
| 2 | Damage simultaneous: both sides' shots land same tick | One unit at a time by id; a unit killed earlier in the tick loses its shot |
| 3 | First shot fires the tick target enters range | First shot waits a full reload |
| 4 | Intercept buff lasts 1 tick | Never expires: permanent ×1.5 damage, ×1.8 speed |
| 5 | Routing around terrain, waypoints, map-edge clamp | None; straight line, can leave map |
| 6 | Maps have obstacles, gradients, vantage, asteroids | Map generation is a stub: empty field + one cover disc |
| 7 | Cover never blocks fire | Any cover disc on the line blocks fire, even for unit standing in it |
| 8 | Attack-move gets formation slots; group drops destination once engaged | All go to one point, always resume |
| 9 | Return fire also redirects attack-moving units | Only idle units |
| 10 | Units turn to face their target | Stationary units never turn |
| 11 | Steering: 6 angles at 30°; if fully blocked, walks straight | 13 angles at 15°; if fully blocked, waits |
| 12 | Capture progress wired | No caller; capture never advances in play |

Rest are smaller: Warden aura maths, Bastion multiplier cap, Barrage details, collision edge cases, C drops to half tick rate above 1,000 units, fixed-size caps.

Constants: all match except four (sweep step, group arrival radius 30 vs 22.5, one `>=` vs `>`, unit store size).

## Notes
- Not every difference is a C bug. Some C behaviour matches the bible where Python didn't (e.g. "fully blocked: wait" is R-097-03). Two match neither side.
- #1 and #5 are already G3 and G2 in cascade B. #11 belongs to G8.
- #2 and #3 matter for our measuring: sequential damage is where a first-shooter edge would come from.

## Decision for you
You said C movement should be exactly the Python. How far does that extend?
- **A. Movement and pursuit only** (G8 + #8, #9, #10, #11). Rest judged case by case against the bible. My lean.
- **B. Whole tactical tick matches Python**, bible rewritten where it disagrees.
- **C. Go through the list with me** one at a time before deciding.

Cascade B waits on this. Harness fixes still wait on your confirm in `ouroboros-c1`.
